The Planning Board requests the initiation of the attached zoning amendments in order to allow residential adaptive reuse of accessory structures by Special Permit. The zoning amendment includes a new section in the “Special Regulations” article, as well as amendments to the “Use Regulations.” Recently, two local landowners have met with the Planning Director to inquire about converting existing accessory structures into residential units either for themselves or their family. The Planning Director proposed an amendment to the existing ADU ordinance to allow for ADUs larger than 900 square feet by Special Permit. However, the proposal to reconsider the ADU ordinance was met with pushback. Therefore, the draft amendment below is independent of the ADU ordinance – it is a new zoning ordinance to allow for existing accessory structures, such as barns or carriage houses, built before August 2016 to be converted into single-family homes by Special Permit. The City of Greenfield is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity Employer, a designated Green Community and a recipient of the “Leading by Example” Award Note: Text with a strikethrough is text to be deleted, black bold italic text is newly proposed text. ---ARTICLE VII ~ 200-7.22. Adaptive Residential Reuse of Accessory Structures A. Purpose. The purpose of this Section is to allow the adaptive reuse of existing accessory structures, such as barns, carriage houses, garages, and other structures for residential purposes in any zoning district where residential uses are allowed. This zoning provides for adaptive residential reuse of accessory structures to accomplish the following purposes: (1) Enable homeowners to utilize existing structures on their land for rental income and alternative living options; (2) Support the maintenance of and prevent dilapidation of historical structures; (3) Increase housing options with gentle density that maintains the existing fabric of the built environment; (4) B. Ensure safe and healthy housing compliant with the Building Code. Applicability. (1) See Sections 200-4.1 through 200-4.17 and Appendix A, Table of Uses, for permitting requirements. C. Adaptive Residential Reuse Standards. The Zoning Board of Appeals, acting as the special permit granting authority (SPGA), may grant a special permit to use an existing accessory structure for single-family residential use on a lot with any number of existing dwellings, provided all of the following conditions are satisfied: (1) The accessory structure must have existed continuously since before August 2016 and have a minimum gross floor area of 900 square feet. (2) The accessory structure may be converted to no more than one dwelling unit and must be a complete, separate housekeeping unit containing both kitchen and bath. The City of Greenfield is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity Employer, a designated Green Community and a recipient of the “Leading by Example” Award (3) The accessory structure may not expand in gross floor area or footprint, except for improvements related to fire safety, ADA accessibility, or utilities. (4) The accessory structure may be converted to residential use notwithstanding nonconformity with dimensional requirements, provided that the conversion does not increase the degree of nonconformity. (5) The accessory structure must be and remain located on the same lot. (6) The exterior façade of the accessory structure shall substantially retain its appearance and architectural features shall be preserved to the maximum extent practicable. (7) The construction of any residential unit must be in conformity with the State Building Code, Title V of the State Sanitary Code, 527 CMR – MA Fire Prevention Regulations and other local ordinances and regulations. (8) Prior to issuance of a permit, a floor plan must be submitted showing the proposed interior and exterior changes to the building. (9) For dwellings to be served by on-site septic system, the owner must obtain a letter from the Board of Health stating that the existing sewage disposal system is adequate for the proposed residential use before a Building Permit can be obtained. (10) In order to encourage the development of housing units for disabled and handicapped individuals and persons with limited mobility, the Inspector of Buildings or Zoning Board of Appeals may allow reasonable deviation from the stated conditions where necessary to install features that facilitate access and mobility for disabled persons. (11) Adaptive residential reuse of accessory structures shall not be used for short-term rentals. EAT | EXPANDED ACCESSIBLE TRANSPORTATION Expanding Accessible Transportation – Bedford and Beyond History needs service design and funding options SB Companion to Expanded Accessible Transportation Presentation | October 25, 2026 Purpose and recommendation Expanded Accessible Transportation (EAT) would connect Bedford residents with medical care in Bedfordadjacent communities while preserving Bedford Local Transit (BLT) for established in-town travel. This report explains the transportation gap, the history of efforts to address it, the proposed service and the resources needed to operate it. It is intended for residents, Council on Aging (COA) Board members, and Town staff reviewing the proposal. The recommendation adds a staffed accessible vehicle and a driver working 26 hours per week. EAT would be available to the community, with priority for older residents and persons with disabilities. Wheels of Life, The RIDE, and the launched Uber Health pilot would continue to serve complementary needs. The proposed service emphasizes dependable medical journeys, including the return home, and reduced reliance on family members who may be working, live elsewhere, or lack an accessible vehicle. First-year base requests, excluding a vehicle shelter, are $12,329 with the vehicle grant and $89,048 without the vehicle grant. Adding the one-time $1,250 shelter produces complete first-year requests of $13,579 and $90,298, respectively. Both scenarios retain the $13,539 COA formula-grant contribution, or 15% of the vehicle cost. Benefits and grant accounting remain subject to Town Finance review. The historical March 2026 MassDOT vehicle award supports the project history but does not guarantee a future award. EAT is presented as a proposed Town priority; final service, funding, and operating decisions would follow the appropriate Town process. Bedford has several transportation resources, but they do not consistently provide the same complete journey: appropriate geography, accessible equipment, affordable payment, and a dependable return. October 2026 | 1 EAT | EXPANDED ACCESSIBLE TRANSPORTATION Guide and Principal Findings The central gap is a usable medical journey beyond Bedford: an appropriate vehicle, a driver, an affordable payment arrangement and a dependable return. A resident may have several nominal transportation options yet lack one that meets all four conditions. Requested Select Board support This report asks the Select Board to recognize expanded accessible transportation as a Town priority and support Town staff advancing both FY2028 funding pathways in parallel: the vehicle-grant pathway and a Townfunded vehicle pathway if grant funding is unavailable or delayed. Advancing both pathways keeps a single acquisition decision open while preserving the Town’s ability to act promptly if grant timing or award conditions create a delay. Final appropriations, procurement, and operating policies would remain subject to the appropriate Town processes. Finding Why it matters 24 of 46 BLT survey respondents requested regional medical rides 52.2% selected out-of-town medical transportation as an improvement. [2] Wheels of Life received 22 responses from 40 invitees All 22 rated it important or very important. Nine of 20 reported missing, delaying or cancelling care because of transportation limitations. [28] Existing financial assistance has limits Wheels of Life offers up to $500 per calendar year. The Uber Health pilot offers $10 on up to four one-way rides per month. [38] Reading guide The report proceeds from history and existing services to separate local surveys, DASH lessons and regional evidence. It then describes the intended population, road safety and operating model, followed by the three fictional rider profiles. The financial sections explain capital, annual operations, offsets, and illustrative fares. The final sections address Board options, implementation, evaluation, common questions and source documentation. The report brings together the history, resident experience, service alternatives and financial structure of the proposed expansion. Its purpose is to explain why the gap exists and how a staffed, accessible service could address it. Operating counts in this report use one-way passenger trips; a person travelling out and back generates two trips. Fictional rider profiles also show round trips explicitly. Passenger seats, unique riders and trips per day are different measures. Surveys retain their own populations and question denominators. Fiscal years run July through June. FY2028 is July 1, 2027–June 30, 2028; FY2029 follows one year later. Wheels of Life resident allowances follow the calendar year. Dollar amounts are shown precisely in the financial sections. The estimated annual salary is $33,314; benefits remain to be confirmed by Town Finance. Reporting in December 2013 described BLT as close to maximum use and discussed Carleton-Willard medical taxi support. The present proposal builds on that history, including the DASH regional pilot and the 2018 aging needs assessment. [11, 21] Period Milestone 2015 Economic Development Coordinator Alyssa Sandoval presented an expanded transit proposal following Healthy Bedford work. [14] Spring 2016 Finance Committee recommended a pilot; Annual Town Meeting approved Article 21. [15, 16] August and September 2016 Select Board awarded the operating contract August 8. DASH service began September 12. [17, 18] June 2018 Aging in Bedford documented driving adaptations, transportation satisfaction and caregiver concerns. [21] June 30, 2019 DASH ended after a third operating year. Healthy Bedford administered its final year. [20] 2024 The current operating-grant framework was completed, according to the recent COA planning update. Expanded-service funding has not yet been used for the proposed expansion. March 13, 2026 MassDOT notified Bedford of an award for one Type A van, with an estimated $13,539 (15%) local match. [39] July to September 2026 Updated Wheels of Life funding and surveys, the Uber Health pilot and new operating-offset information inform the current proposal. [35, 38] What the historical award establishes The March 13 email concerned the FY26 Community Transit Grant Program. It reported 131 vans awarded out of 238 requested and stated that final award and match values would follow after inflation adjustment. These are vehicle counts, not numbers of communities. [39] The COA project history identifies FY2027, beginning July 1, 2026, as the intended service start. It reports that the vehicle could not be accepted because the request did not obtain inclusion on the Annual Town Meeting warrant. This should not be described as a Town Meeting vote rejecting the vehicle. The next application needs an explicit path connecting grant acceptance, local authorization and annual operating support. The motion was seconded by Member Rosa and unanimously voted 5-0-0. 2 Meeting Held - 365 Boston Road, Billerica, MA 01821 – 978-671-0939 www.town.billerica.ma.us TOWN OF BILLERICA SELECT BOARD MINUTES SEPTEMBER 22, 2025 8. Public Hearing – National Grid and Verizon - #31168498 – National Grid to install (1) JO Pole (Pole #P250) on Cook Street beginning at a point ~240’ northeast of the centerline of the intersection of Boston Road mid-span between poles P2 and P3 Cook Street. Pole will be located on town property intersected by Boston Road and Covington Avenue. MOTION - Secretary Darris-O’Connor made a motion to open the public hearing for National Grid #31168498 at 6:38 PM. The motion was seconded by Member Rosa and unanimously voted 5-0-0. Bryan Sathler of National Grid appeared for the public hearing. Mr. Sathler stated that this application is for a new pole. Member Rosa asked if any abutters had reached out. Mr. Sathler replied no. Member Rosa asked if you have read the DPW comments. Mr. Sathler replied yes. Member Rosa stated that the DPW has stated that the pole is proposed to be installed on a paved sidewalk with less than 36”. He will not support this. We have worked really hard to have poles removed from sidewalks and will not support adding a new one. Member Favreau stated that adding a pole in the sidewalk is not in line with complete streets policy and will not support this. There were no questions from abutters in person or via Zoom. MOTION - Secretary Darris-O’Connor made a motion to close the public hearing for National Grid public hearing #31168498 at 6:40 PM. The motion was seconded by Member Rosa and unanimously voted 5-0-0. MOTION - Secretary Darris-O’Connor made a motion to approve the National Grid pole petition for #31168498 as presented. There was no second. The motion fails. Interviews 9. Town Counsel Interviews: - Brooks & DeRensis Paul DeRensis appeared for the interview for Town Counsel. Attorney DeRensis stated that they have been Billerica’s Town Counsel for a year and a few months. We’ve been operating under a retainer system, but they are willing to negotiate as long as it works for both sides. Our rates are 20% less than Harrington Heep. We took over from your previous Town Counsel, and it took longer and was more difficult than it should have been. It was a hard transition. There was a flood of backlogs and many upheavals. There have been changes in the Town Manager, in Select Board Chairs as well as many disputes between Board members. They have hired Attorney Moreira as Billerica’ point of contact. They have accomplished a lot for the Town and have had success in courts. We have invested a lot of time in Billerica and with our reputation, there is no need to go elsewhere. We have 20 lawyers and 9 paralegals, and we just hired a 30-year experienced land use attorney. Our Real Estate department with 7 attorneys will be available to Billerica. John Ruggieri joined the meeting via Zoom. Attorney Ruggieri stated that he is the Chair of the Real Estate Department with over 30 years of experience and has been involved in the Yankee Doodle Bike Path, and procurement. They also have Attorney Clements on staff that have over 30 years’ experience in land use and zoning matters. Member Rosa stated that there have been bumps in the road and he knows that Mr. Dillon has some issues with the billing. We have a retainer, but we have had multiple meetings to discuss issues and concerns we are having. Mr. Kopelman was agreeable to some of our ideas and maybe some of them have been incorporated but there have been issues that were not always clear and concise. The hiring of Attorney Moreira has helped with response time, but we are getting billed for his time at attorney rates. Attorney DeRensis stated that only when he provides legal opinions. Member Rosa stated that when you took over from KP Law, you said that they did not provide a lot of our files and you had to recreate them. We asked you to track the time separately, but you never did that. This was frustrating because we made it very clear that we wanted to try to recoup that. There have been issues like with AT&T lease on the water tower. This was sent to Attorney Hucksam, and he didn’t do anything about it. We need to have trust that 3 Meeting Held - 365 Boston Road, Billerica, MA 01821 – 978-671-0939 www.town.billerica.ma.us TOWN OF BILLERICA SELECT BOARD MINUTES SEPTEMBER 22, 2025 our Town Counsel explores all avenues. He likes that the cost is less, but they have spent significantly more than what we have paid in the past. Before Mr. Dillon came, no one was reviewing what was covered by the retainer. Secretary Darris-O’Connor thanked them for coming but to be honest, he has dire concerns that Brooks and DeRensis can represent Billerica. Does Brooks & DeRensis have a dedicated municipal law unit. Attorney DeRensis stated that everyone is a municipal law member, but we do other private business but we can handle a wide range of issues. Secretary Darris-O’Connor asked how many towns you represent. Attorney DeRensis replied seven towns with 20 lawyers. Harrington Heep represents 27 towns with 13 lawyers. Secretary Darris-O’Connor stated that we need timely responses. There was a question asked about the reorganization of the Select Board, and it took over a week to answer. Attorney DeRensis stated that every Select Board member has access to Town Counsel and we were getting conflicting information and politics aside, we did provide legal opinions. Secretary Darris-O’Connor asked why there were multiple opinions on the preliminary warrant. Attorney DeRensis stated that they were editing articles and they did not get the full story. Secretary Darris-O’Connor stated that we need timely opinions regardless of who asks. Secretary Darris-O’Connor stated that at Town Meeting there was a motion to move the question and was asked if a simple majority vote was required or a 2/3 vote and we couldn’t get a clear answer. Attorney DeRensis stated that this dealt with MBTA and it was a not a clear issue. Vice Chair Burrows stated that he is concerned with response time with department heads. He doesn’t want a personal opinion; he wants to know what the law is. When bad information is given, it drops your credibility. The bills have been astronomical, and he wonders what is covered under the retainer. Attorney DeRensis stated that they put Attorney Moreira in charge of getting timely answers and early on it was a flood gate. There are changing opinion because we are not given all the relevant information and we need to give an opinion based on the information given. Vice Chair Burrows stated that the Chair was supposed to be cc’d on every email and that was not happening. Attorney DeRensis agreed that was an issue and we fixed that. Member Favreau prefaced her comments that the opinion for the preliminary warrant was thorough. You’re firm has not been responsive in the last six months. We met in January in Executive Session to discuss deficiencies. Some issues have improved but some haven’t. What would your firm do differently if selected. Attorney DeRensis stated that we have provided tracking for questions received and we provide it weekly. Member Favreau stated that she hasn’t seen that. Chair Pavidis stated that it goes to herself and the Town Manager. She can send it to the entire Board. Member Favreau asked what would be done differently. There are issues with response time, different opinions, lack of trust, accuracy of law. Attorney DeRensis stated that we are told one story and then someone comes to us with different information, it’s hard to give an accurate opinion. Member Favreau asked what the recommendation would be moving forward because we need adequate legal counsel. There have been some improvements but not quite enough. Attorney DeRensis stated that the full board should get the tracking log and sometimes the law is not clear. Mr. Dillon stated that you have 20 attorneys representing 7 towns but how many municipal attorneys are on staff. Attorney DeRensis replied 16. Mr. Dillon asked how many do only municipal law. Attorney DeRensis replied 6. Mr. Dillon asked if you are not selected, what is the transition plan. Attorney DeRensis replied that they would never do what KP Law did and will always protect the town. Chair Pavidis stated that there have been a lot of changes. What happens when five Select Board members have facts that they believe are true. The response time has improved but is still lacking. Attorney DeRensis stated that the Board should use the Town Manager as a clearing house. All correspondence should go through the Town Manager, and the Town Manager would send it to Town Counsel. Member Rosa stated that per our policies and procedures, both the Town Manager and Town Counsel are appointed by this Board. Our policies require that the Chair and Town Manager be copied on all emails to Town Counsel. If you receive conflicting questions, reach out to Town Manager. Member Rosa asked if Brooks & DeRensis has the bandwidth to handle Billerica. Attorney DeRensis replied yes. 4 Meeting Held - 365 Boston Road, Billerica, MA 01821 – 978-671-0939 www.town.billerica.ma.us TOWN OF BILLERICA SELECT BOARD MINUTES SEPTEMBER 22, 2025 Attorney DeRensis stated that they are willing to work with the Town on the policies and procedures and with the retainer. On motion by Vice-President Jadczak and seconded by Councilor Markee, it was unanimously voted to suspend Public Speak to allow for Mayor Derby to present information regarding the proposed Special Election. Public Hearing – Supplemental Appropriation for $5,000.00 from Free Cash to fund a new parttime position in the Tax Collector’s Office for FY26 President Denham stated that this item was removed from the agenda without prejudice. It was stated that the individual was hired before funds were appropriated. Mayor Derby spoke regarding the request for the part-time position in the Tax Collector’s Office. He stated that there is a desperate need for the position. If collections get behind, it affects the Treasurer and Auditor. He said that the position will be covered by Enterprise Funds in the future since the employee will be handling water bills. Vice-President Jadczak said that while she is in support of getting assistance in the Collector’s Office, she asked why it was not previously mentioned by the Mayor or Human Resources that the person has already been hired. Mayor Derby said that because the position will be funded through Enterprise Funds it is not at risk for paying unemployment. Human Resources Director Emily Russo stated that the city will now implement requisition forms to assure that funding is in place before employees are hired. On mo on by Councilor Kwiecinski and seconded by Councilor Schmidt, it was unanimously voted to set a public hearing for the supplemental appropria on request for $5,000.00 from Free Cash to fund a new part- me posi on in the Tax Collector’s Oﬃce for FY 26 for May 11, 2026 at 6:15 p.m. at 50 Payson Avenue, second ﬂoor, in City Council Chambers. Mayor’s Request for the City Council to set a Special Election for June 9, 2026 for a vote of a proposed Tax Levy Override of $6,900,000.00 President Denham asked Mayor Derby to speak to this before Public Speak. 1 Mayor Derby stated that since COVID, budgets have been growing in relation to inflation. Over the last few years, the city has been utilizing stabilization money along with other one-time funds to balance the budget. The city was without a Treasurer for approximately a year, a new Treasurer was hired in August. He said that Free Cash was certified in March when it usually happens in October/November of the previous year. He added that debt and interest figures came in significantly higher than anticipated. Mayor Derby stated that the requested amount of $6.9 million will allow the city to not have to request another override next year. Public Comment Summary: Dan Rist, 26 Line Street, was a 27-year member of the City Council and was on the Finance Commitee for 20 years. He said that he wants to “lend credibility” to what this budget situa on is: increase in inﬂa on, increase in health care costs. He said that what the number requested is up to you, but he wants to only put one number on the ballot. He said the city will lose a lot of teachers, the School Department is half of the city’s budget. There will be decreases in response me from the Fire and Police Departments. The Senior Center and Nonotuck Park have reduced hours. He said that a “No” vote is extremely dangerous. William Joss, 60 Division Street, said that he wants people to know that this is an ongoing expense. He ques oned how the city could not have a Treasurer and get into this situa on. Cathy Wauczinski, Overlook Drive, said that the property tax increase will also increase the amount residents pay in CPA (Community Preserva on Act) tax. She said that a water rate increase was approved by the Board of Public Works. She said that the City Council, School Commitee, and former Mayor are responsible for this. She said that Easthampton Ac ve Ci zens will pe on to remove the CPA tax. Darlene Orvieto, Muter Street, said that there have been mistakes by the Governor and former Mayor. She said there should not be an override vote un l “we can see the budget.” Mateusz Marcinowski, 7 West Lake Street, said that his son is a recipient of special educa on. He said that he supports the override and how important it is but realizes that this is not an easy choice for anyone. James Ramsey, Campbell Drive, said that he has lived in Easthampton his en re life me. He asked where the state and cannabis funds are. He said that Main Street is not in good condi on and added that he lives within his means. Nori Torman, 52 East Street, said that “charity begins at home” and that Easthampton is our home. 2 ? Lavalley, Maxine Circle, said that they are impressed with the City Council in its considera on of senior ci zens. They said that many people cannot aﬀord to re re and may lose their homes. They asked if there is another way to resolve this. Jess Atkins-Barber, 22 Vadnais Street, is a tenth grader at Easthampton High School. They would like us to stay connected as a community and to move forward on the override. Kathleen Joss, 60 Division Street, said that she is concerned about the increase of 6-8 more liquor licenses. She said that she frequently walks and that there is a lot of speeding in Easthampton, adding that there was an accident on Northampton Street today. Carol Brodeur, 72 Oliver Street, said that we need to live within our budget and make cuts. She stated that she is against the override. Chris O’Connor, 21 Ashley Circle, said she is opposed to the override, sta ng that elected oﬃcials need to balance the budget. Jen Sandler, 26 Williston Avenue, said that she does not know exactly how we got here, saying that inﬂa on is more than 2 ½ %. She asked if the city could involve ci zens more regularly in hopes that this will lead to a more democra c discussion. Karl Prahl, 15 Torrey Street, said that the city needs to look at diﬀerent sources of revenue. Carolyn Cushing, Main Street, said that it seems important to have the override and hear people’s voices. She said that there are challenges with communica ng the ballot ques on if it is a “pyramid” type. Sam Hunter, 8 Mayher Street, member of the Easthampton School Commitee, asked the City Council to vote to set the Special City Elec on for the override. Sam said that some programs such as the summer food program may have to be cut next year. Dan Zdonek, member of the Easthampton Board of Assessors, but stated that he is not represen ng the Board. He said that he has seen a rough dra of the numbers and it does not look good. He said that the vote should set the number at $6.9 million and a lower number that might pass if the City Council feels that $6.9 million is too high. He said that if informa on does not get out, the override will not pass. President Denham addressed some of the ques ons posed during Public Speak. Why was there no Treasurer for a signiﬁcant amount of me? The last Treasurer le during the previous administra on for personal reasons and the eﬀort to ﬁll the posi on took a signiﬁcant amount of me. 3 Regarding the proposed 6-8 addi onal liquor licenses, this is a way for restaurants to raise revenue since the markup on food is very small. In response to a ques on of the meline, why only a month to ﬁgure this out? Free Cash was cer ﬁed in March. Public Speak con nued Liz Perry, Precinct 3, ques oned why budgets are being proposed to be cut by the size of the department’s budget rather than its importance to the community? Julie Slavet, 14 Nicols Way, (online) said that local property tax is not a good way to support local government. She added that it would have been useful to have some visual aids at the mee ng such as slides. She asked for a task force on revenue to be set up. Leslie Sharr, Nashawannuck Street, said that the override will aﬀect everyone including landlords increasing rent. She asked that the library not be part of the proposed cuts. Sean Abbot, Summer Street, (online) said that this was not brought on by us and will be diﬃcult for folks but cuts will also be diﬃcult. Leslie Buton, 5 Fox Run, said that she has a lot of experience managing budgets at a signiﬁcant level. She asked about contractual costs such as the level of increases for teachers’ contracts. Councilor Kwiecinski asked if the meline is ght because the budget is scheduled to be out soon. Mayor Derby said that the schools have a statutory deadline to let teachers know by June 15th if they are going to be re-hired for the following school year. He added that the city budget needs to be passed by July 1st. On mo on by Councilor Peake and seconded by Councilor Jamrog-McQuaid it was unanimously voted to set a Special City Elec on on June 9, 2026 to vote on a Proposi on 2 ½ Override Ques on reques ng $6,900,000.00. Councilor Peake retracted his mo on and Councilor Jamrog-McQuaid retracted his second of the mo on. Mo on was made by Councilor Peake and seconded by Councilor Jamrog-McQuaid to set a Special City Elec on for June 9, 2026. The ballot ques on shall read as follows: “Shall the City of Easthampton be allowed to assess an addi onal $6,900,000 in real estate and personal property taxes for the purposes of opera ng the Municipal Government and Public Schools for the ﬁscal year beginning July ﬁrst, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six?” 4 Mo on was made by Councilor Kwiecinski and seconded by Councilor Peake to amend the mo on to add an addi onal ques on of reques ng $3,450,000.00 in real estate and personal property taxes for purposes of opera ng the Municipal Government and Public Schools for the ﬁscal year beginning July ﬁrst, Two Thousand and Twenty Six? Councilor Peake inquired of Councilor Kwiecinski how he arrived at the amount of $3,450,000.00. Councilor Kwiecinski said that the amount he proposed is “closer in line” to the amount the city is using from reserves. He said that this is one half of the amount proposed of $6,900,000.00. He added that in reviewing override ques ons from other communi es, most had two op ons on the ballot. Councilor Peake said that in theory he is not opposed to a second amount but if the city proposes two ques ons on the ballot, there will be a very short meline to educate voters. In a pyramid type ques on, if both ques ons pass, the larger number prevails. People may think that the city is asking for both amounts which is a concern that has played out in other communi es. Councilor Peake asked the Mayor if the City Council wants to propose a separate, lower number, would this require three diﬀerent budgets? Mayor Derby replied, that “yes” he would meet with department heads again for a third round of budgets. Councilor Kwiecinski said that he “wants to put on record” that he is amenable to another second number, he is not ed to the amount he proposed. Councilor Peake stated that he wants to use a number that has a ra onale behind it. Councilor Newton asked Mayor Derby if $3.9 million would cover the city for the next year. Mayor Derby responded that there would s ll be signiﬁcant cuts. Mayor Derby said that approximately $4.5 million was used to balance the budget. With the proposed amount of $3.9 million there will be a signiﬁcant gap and that they city would be back reques ng another override. President Denham said that we have a mo on and second on the amendment. Vice-President Jadczak said that one concern with op ons on the ballot is that if the lower number passes and the city has to come back reques ng more funds, this will not look good. Councilor Newton said that she is comfortable with one number considering what everyone else has said. 5 Councilor Schmidt said that he does not want to give the impression that the lower number will ﬁx things long-term. Councilor Markee said that he is not comfortable with any amount below $6.9 million, sta ng that this is the lower number considering an amount between $8 million and $8.5 million is closer to what it necessary to give the city 4-5 years of ﬁscal stability. A vote was taken on the mo on for the Proposi on 2 ½ ballot ques on to request $3,450,000.00 and the mo on failed with 7 against, 2 in favor. Councilor Peake said that year a er year we have passed budgets to keep the level of service from the previous year but with costs increasing. He said that many communi es are dealing with overrides now. He referenced the Massachusets Municipal Associa on (MMA) ar cle “The Perfect Storm” detailing how many ci es and towns are now in the same situa on and how state aid has not kept up with costs. President Denham said that this is a par cularly diﬃcult conversa on to have. She said that she was the only Councilor to not vote for the budget last year because she did not want to take $4.5 million from the stabiliza on fund. President Denham said that this pains her and that there will be people who cannot aﬀord the override and will be forced to leave the community. President Denham asked Councilor Peake, as Finance Commitee Chair, to meet with the City Auditor more frequently. The vote returned to the main mo on of a request for $6.9 million. On mo on by Councilor Peake and seconded by Councilor Kwiecinski it was unanimously voted to set a Special City Elec on for June 9, 2026 for a Proposi on 2 ½ Override Ques on as follows: “Shall the City of Easthampton be allowed to assess an addi onal $6,900,000 in real estate and personal property taxes for the purposes of opera ng the Municipal Government and Public Schools for the ﬁscal year beginning July ﬁrst, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six?” On motion by Councilor Kwiecinski and seconded by Councilor Smith it was unanimously voted that this meeting adjourn. Town Hall, 334 Main Street Great Barrington, MA 01230 Telephone: (413) 528-1619 Fax: (413) 528-2290 TOWN OF GREAT BARRINGTON MASSACHUSETTS ___ PLANNING BOARD October 29, 2026 Zoning Board of Appeals Town Hall 334 Main Street Great Barrington, MA RE: 110 Cottage Street Dear Members of the ZBA: At its meeting of October 22, 2026, the Planning Board voted to send a favorable recommendation for the application filed by James Toby Zucco for permission to construct a larger garage on the same nonconforming footprint as the previous structure at 110 Cottage Street, Great Barrington, per Sections 5.7 and 10.4 of the zoning bylaws. Thank you for your attention to this matter. Sincerely, Kimberly L. Shaw Kimberly L. Shaw Planning Board Secretary Cc: Chris Rembold, Assistant Town Manager & Director of Planning and Development Town of Great Barrington Town Manager’s Office www.townofgbma.gov 334 Main Street, Great Barrington, MA 01230 (413) 528‐1619 lhartsgrove@townofgbma.gov Liz Hartsgrove Town Manager ___ Chris Rembold Assistant Town Manager Memo To: Zoning Board or Appeals Members From: Date: Liz Hartsgrove, Town Manager October 28, 2026 Re: Cc: 110 Cottage Street Special Permit Recommendation Selectboard Members The Great Barrington Selectboard, at its meeting on October 26, 2026, voted unanimously (5‐0) to send a positive recommendation of the Special Permit application from James Toby Zucco to construct a larger garage on the same nonconforming footprint as the previous structure at 110 Cottage St, Great Barrington, per Sections 5.7 and 10.4 of the zoning bylaw. Zoning Board of Appeals Town of Great Barrington Minutes of Monday, July 27, 2026 The following members were present: JB Brodeur, Stephen McAlister, Madonna Meagher, Peter Most, and Michael Wise. James Manning (alternate) was not present. Also Present: Assistant Town Manager/Planning Director Christopher Rembold. 150 Hurlburt Road: application for a Variance Chair Peter Most reopened the hearing at 3:00 pm, noting that the case was continued from June 30. The hearing was on this agenda because the continuation originally scheduled for July 21 could not occur due to the agenda not being timely posted. Most opened the public hearing and invited the applicant to present the project. Most noted that since June 30, the state has passed a new law that changed the criteria for Variances in MGL Ch 40A section 10. He said the new law became effective July 1 and lowers the threshold for variances to a standard of “practical difficulty.” He said the board received the applicant’s written response as to how the proposal meets the Variance criteria. He said that it is written based on the previous criteria, but the board must use the new standard per the law currently in effect. Applicant Max Ritt described the proposal and reviewed the additional information he sent to the Board based on the last session. It is made part of the record of the permit. Board members discussed the applicant’s responses, referencing the new criteria of Section 10 as follows: (i) whether the practical difficulty relates to soil conditions, shape or topography of such land or structures; Members agreed that the nonconforming lot shape and the placement of the well and the septic system make it practically difficult to place the garage in a conforming location behind the existing house. (ii) whether the strict enforcement would impose a financial hardship on the appellant or petitioner; Members agreed based on the information provided that the cost to move the well and the septic system in order to build the garage in a conforming location would be a financial hardship. (iii) whether the benefit sought by the appellant or petitioner can be achieved by some other method feasible for the appellant or petitioner to achieve; and Members agreed there was no other method feasible to locate the garage. (iv) whether the practical difficulty was self-created. Members agreed the current owner and applicant did not locate the existing structure or utilities and therefore did not self create the practical difficulties. Most said if he had to decide the Variance based on the old criteria he would have been skeptical but believes the applicant meets the current criteria. Brodeur and Meagher agreed. McAlister agreed stating the Exhibit A provided to the board tells the story clearly. Wise said the changes in the law make all the difference in this case. Wise moved to close the hearing. Meagher seconded. On a roll call vote, all were in favor. ZBA Minutes July 27, 2026 Wise moved that the strict enforcement of the front and side yard setbacks of the R2 zone does result in a practical difficulty for the proposal, based on the discussion of the four criteria. Meagher seconded. On a roll call vote, all were in favor. Citizen Speak: None Adjourn: Most adjourned the meeting at approximately 3:40 PM. Minutes taken by: Christopher Rembold 2

title: Warrant for 2026 State Election
text: COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS WILLIAM FRANCIS GALVIN SECRETARY OF THE COMMONWEALTH WARRANT FOR 2026 STATE ELECTION SS. To the Constables of the City/Town of HAMPDEN GREETINGS: In the name of the Commonwealth, you are hereby required to notify and warn the inhabitants of said city or town who are qualified to vote in Elections to vote at: _ 0/001 __ TOWN HALL 85 WILBRAHAM ROAD On TUESDAY, THE THIRD DAY OF NOVEMBER, 2026, from 7:00 A.M. to 8:00 P.M. for the following purpose: To cast their votes in the State Election for the candidates for the following offices and questions: SENATOR IN CONGRESS For this Commonwealth GOVERNOR and LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR For this Commonwealth ATTORNEY GENERAL For this Commonwealth SECRETARY OF STATE For this Commonwealth TREASURER For this Commonwealth AUDITOR For this Commonwealth REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS FIRST DISTRICT COUNCILLOR EIGHTH DISTRICT SENATOR IN GENERAL COURT HAMPDEN, HAMPSHIRE & WORCESTER DISTRICT REPRESENTATIVE IN GENERAL COURT SECOND HAMPDEN DISTRICT DISTRICT ATTORNEY HAMPDEN DISTRICT REGISTER OF PROBATE HAMPDEN COUNTY QUESTION 1: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. This proposed law would exempt documents related to the development of public policy and communications between legislators and their constituents, if those communications are reasonably related to a constituent’s request for assistance in obtaining government-provided benefits or services or interacting with a government agency. A YES VOTE would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. A NO VOTE would make no change to the Massachusetts Public Records Law. QUESTION 2: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would specify that employees of the Committee for Public Counsel Services (“CPCS”) are permitted to engage in collective bargaining with their employer. It would also require CPCS, after executing a collective bargaining agreement, to request the appropriation necessary to fund such agreement from the Governor. A YES VOTE would specify that Committee for Public Counsel Services employees may form a union to collectively bargain with their employer. A NO VOTE would make no change to the law governing labor relations for Committee for Public Counsel Service employees. QUESTION 3: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would eliminate political party primaries for state elections and instead establish a system where there would be a single, all-party primary in which all candidates, regardless of their party affiliation, would be listed on one ballot, and voters could vote for any candidate on the ballot. The two candidates receiving the most votes in the primary would advance to the general election ballot. This proposed law would require candidates for governor and lieutenant governor to run and be listed jointly on the ballot in the primary. This proposed law would provide political party status to any group whose candidates for any statewide office received at least 3% of the ballots cast in the state primary. A YES VOTE would eliminate separate party primaries for state elections and require a single primary in which all candidates appear on one ballot, voters could vote for any candidate, and the top two candidates would advance to the general election. A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing primary elections. QUESTION 4: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would permit eligible individuals to register to vote or update their voter registration address on Election Day. An individual who is eligible to vote could register to vote on Election Day by going to the polling place in the precinct where they live during voting hours and presenting proof of residency and signing a written oath. Proof of residency could be a valid photo identification, or documentation showing the individual’s name and the address where the individual resides, such as a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, residential lease, wireless telephone statement, paycheck, current student fee statement or other document from a post-secondary school, or another government document or correspondence. The written oath would require the individual to certify that they are a citizen of the United States, are at least 18 years old, are not legally prohibited from voting, and have not and will not vote in the same election 2 at another location. The oath would require the individual to acknowledge that providing false information is a felony punishable by not more than 5 years imprisonment or a fine of not more than $10,000, or both. If an individual did not present proof of residency, they would be allowed to cast a provisional ballot, which would be counted only if the individual returned to provide the required information before the close of polls for a municipal election; within two days after a state primary; or within six days after a state election. Individuals who register to vote on Election Day would be registered to vote in future elections as well as in the election taking place that day. Individuals who are already registered to vote would not be able to change their political party affiliation on Election Day. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028. A YES VOTE would permit eligible citizens to register to vote or to update their voter registration address at their polling place on Election Day. A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing voter registration. QUESTION 5: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would change the limit on how much revenue the state can collect in a given year. The proposal would limit state revenue in a given year to the net amount of state revenue from the year before, increased by a rate equal to the average growth of wages and salaries in Massachusetts over the most recent three years. If revenue collected by the state in a given year exceeds the limit, the excess amount would be refunded to taxpayers the following year. The proposed law would include all revenue from the surtax on incomes over $1 million when calculating the revenue limit and when determining whether state revenue exceeds the limit. The provisions of the proposed law would all be effective as of July 1, 2027. The proposed law states that, if any of its parts were declared invalid, the other parts would stay in effect. A YES VOTE would change the limit on state revenue collection, tying it to prior year collections plus average wage and salary growth, and provide for a rebate of revenue exceeding that limit. A NO VOTE would make no change in the law relative to state revenue collection. QUESTION 6: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would establish a Nature for All Fund that, subject to appropriation by the Legislature, would receive 50% of state taxes collected from the sale and use of sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses for the first year of its operation. After July 1, 2028, the Nature for All Fund would begin receiving, subject to appropriation by the Legislature, 100% of state taxes collected on the sale and use of sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses. The sales tax revenue received by the Nature for All Fund would exclude sales tax revenue transferred to the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority State and Local Contribution Fund and the School Modernization and Reconstruction Trust Fund. The proposed law would allow the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to spend the money in the Nature for All Fund for natural resource conservation. 3 The proposed law would allow public and private donations to the Nature for All Fund. The proposed law would prevent the state comptroller from transferring surplus funds in the Nature for All Fund at the end of the fiscal year. It would also allow state agencies, municipalities, public charities involved in natural resource conservation, tribal governments, and other regional public entities to receive money from the Nature for All Fund. Natural resource conservation would include the conservation or restoration of land to protect drinking water, streams, rivers, lakes, coasts, farms, forests, connectivity between open spaces, and lands and natural resources of indigenous cultural significance. Natural resource conservation would also include the creation, improvement, and management of parks, trails, greenspaces or outdoor recreation access. The proposed law would establish a 15-member Nature for All Board that consists of five state officials and ten members of the public appointed by the Governor. The proposed law would require the ten members of the public to include representatives of underserved communities and indigenous peoples and at least one person with expertise or experience in natural resource conservation. The proposed law would allow the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to spend money from the Nature for All Fund to hire staff to manage the fund. The proposed law would also require the Nature for All Board to establish rules about how the money in the Nature for All Fund should be spent, including rules regarding alignment with environmental justice principles, access to and restoration of lands and natural resources of indigenous cultural significance, promotion of affordable housing development, and other matters regarding spending and bond issuance. The proposed law would require the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to submit an annual report to various state committees regarding the funds spent to buy or improve land in cities and towns containing environmental justice populations. The proposed law would take effect on July 1, 2027. A YES VOTE would create a fund that could be utilized for natural resource conservation that would receive some state taxes collected on the sale and use of sporting goods and recreational vehicles, and the use of golf courses. A NO VOTE would not create this natural resource conservation fund or change how sales and use taxes are spent. QUESTION 7: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would allow single-family homes to be built in a residentially zoned area as long as the land on which it is to be constructed is at least 5,000 square feet, has at least 50 feet of land bordering the street, road, or public way that it faces, and has access to public sewer and water services. The proposed law would allow cities and towns to reasonably regulate certain aspects of those single-family homes, including their height, distance from neighboring buildings, open space, parking requirements, and whether they can be rented out on a short-term basis. The proposed law would also allow the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities to issue guidance or regulations to administer the proposed law. A YES VOTE would allow single-family homes to be built on lots of 5,000 square feet or more in residential areas, subject to reasonable local regulation of certain aspects of those homes. A NO VOTE would make no change to the law relative to building single-family homes. QUESTION 8: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY The proposed law would change the type and amount of marijuana that may legally be possessed in Massachusetts by repealing the laws that legalize, regulate, and tax the retail sale of adult recreational use marijuana in Massachusetts. The proposed law would also permit persons 21 years of age and older to possess 1 ounce or less of marijuana including no more than 5 grams in the form of concentrate, and to gift or transfer to another person 21 years of age and older 1 ounce or less of marijuana including no more than 5 grams in the form of concentrate. The proposed law would also impose a civil penalty of $100 and forfeiture of the marijuana for the possession of marijuana between the weight of 1 and 2 ounces. For persons 21 years of age and younger, the proposed law would make the possession of 2 ounces or less of marijuana a civil infraction subject to a $100 fine, forfeiture of the marijuana, completion of a drug awareness program and community service, and notification to their parents or legal guardian of the offense and penalties. The proposed law would allow currently licensed adult recreational marijuana businesses to apply on an expedited basis to become a licensed medical marijuana dispensary and to sell their remaining inventory of adult recreational marijuana to medical marijuana dispensaries. The proposed law would retain the Cannabis Control Commission but modify its authority so it would regulate only the medical marijuana market. The proposed law states that, if any of its parts were declared invalid, the other parts would stay in effect. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028. A YES VOTE would prohibit the legalization, regulation, and taxation of the retail sale of adult recreational use marijuana, and change the penalties for possession of marijuana. A NO VOTE would make no change to the law relative to marijuana. QUESTION 9: REFERENDUM ON AN EXISTING LAW Do you approve of a law summarized below, which was approved by the House of Representatives on July 18, 2024 by a vote of 124 to 33, and approved by the Senate on July 18, 2024 by a vote of 35 to 5? SUMMARY This law makes a number of changes to Massachusetts laws governing firearms. The law adds school administrators and licensed healthcare providers as parties permitted to ask a court to issue an Extreme Risk Protection Order — requiring an individual to surrender or relinquish their firearm licenses, permits, and firearms - if an individual is a present danger to self or others. The law also provides that, when issuing an Harassment Prevention Order, a court may also order the surrender of firearms licenses, permits, and firearms. The law imposes penalties for possessing, creating, and transferring untraceable “ghost gun” firearms and requires all firearms except antiques and relics, including unfinished frames and receivers that can be readily made into a finished product, to have serial numbers. The law includes privately-made guns like 3D-printed guns within the provisions governing untraceable “ghost gun” firearms. The law changes firearms licensing requirements to: (1) allow local licensing authorities to request prior license and permit information from the state, as well as access petitions for involuntary mental health commitments denied by a court in addition to prior involuntary commitments, as a part of their review of applications for licenses to carry firearms, firearm ID cards, and licenses to sell firearms; (2) require an individual to be 21 years of age to own semiautomatic rifles or shotguns; (3) add the possibility of incarceration of up to six months for a second offense of failing to report a firearm loss or theft; and (4) enable 12-15 year olds to apply for a self-defense spray permit with parental permission, and 15 to 18 year olds to apply independently. The law allows local firearm licensing authorities to transfer the responsibility to inspect firearm dealers to the State Police. The law requires local licensing authorities to attend statewide training regarding those inspections. It requires dealers to confiscate expired or suspended licenses and report them to the state and to local licensing authorities. The law changes the definition of “machine gun” to include bump stocks, trigger cranks, Glock switches and auto sears among the devices whose possession and use are subject to penalties. It expands the definition of “silencer” to include the parts used to construct a silencer. The law clarifies how to determine whether a firearm is an assault-style weapon and the circumstances under which a person may continue to possess assault-style weapons and large capacity feeding devices they already own. The law requires the state Firearm Control Advisory Board and the state Secretary of Public Safety and Security to review and update the rosters of prohibited assault-style firearms, approved firearms, and approved firearms sold for target shooting. The law clarifies requirements relating to the carry and transport of firearms in motor vehicles and ATVs. It prohibits the carrying of firearms in government buildings, polling locations, and schools, with certain exceptions. The law expands data compilation and reporting requirements to and from the state, and creates a publicly-accessible dashboard of anonymized aggregate firearm data, along with a commission to study that data. The law requires the State Police to provide training and a test for new applicants for licenses to carry or Firearm ID cards. The law establishes two special legislative commissions — one to examine funding for violence prevention services, and one to study emerging firearms technology. The law criminalizes discharging a firearm and striking a building in use. A YES VOTE would keep in place the law, which increases the regulation of firearms, including ghost guns, machine guns, and assault-style weapons. A NO VOTE would repeal this law. title: Special Town Meeting Warrant
text: Town of Mansfield SPECIAL TOWN MEETING WARRANT November 12, 2026 MANSFIELD HIGH SCHOOL 250 East Street Mansfield CALL TO ORDER: 7:00 PM Town of Mansfield WARRANT FOR THE SPECIAL TOWN MEETING Thursday, November 12, 2026 BRISTOL, SS: To either of the Constables of the Town of Mansfield in the County of Bristol; GREETINGS: IN THE NAME OF THE COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS, you are hereby directed to notify and warn the inhabitants of said town, qualified to vote in elections and in town affairs, to meet at the Mansfield High School Auditorium, 250 East Street, Mansfield, Mansfield, Massachusetts (Precincts One, Two, Two-A, Three, Four, Five, Six, Six-A and Seven) in said Mansfield on Thursday, November 12, 2026 at Seven O’clock in the afternoon, at the said Mansfield High School Auditorium, or some other convenient date and time, then and there to act on the following articles: Article 1: To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate or transfer from available funds to further amend, increase, decrease, or otherwise adjust the appropriations voted at the May 5, 2026 Annual Town meeting for several Municipal Town departments for Fiscal Year 2027, or take any other action relative thereto. Explanation: At the time the appropriations were voted at the May 5, 2026 Annual Town Meeting, many assumptions were made in order to balance the various budgets. This article (if approved) would allow the Town to now further amend, increase, decrease, or otherwise adjust these appropriations based upon new information not previously known. This article will seek additional funding for Budget 610 Public Library, Budget 152 Public Buildings, and Budget 131 Finance Committee. If approved, the additional $18,442 library funding will satisfy the Municipal Appropriations Requirement (MAR) per Massachusetts General Law Chapter 78 Section 19A to maintain eligibility to receive State Aid to Public Libraries. Without the funding the Town would be required to file a waiver from the state. The FY2026 budget required a waiver to be filed. If approved, the $60,000 funding for Public Facilities Maintenance will allow the Town to restore funding for routine maintenance and inspections for town-owned buildings that was previously cut in the creation of the FY2027 budget. If approved, the Finance Committee’s Reserve fund will be further funded by an additional $250,000. Pursuant to the Town’s Reserve Fund policy, the Town shall endeavor to fund the Finance Reserve at a rate of 1% of the operating budget minus debt, which constitutes about $540,000 for FY2027. Page 1 of 21 Article 2: To see if the Town will vote to amend Chapter 52 of the General Bylaws, Revolving Funds, by adding the following revolving funds to the table contained in § 52-5: Revolving Fund Name Programs and Purposes of Fund Departmental Officer Fiscal Year Receipts to be Authorized to Credited to Fund Expend from Fund District Expenses of District All advertising Superintendent Fiscal Year Advertising programs, fees, of Schools 2027 and activities, events, sponsorship Sponsorship facilities, payments and publications, other receipts websites, and other received District-sponsored pursuant to initiatives in approved School connection with District which advertising advertising and or sponsorship sponsorship revenue is agreements generated, including related equipment, technology, materials, improvements, and program expenses Animal Materials, supplies Adoption fees Animal Control Fiscal Year Shelter and veterinary care Officer 2028 Needs Fund for animals under the care of the Town or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This Article establishes two new revolving funds: one for School District advertising and sponsorship receipts, and one for animal adoption fee receipts. Because the District Advertising and Sponsorship fund will be funded with a new revenue source that was not available at the beginning of the fiscal year, it may go into effect during the current fiscal year. Accordingly, Article 3 also establishes the current-year expenditure limit for the District Advertising and Sponsorship revolving fund. Because the Animal Shelter Needs revolving fund is funded from an existing revenue source, it cannot become effective until next fiscal year and no expenditure limit is established for the current fiscal year. Page 2 of 21 Article 3: To see if the Town will vote to amend the annual spending limits for the Radio Master Box Fee revolving fund, and establish the Fiscal Year 2027 expenditure limit for the District Advertising and Sponsorship revolving fund, as set forth below: Revolving Fund Name Radio Master Box Fee District Advertising and Sponsorship FY2027 Total Annual Limit on Expenditures from Fund $150,000 $50,000 or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article establishes the annual maximum that is allowed to be expended from these revolving funds. The Radio Master Box Fee account is used for specific purchases related to Fire Suppression systems, alarms and equipment and is under the jurisdiction of the Fire Chief. The established annual upper limit adjustment requested for this fund reflects actual anticipated costs over Fiscal Year 2027. The District Advertising and Sponsorship account is a new revolving fund that will be used for certain School program expenses incurred in connection with activities that generate advertising or sponsorship revenue. Article 4: To see if the Town will raise and appropriate or transfer from available funds a sum of money for deposit into the following funds: Employee Other Post-Employment Benefits (OPEB) Liability Trust Fund; Future Payment of Accrued Liabilities for Compensated Absences Reserve Fund; Town’s Special Education Reserve Fund; or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board for Finance Committee Explanation: The Town is required to pay a percentage of retirees’ medical, dental, and life insurance costs. The Town’s net OPEB liability as of FY2026 is estimated at $135.8 million. This article, if approved, will transfer a sum of money into the OPEB Trust Fund to offset some of those future costs. This article, if approved, will deposit a sum of money into this Reserve Fund and allow the Town Manager to pay compensated absence expenses as outlined in MGL Chapter 50, Section 13D. The qualifying expenses under this account include contractual employment obligations. At the May 2, 2017 Annual Town meeting, voters authorized the creation of a Special Education Reserve Fund for payment of certain Special Education-related expenses. This article, if approved, will deposit a sum of money into this Reserve Fund and allow the Mansfield School Committee, with the approval of the Select Board, to pay Special Education – related expenses per MGL Chapter 40, Section 13E. Page 3 of 21 Article 5: To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, or borrow pursuant to any applicable statute a sum of money for the following Capital Improvement projects for the Town of Mansfield; or take any other action relative thereto. Item Highway Vehicle with Related Equipment Public Safety Radio Upgrades (DPW, MEMA, SCHOOLS, POLICE & FIRE) Town Hall Sidewalk Repair Police Line Cruiser Replacement (3) Fire Cruiser Replacement School District Fire Alarm System Updates/Repairs School Districtwide Buildings and Grounds Maintenance Memorial Park/Plymouth Street Tennis Court Replacement Design Project Memorial Park Parking Lot Repair and Pavement Project SPONSOR: Cost $70,500 Anticipated Funding Source Certified Free Cash $700,000 Certified Free Cash $25,000 $248,000 Certified Free Cash Certified Free Cash $76,000 $200,000 Certified Free Cash Certified Free Cash $400,000 Certified Free Cash $172,000 Certified Free Cash $300,000 Parking Enterprise Retained Earnings Select Board for Capital Improvement Program Committee Explanation: This article will contain several motions to fund the Capital Improvement Program Committee’s recommended Town, School, Sewer Enterprise, Water Enterprise, Airport Enterprise, and Parking Enterprise projects. This article (if approved) will fund the Capital Improvement Program Committee’s recommendations. Article 6: To see if the Town will vote to appropriate a sum of money to pay costs of repairing and/or replacing various roads, sidewalks, public parking and bridges within the Town; and for the payment of all costs incidental and related thereto; to determine whether this appropriation shall be raised by borrowing or otherwise; or to take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board as Road Commissioners Explanation: This article (if approved) will authorize the Treasurer to borrow funds to continue the Town’s work in repairing and replacing roads, sidewalks, parking lots, bridges and other transportation infrastructure throughout the Town. Such funding is used as a supplement to state aid for highway construction and maintenance. Page 4 of 21 Article 7: To see if the Town will vote to transfer from available funds a sum not to exceed Seven Hundred Twenty-Five Thousand Dollars ($725,000) from the Water Enterprise Fund – Retained Earnings to meet the expenses of materials for the Gilbert Street Water Main Project previously authorized by Article 6 of the May 5, 2026 Annual Town Meeting to defray costs related to borrowing funds for said project, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This project was procured in September 2026 and the materials portion of the bid came in lower than originally projected. The Water Enterprise fund has retained earnings available and recently certified by the Department of Revenue. This article allows the Town to fund the materials purchase with available funds and thereby reduce the amount of borrowing required for this project, ultimately reducing associated interest and principal costs. Article 8: To see if the Town will vote transfer from available funds a sum not to exceed Fifty Thousand Dollars ($50,000) to pay for the Town’s Tax Title expenses, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: These funds will be used to meet legal and administrative expenses relative to tax collections and foreclosures, specifically for abandoned properties or those that are in arrears on taxes. Article 9: To see if the Town will vote to transfer a sum of money not to exceed Two Hundred Thousand Dollars ($200,000) from the Sewer Enterprise Fund – Retained Earnings to the Sewer Enterprise Fund – Reserve Fund For Transfer Fund, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article will transfer a sum of money from the Sewer Enterprise Fund’s certified retained earnings into the Sewer Enterprise Fund’s Reserve Fund. It can then be used for any lawful purpose. Article 10: To see if the Town will vote to transfer a sum of money not to exceed Four Hundred Thousand Dollars ($400,000) from the Water Enterprise Fund – Retained Earnings to the Water Enterprise Fund – Reserve Fund For Transfer Fund, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article will transfer a sum of money from the Water Enterprise Fund’s certified retained earnings into the Water Enterprise Fund’s Reserve Fund. It can then be used for any lawful purpose. Page 5 of 21 Article 11: To see if the Town will vote to transfer a sum of money not to exceed Fifty Thousand Dollars ($50,000) from the Airport Enterprise Fund – Retained Earnings to the Airport Enterprise Fund – Reserve Fund For Transfer Fund, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article will transfer a sum of money from the Airport Enterprise Fund’s certified retained earnings into the Airport Enterprise Fund’s Reserve Fund. It can then be used for any lawful purpose. Article 12: To see if the Town will vote to transfer a sum of money not to exceed Seventy-Five Thousand Dollars ($75,000) from the Parking Enterprise Fund – Retained Earnings to the Parking Enterprise Fund – Reserve Fund For Transfer Fund, or take any other action realtive thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article will transfer a sum of money from the Parking Enterprise Fund’s certified retained earnings into the Parking Enterprise Fund’s Reserve Fund. It can then be used for any lawful purpose. Article 13: To see if the Town will vote, pursuant to M.G.L. c. 44 § 53 as amended by c. 77, §§ 9 and 197 of the Acts of 2023, to establish an Opioid Settlement Special Revenue Fund, to be spent under the direction of the Town Manager; and further, to transfer a sum of money not to exceed Five Hundred Forty-Five Thousand Dollars ($545,000.00) previously received from opioid settlements from the Opioid Mitigation Stabilization Fund to said fund; or to take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: The Legislature has authorized municipalities to place opioid settlement receipts in a special revenue fund. The funds may then be expended without further appropriation at the direction of the chief executive officer, only for the purpose identified in said settlement agreements. Mansfield had previously received opioid settlement funds, which had been transferred to the Opioid Mitigation Stabilization Fund, and this article will transfer those funds into the new special revenue fund. Any additional opioid settlement funds received by the Town in the future will be transferred directly to the special revenue fund. Amount in fund as of September 30, 2026 is $540,164.14. Actual amount inclusive of accrued interest will be reflected in motion at Town Meeting. Article 14: To see if the Town will vote to establish the Treasurer/Collector’s fee charged for each written demand issued pursuant to Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 60, Section 15(2), at $30, effective January 1, 2027, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Page 6 of 21 Explanation: This article establishes the fee charged for each written demand for payment of a delinquent tax at $30, the maximum amount permitted by Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 60, Section 15(2). The adjustment is to bring the cost of the fee in line with the administrative costs of managing unpaid tax accounts. Article 15: To see if the Town will vote to accept Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 44, Section 54(b), authorizing trust funds held in the custody of the Treasurer/Collector to be managed as a combined investment pool and invested in accordance with Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 203C, or take any other action relative thereto. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: Acceptance of this section would permit certain trust funds held in the custody of the Treasurer/Collector to be managed as a combined investment pool and invested in accordance with the “Prudent Investor” standards of Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 203C, rather than the investment limitations otherwise applicable under Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 44, Section 53(a). This provision applies only to qualifying trust funds and does not override investment restrictions contained in a bequest, trust instrument, or other expression of donor intent. Acceptance would provide greater investment flexibility and diversification opportunities with respect to such funds. Article 16: To see if the Town will vote to accept an access easement along Oakland Street for purposes of public use of the existing sidewalk, as shown on the plan titled Sidewalk Easement Plan on file with the Town Clerk’s Office, and further to authorize the Select Board to execute any and all instruments as may be necessary to effectuate the purposes of this article. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article asks voters if they will accept an access easement for purposes of public use of the existing sidewalk which currently traverses into private property. Article 17: To see if the Town will vote to accept a drainage easement on the property at 150 Oakland Street, shown on Assessor’s Map 030 as Parcel 039, owned by 150 Oakland Owner LLC, said easement being shown on the plan titled Drainage & Access Easement Plan on file with the Town Clerk’s Office, and further to authorize the Select Board to execute any and all instruments as may be necessary to effectuate the purposes of this article. SPONSOR: Select Board Explanation: This article asks voters if they will accept a drainage easement for such purposes to maintain existing drainage infrastructure which outlets into the Town drainage system located in Oakland Street. Page 7 of 21 Article 18: To see if the Town will vote to amend Chapter 89, Animals, of the General Bylaws, by adding the following two new definitions to section 89-1: DOMESTIC CHARITABLE CORPORATION KENNEL — A facility operated, owned or maintained by a domestic charitable corporation registered with the Department of Agricultural Resources or an animal welfare society or other nonprofit organization incorporated for the purpose of providing for and promoting the welfare, protection and humane treatment of animals, including a veterinary hospital or clinic operated by a licensed veterinarian, which operates consistent with such purposes while providing veterinary treatment and care. VETERINARY KENNEL — a veterinary hospital or clinic that boards dogs for reasons in addition to medical treatment or care; provided, however, that ''veterinary kennel'' shall not include a hospital or clinic used solely to house dogs that have undergone veterinary treatment or observation or will do so only for the period of time necessary to accomplish that veterinary care. and by amending subsections of sections 89-3, 89-5, 89-6, 89-8 and 89-13 as follows (additions show in bold and underline and deletions shown in strikethrough): § 89-3. Animal Control Officer. E. Review all dogs that have not been licensed by their owners and report findings to the Animal Welfare Committee/Animal Control OfficerTown Clerk on a monthly basis. § 89-5. Permits. A. No person, partnership, or corporation shall operate a commercial animal establishment, kennel, or animal shelter without first obtaining a permit in compliance with this section. C. A permit shall be issued by the licensing authority upon payment of the applicable fee and when a permit applicant has shown that they are willing and able to comply with the regulations promulgated by the permit granting authority and the Massachusetts Department of Agricultural Resources, and an inspection of facility has been satisfactorily completed by the Animal Control Officer and signed off by the Animal Welfare Committee/Chief of Police. F. If there is a change in ownership of a commercial animal establishment or kennel, within 30 days the new owner must have the current permit transferred to their name upon payment of a transfer fee of $10 after the Animal Control Officer has inspected the premises. G. The licensing authority shall specify on the permit the type of kennel permit and the maximum number of animals allowed in the kennel. Page 8 of 21 H. Commercial boarding or training kennels shall maintain records of individual dog licenses for all dogs in its care that are required to be licensed under § 89-4. GI. Fees. (1) Annual permits shall be issued upon payment of the applicable fee, provided, however, that in determining the amount of the license fee for a kennel, a dog under the age of 3 months shall not be counted in the number of dogs kept in a kennel: (a) Kennel authorized to house four or fewer dogs: $2550. (b) Kennel authorized to house more than four dogs but not more than 10 dogs: $5075. (c) Kennel authorized to house more than 10 dogs: $85100. (d) Pet shop: $50. (e) Riding stable: $50. (f) Grooming shop: $50. § 89-6. License and permit issuance and revocation. A.
