Williams Kathy Williams TOWN OF YARMOUTH 1146 ROUTE 28, SOUTH YARMOUTH, MASSACHUSETTS 02664-4492 Telephone (508) 398-2231, Ext. 1276, Fax (508) 398-2365 Planning Division MEMORANDUM To: Planning Board From: Kathy Williams, Town Planner Date: October 30, 2026 Subject: Potential 2027 Annual Town Meeting (ATM) Zoning Amendments As we head into the final stretch for the 2026 Special Town Meeting on November 16th, it is never too early to look at potential amendments for the 2027 ATM on April 27, 2027. This is especially true as the timelines have been moved up a bit with placeholder articles due from the Planning Board by December 18th with the Warrant closed on January 5th and executed on March 16th. With this limited timeline we can only address a few changes. Some suggestions for discussion include: 1. STATE MANDATES: a. FY 25 Budget Appropriation - Family Child Care Home and Large Family Child Care Home: Included within an FY25 annual budget appropriation was a modification to Section 3 of Chapter 40A (so-called Dover Amendment) as shown below. Family child care home and large family child care home as defined in section 1A of chapter 15D shall be an allowable use and no city or town shall prohibit or regulate such use in its zoning ordinances or by-laws. Currently, we require a Special Permit for P7A – Family Day Care Home. We will need to modify our Use Table to reflect this Use as being by-right and may need some definition modifications. b. Affordable Homes Act – Merged Lots: Zoning Bylaw Section 104.3.4 – Nonconforming Lots already allows for some provisions for merged lots. The Affordable Homes Act added the following option but includes size limitations and Short-Term Rental prohibition. Adjacent lots under common ownership shall not be treated as a single lot for local zoning purposes if, at the time of recording or endorsement, the lots: (i) conformed to then existing requirements of area, frontage, width, yard or depth, where each such lot has not less than 10,000 square feet of area and 75 feet of frontage; and (ii) are located in a zoning district that allows for single-family residential use. Any single-family residential structure constructed on said lot shall not exceed 1,850 square feet of heated living area, shall contain not less than 3 bedrooms and shall not be used as a seasonal home or short-term rental. We will need to modify Section 104.3.4 to include this additional allowance related to merged lots as well as the required restrictions. I would anticipate most property owners would try to use the least restriction mechanism that allowed for construction on a lot. Planning Board Potential 2027 ATM Amendments October 30, 2026 c. FY 27 Budget Appropriations – Miscellaneous Modifications to MGL CH 40A: Some of the changes in the attached redline edits to CH 40A are administrative (such as electronic mailing, extension of time for Variances to be exercised, and confusing timelines for zoning freezes), while others will require changes to the Zoning Bylaw, with input from Town Counsel needed to ensure compliance. • Will need to modify Section 102.2.2 related to Variances as the language has completely changed. Can simply reference the Variance criteria in MGL CH 40A, Section 10. • Will need to modify Section 104.3.1 Abandonment to extend allowance of an abandoned non-conforming use from 2 years to 4 years. • Will need to modify Section 104.3.4 - Nonconforming Lots to apply to all lots not just single or two family. Should also review the language of this entire section to see if it can be simplified. • Will need to modify Section 104.3.2 Change, Extension or Alteration to allow by-right extension or alternation of nonconforming structures or residential uses that do not conform to lot size or shape, frontage, lot coverage or floor area ratio, if such extension or alteration complies with current dimensional regulations regarding only height, stories, and setback. 2. FEMA OA ZONES: Very minor request by MA Dept of Conservation and Recreation Floodplain Management. Will need to amend Section 403.10 Recreational Vehicles in a Flood District to also reference Flood District AO. We have a very small area of AO east of Parkers River Beach. 3. VCOD MINIMUM/MAXIMUM FRONT YARD SETBACKS: At the 2026 Annual Town Meeting we allowed special permit relief related to minimum/maximum front yard setbacks to address strip takings from the MassDOT Route 28 Corridor Improvement Project. We should further evaluate modifications to the minimum/maximum front yard setbacks in VC1, VC2 and VC3 (VC2 only has a 30’ minimum). There should be a caveat related to the section of Route 28 that has an 80’ wide right-of-way (eastward of the intersection of Route 28/Old Main) where reductions in the min/max are not needed. 4. MURALS AND PUBLIC ART ON TOWN LAND: Now that the Public Art Committee is well underway, can consider modifications to the Zoning Bylaw to define a mural and allow them on town properties as governed by the Public Art Committee. This gets the issue of whether it is a sign out of the Zoning Bylaw and allows the Public Art Committee to offer their recommendations to the Select Board for murals on town properties. 5. SHORT TERM RENTALS (STR): a. STR Limitations: Continue discussions on limiting the number of STRs in the new General Bylaw while coming up with resolutions to such issues as transfers to families and inherited legacy properties. Select Board member Mark Forest suggested only allowing STRs in certain areas that are more commercial in nature and outside the more traditional residential neighborhoods. This is a much larger endeavor to evaluate all implications and not something that can be looked at for ATM. b. Economic Development Bond Bill: If mandated via the Economic Development Bond Bill, we can add in the prohibition of STRs for new as of right duplexes created from this directive. ATTACHMENTS: • Dept of Early Education and Care Notice of Change to Dover Amendment • MTC Town Counsel Advisory on FY 27 Zoning Act Amendments Page 2 of 2 The Commonwealth of Massachusetts Amy Kershaw, Commissioner NOTICE OF CHANGE TO THE DOVER AMENDMENT, M.G.L. c. 40A, § 3 As part of the FY25 enacted budget signed by Governor Healey on July 29, 2024, changes were made to the so-called Dover Amendment, M.G.L. c. 40A, § 3. The amended Section 3 reads: Section 3 of chapter 40A of the General Laws, as so appearing, is hereby amended by striking out the fifth paragraph 1 and inserting in place thereof the following paragraph:Family child care home and large family child care home as defined in section 1A of chapter 15D shall be an allowable use and no city or town shall prohibit or regulate such use in its zoning ordinances or by-laws. M.G.L. c. 40A, § 3 (emphasis added). 2 As detailed above, the Legislature has amended G.L. c. 40A, § 3 to explicitly provide that family child care homes and large family child care homes are an allowable use, which shall not be prohibited or regulated by a city or town’s zoning ordinances or by-laws. 1 The now stricken paragraph 5 of M.G.L. c. 40A, § 5 previously read: “Family child care home and large family child care home, as defined in section 1A of chapter 15D, shall be an allowable use unless a city or town prohibits or specifically regulates such use in its zoning ordinances or by-laws.” 2 FY2025 enacted budget Outside Section 76, available at https://budget.digital.mass.gov/summary/fy25/outside-section/section-76-family-childcarezoning/. ADVISORY 30 Green Street Newburyport, MA 01950 Phone 978.463.7700 Fax 978.463.7747 www.mtclawyers.com TO: TOWN MANAGERS, TOWN ADMINISTRATORS, MAYORS AND PLANNERS FROM: MEAD, TALERMAN & COSTA, LLC SUBJECT: AN ACT MAKING APPROPRIATIONS FOR FY2027 (H. 5555) ZONING ACT AMENDMENTS DATE: JULY 10, 2026 Yesterday, Governor Maura Healey signed House Bill 5555, also known as an Act Making Appropriations for Fiscal Year 2027 (the “New Law”). In addition to effectuating the FY2027 state budget, the New Law makes a variety of meaningful and consequential changes 1 to the state Zoning Act, see G.L. c. 40A, specifically Sections 5, 6, 10 and 11 thereof, relative to vested rights; the extent of protection(s) afforded pre-existing, nonconforming uses and structures; the standard by which zoning variances may be granted; and the sending of certain notices via electronic means. These Zoning Act amendments are now in-effect, per the New Law’s retroactive July 1, 2026 effective date and accompanying emergency preamble. They are summarized below; but, for convenience, the full text of Sections 5, 6, 10 and 11 of the Zoning Act is affixed hereto, with the revisions shown. 1. Vested Rights A vested right is best defined as “the right to initiate or continue the establishment of a use or construction of a structure which, when completed, will be contrary to the restrictions or regulations of a zoning ordinance [or bylaw] or an amendment to it which has become effective in the meantime.” 2 Section 6 confers vested rights, commonly referred to as zoning freezes, upon owners and applicants whose property meets certain qualifications. Before adoption of the New Law, under Paragraph 1 of Section 6 of the Zoning Act, a zoning ordinance or bylaw was said not to apply to “a building or special permit issued” before the first publication of notice of a public hearing on a new ordinance, 1 In a legislative press release issued on June 30, 2026, these changes were characterized as follows: “Building on last session’s Affordable Homes Act, the budget agreement includes numerous provisions to streamline local permitting, support development on nonconforming properties, provide reasonable timelines for projects to move forward under existing zoning rules and modernize the variance standard – all aimed at meeting housing demand, boosting production and driving down costs.” 2 Edward H. Zeigler, 4 Rathkopf’s Law of Zoning and Planning, § 70:2 (2001). bylaw or amendment thereto. The New Law replaces the quoted phrase with “a building or special permit or other entitlement applied for under this chapter.” 3 The result is two-fold. First, it is no longer only a building or special permit that vests rights under the cited clause in Paragraph 1; “other entitlement[s]” will now qualify an owner or applicant for a zoning freeze. What constitutes an entitlement is not specified in the amendment, or elsewhere in the Zoning Act, thus creating ambiguity; but the term might be interpreted to include administrative appeals (if ultimately successful), potentially site plan approvals 4 or even requests for confirmation of zoning status or applicability of a zoning exemption. Second, a building permit, special permit or, now, other entitlement no longer must be “issued” before publication of notice of a public hearing on a zoning adoption or change. Under the New Law, rights now vest upon “appli[cation]” for a building permit, special permit or other entitlement. Related to the above, prior to adoption of the New Law, and in order for an owner or applicant to successfully avoid compliance with later-enacted provision(s) or a zoning ordinance or bylaw, construction or operations under a building permit had to be commenced “within… 12 months after the issuance of the permit” and continued through to completion as continuously and expeditiously as is reasonable. The New Law not only increases the period within which work must commence under a building permit to 24 months, it also calculates the deadline from the date of issuance “of the last permit necessary for construction.” And it expressly states that “[t]he 24-month period shall be tolled during any time the applicant is actively seeking or obtaining other necessary permits.”5 Lastly, under Paragraph 4 of Section 6 of the Zoning Act, vacant lots are protected from “[a]ny increase in area, frontage, width, yard or depth requirements” of a zoning ordinance or bylaw if, as of the time of their recording or endorsement, whichever occurred first, they had qualifying area and frontage under the statute. Prior to adoption of the New Law, the protection only applied to lots “for single and two family residential use.” That is no longer. Now, the protections that Paragraph 4 affords certain lots in separate ownership and certain other lots in common ownership extend to all lots, not just lots for single and two family residential use.6 The zoning freeze for vacant lots now also applies to lots for non-residential use. 2. Expansion of Protection(s) for Certain Nonconformities The New Law also expands protection(s) for pre-existing, nonconforming uses and structures, in two ways. First, some types of changes to pre-existing, nonconforming structures or residential uses are now statutorily exempt from any requirement that they be authorized by finding (or by special permit). Before the New Law was enacted, Paragraph 1 of Section 6 of the Zoning Act, second sentence, stated only that “[p]re-existing nonconforming structures or uses may be 3 See H. 5555, § 42. 4 Although site plan review is not a process established “under this chapter,” meaning under the Zoning Act, multiple site plan review references now exist in the Zoning Act, including in Section 6 itself. 5 See H. 5555, § 45. 6 See H. 5555, § 46. extended or altered, provided that no such extension or alteration shall be permitted unless there is a finding by the permit granting authority or by the special permit granting authority… that such change, extension or alteration shall not be substantially more detrimental than the existing nonconforming use [or structure]7 to the neighborhood.” Under the New Law, “preexisting nonconforming structures or residential uses that do not conform to zoning because of lot size or shape, frontage, lot coverage or floor area ratio requirements may be extended or altered as of right… if such extension or alteration complies with the current dimensional regulations regarding height, stories and setback.” 8 Placement of the new language, above, into the second sentence of Paragraph 1 of Section 6 of the Zoning Act suggests that it applies to all pre-existing, nonconforming structures, including single- and two-family residential structures, even though these latter structures may not have historically, and may not now, require resort to the second sentence at all (if, under the first sentence’s so-called “second except clause,” alteration, reconstruction, extension or structural change is deemed “not [to] increase the nonconforming nature of said structure”). Among other examples, conforming structures on undersized or otherwise dimensionally noncompliant lots, which heretofore may have required zoning relief for extensions or alterations thereto, e.g. a finding or a special permit, 9 will no longer be subject to discretionary approval but may be modified by-right so long as the proposal complies with the ordinance’s or bylaw’s height, story and setback requirements. Note that the new language, above, does not apply to extension or alteration to or of nonresidential use(s). Even communities that prohibit the extension or alteration of all or some pre-existing, nonconforming uses or structures are probably subject to the exemption, above. While we recognize that “[w]hen [an] ordinance or bylaw does not expressly speak to such changes… the otherwise applicable regulations will govern and invariably lead to a prohibition of the change,” and that “[r]esort to the statute will not overcome local silence on the matter,” 10 the New Law’s amendment to the second sentence, above, expressly allows extensions or alterations “as of right” if its conditions are satisfied. 7 While the New Law adds the phrase “or structure,” it is of no functional effect on interpretation or application of Section 6 inasmuch as the judiciary effectively did so decades ago. See Willard v. Board of Appeals of Orleans, 25 Mass. App. Ct. 15, 21 (1987). 8 See H. 5555, § 43. 9 See, e.g., Bjorklund v. Zoning Bd. of Appeals of Norwell, 450 Mass. 357 (2008). In Bjorklund, it was the second except clause that was at-issue, not the second sentence of Paragraph 1. Nevertheless, the question before the Supreme Judicial Court was whether-or-not the proposed reconstruction of a single-family residence on an undersized lot, quintupling its size, but otherwise in compliance with the Norwell Zoning Bylaw, “increase[d] the nonconforming nature of [the] structure.” See G.L. c. 40A, § 6, ¶ 1, first sentence. The Justices concluded that it did; and thus affirmed the Norwell Zoning Board of Appeals’ conclusion to that effect, and its ensuing finding that the proposal was “substantially more detrimental… to the neighborhood.” Were Bjorklund decided today, enactment of the New Law would render the latter finding unnecessary. Since the residence in Bjorklund was nonconforming “because of lot size,” and where the proposed reconstruction “complie[d] with… dimensional regulations regarding height, stories and setback,” it would now be permissible “as of right.” 10 Mark Bobrowski, Handbook of Massachusetts Land Use and Planning Law, § 6.03[A] (6th ed. 2024). 3 Second, whereas the Zoning Act previously authorized cities … where there are 2 branches or by a vote of a simple majority of town meeting: (1) an amendment to a zoning ordinance or by-law to allow any of the following as of right: (a) multifamily housing or mixed-use development in an eligible … a detached structure on the same lot; or (c) open-space residential development; (2) an amendment to a zoning ordinance or by-law to allow by special permit: (a) multi-family housing or mixed-use development in an eligible location; (b) an … and (4) the adoption of a smart growth zoning district or starter home zoning district in accordance with section 3 of chapter 40R. Committee Reports. *Public Comment: please see attached Public Comment Policy which can also be found at https://www.nantucket-ma.gov/DocumentCenter/View/51055/Public-Comment-Policy---Adopted-bythe-Select-Board-on-February-12-2025-PDF. **New Business: Topics not reasonably anticipated by the Chair 48 hours in advance of the meeting may be brought up for discussion in accordance with the Open Meeting Law. 2 Town of Nantucket Public Comment Policy Adopted by Select Board February 12, 2025 A. Purpose: This Policy is adopted to facilitate orderly and efficient public comment periods at meetings of Town public bodies. It will protect the ability of the residents of Nantucket, and other persons, to provide feedback or information to pertinent public bodies regarding matters of public interest, Town initiatives, operations, services, and programs. To allow speakers a fair opportunity to address a public body, and to ensure the public body may accomplish its stated business in an efficient manner, these guidelines seek to ensure compliance with the Open Meeting Law and meet other legal and constitutional obligations. Meetings of public bodies in the Town of Nantucket should be places to engage in orderly and peaceable discourse. B. Authority: Principles of free speech and freedom to petition the government, fundamental rights protected by the United States and Massachusetts Constitutions, prohibit public bodies from preventing all speech that may be upsetting or offensive. As such, this Policy establishes reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions sufficient to facilitate orderly and peaceable public comment periods at meetings of elected and appointed public bodies of the Town. C. Legal Standards: Meetings of public bodies are subject to the requirements of the Open Meeting Law, G.L. c. 30A, §§ 18-25. The Open Meeting Law empowers the chair of a public body to preside at and regulate the proceedings of meetings. Pursuant to G.L c. 30A, § 20(g), no person shall address a meeting of a public body without permission of the chair, and all persons shall, at the request of the chair, be silent. Any person wishing to speak at an open meeting must first be recognized by the chair. All questions raised and all comments made by a duly-recognized speaker must be directed to the chair of the public body alone, not to individual members of the public body, staff, or the public. The chair is authorized to maintain order, and, although a rare occurrence, has authority, after appropriate warnings are ignored, to take action up to and including removal of a person who is disrupting a meeting. D. Application: To secure the rights of the public to participate in public comment periods in the Town of Nantucket in a manner consistent with law, and, to thereby protect the Town and members of elected and appointed bodies from civil rights claims, this policy shall apply to all public bodies in the Town of Nantucket. E. Procedures: 1. All agendas of multiple-member bodies in the Town of Nantucket shall include a period for Public Comment, subject to the limitations set forth in paragraph 3. Where to place Public Comment on the agenda is at the discretion of the chair. If public comment is invited during a separate agenda item, this Policy shall govern. 2. While statements made during a Public Comment period are not required to address an agenda item for that particular meeting, such comments must relate to a matter within the public body’s jurisdiction. Public comments on matters outside the public body’s jurisdiction may be ruled out of order by the chair. To avoid due process issues, a person seeking to provide comments on a matter appearing on the same agenda will be asked to defer until the specific agenda item is reached. 3. Each speaker will be allowed to speak once for up to 3 minutes. The chair will curtail verbal comments exceeding the allotted time. 4. A recognized speaker may not cede or assign their time to another unless such an assignment is required as reasonable accommodation for such person because of a disability. All speakers who may need an accommodation are strongly encouraged to contact Town staff or the chair of the public body at least 48 hours prior to the meeting. That said, to facilitate an efficient public comment period, groups that have multiple speakers with the same viewpoint may consider consolidating their comments or designating one person to speak on their individual behalf’s. F. Disruptive Conduct/Unprotected Speech: Disruptive conduct and engaging in other unprotected speech, including but not limited to the following, may be grounds for the chair of a public body to curtail speech and take other action as appropriate: 1. Speaking without being recognized; 2. Continuing to speak after the chair has curtailed additional verbal comment; 3. Interrupting a recognized speaker; 4. Speaking about matters not within the jurisdiction of the public body; 5. Engaging in conversations while another person is speaking; 6. Making true threats of violence directed toward a particular individual; and 7. Making comments inciting imminent lawlessness. G. Public Body Response: 1. A public comment period is a listening session, and the public body is there to listen. The public body, in fact, should not respond to matters raised at the meeting unless they are on the agenda for the same meeting. 2. Matters raised during public comment periods are not required to, and are unlikely to, be addressed or resolved by the public body at the same meeting. Such matters may be appropriately deferred to a noticed-agenda item at a future meeting due to Open Meeting Law considerations. 3. At the sole discretion of the chair of the public body, matters raised during public comment may or may not appear on a future agenda or be referred to the Town Administrator for appropriate action, if any. 4. A public body cannot demand that persons attending meetings or participating in public comment be civil to one another. Nevertheless, the Town, or the members of the public, and those that appear before them are encouraged to make any/or all residents of the Town feel welcome, including listening to them speak, and acknowledging that speakers may have a different viewpoints. Disclaimer: A Public Comment period is not a time for debate or response to comments by the public body. Comments made during the Public Comment period do not reflect the views or the positions of the public body. Because of constitutional free speech principles, the public body does not have the authority to prevent all speech that may be upsetting and/or offensive during the public portion of the meeting. H. Enforcement: Concerns about Public Comment Periods may be brought to the attention of the Town Manager, who will discuss the concerns with the chair of the public body, and take appropriate action. Failure to comply with this Policy may be deemed a violation of the Town’s Code of Conduct, and grounds for the removal of an appointed official. text: FITCHBURG CITY CLERK Nov 02 2026 1:50 pm WELCOME TO THE FITCHBURG CITY COUNCIL November 4, 2026 Fitchburg Legislative Building 700 Main Street Fitchburg MA 01420 7:00 PM This meeting can also be viewed live on FATV. Go to www.fatv.org/watch-fatv for more information on accessing this meeting. This is intended to help you understand the meeting format and assist you with the rules of the Council as they pertain to your participation. All meetings of the Fitchburg City council are open to the public. This does not mean that the public participates in all aspects of the meeting. It simply means that the meeting itself, including all discussions and votes, is open for public view. Executive Session The only time a Council meeting can be closed to the public is when the Council votes for Executive Session in order to discuss sensitive matters in private, such as pending litigation. Any votes taken however, must be taken in open session. OPPORTUNITIES FOR THE PUBLIC TO SPEAK DURING A COUNCIL MEETING: Public Forum The Public Forum occurs immediately following the Pledge of Allegiance. The President will ask if anyone in the audience wishes to speak on any matter appearing on the Agenda. If you wish to address the Council, you must stand and be recognized and follow these rules before speaking: 1. 2. 3. 4. State your name and city of residence. Approach the center table and either stand or sit. This allows you to be seen and heard clearly by everyone in attendance. You may speak only on items appearing on the agenda for no more than (2) minutes. Copies of the agenda are available on the center table prior to the meeting. Please state the petition, order, ordinance, or resolution number to which you refer. Public Hearings Public hearings are held on various issues such as Special Permits and Zoning changes. The same rules apply with the following exceptions: 1. You must stand and be recognized either “in favor” or “in opposition” when asked by the Council President. 2. You need not refer to the petition number. If you have any questions or comments either before or after the meeting, any Councilor would be happy to assist you. Thank you for your interest! I. title: Packet
text: RURAL DEVELOPMENT, INC. 241 Millers Falls Road · Turners Falls, MA 01376 Telephone: (413) 863-9781 · Fax (413) 863-9289 October 6, 2026 Jeff Sauser, Chair George Touloumtzis, Vice Chair Planning Board City of Greenfield 14 Court Square Greenfield, MA 01301 RE: Site Plan Approval Extension Request for Rural Development, Inc.’s 176 Main Street Project Chair Sauser, Vice Chair Touloumtzis, members of the Board: Rural Development, Inc., (RDI), a non-profit affordable housing developer based in Montague, MA, requests an extension to the January 2, 2025, site plan approval of its 176 Main Street affordable housing development project. Under Section 200-8.4H of the City of Greenfield Zoning Ordinance, “Site plan approval issued under this section shall expire within two (2) years if a substantial use thereof has not commenced except for good cause.” This memo provides a timeline of progress made by RDI since the January 2, 2025, approval, and supports the argument that the delay in initiating substantial use has been for good cause. Funding Applications: The project is a 100% affordable housing development, serving households with incomes ranging from under 30% of Area Median Income (AMI) up to 80% AMI. The process of obtaining funding for affordable housing development in Massachusetts is extremely competitive and complex and typically takes several years. For the project to pencil out financially, multiple funding sources are needed, each with different application timeframes. It is typical for projects to submit applications to multiple funding rounds, especially for State funds and Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) allocations from the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (EOHLC). Funding is also needed for predevelopment, and the rate at which we can obtain loan increases or grants to pay for predevelopment work impacts how quickly we can progress Equal Housing Opportunity plans to a level that is competitive for construction financing. Throughout the process RDI has diligently pursued funding for both predevelopment and construction of the project. Predevelopment Funding Applications: Prior to site plan approval, we obtained an initial predevelopment loan through the Community Economic Development Assistance Corporation (CEDAC), a $100,000 MassDevelopment Site Readiness grant, and a $50,000 CPA grant from the City of Greenfield. The following are applications submitted since January 2, 2025, to continue to cover permitting, design, engineering, legal, environmental, and other project costs during predevelopment: Funding Source CEDAC City of Greenfield CPA CEDAC Application Loan Increase Request July 2025 November 2025 Loan Increase Request March 2026 Approval October 2025 June 2026 May 2026 Construction Funding Sources: The following applications were submitted to pay for the construction of the project. Funding rounds are held once or twice per year, depending on the source: Funding Source Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (EOHLC) 2025 Rental Funding Round Executive Office of Energy & Environmental Affairs (EEA) Municipal Vulnerability Preparedness (MVP) MassDevelopment Site Readiness Community One Stop Federal Home Loan Bank of Boston (FHLB) Affordable Housing Program EOHLC 2025 High Readiness Rental Funding Round MassDevelopment Site Readiness Community One Stop *LIHTC = Low Income Housing Tax Credits Application Approval / Award February 2025 No award April 2025 No award June 2025 No award July 2025 October 2025 June 2026 April 2026 / $850,000 February 2026 / $4.7M State funds, $14.3M LIHTC* October 2026 / $450,000 Permitting / Approvals: Historic Approval: RDI met with the Greenfield Historical Commission (GHC) on April 3, 2025, to review updated architectural plans for the buildings which incorporated feedback previously provided by the GHC. Based on that meeting, a cornice detail was added to the 4-story building on Main Street, which was reviewed at the May 1, 2025, GHC meeting. On June 3, 2025, the GHC issued a letter to the Massachusetts Historical Commission expressing support for the project. Site Plan Updates: In October 2025, RDI submitted updates to the site plan and met with the Planning Director, Eric Twarog, to review. The primary update was the incorporation of the city-owned 188 Main Street parcel into the plan set. RDI responded to a Request for Proposal in January 2025 and was selected in February 2025 by the City to acquire the parcel. The updates were incorporated into the project file. The executed Development Agreement and Purchase and Sale Agreement between the City and RDI are included in the Site Plan extension application as an attachment. Approval Not Required: RDI submitted an Approval Not Required application to separate the 156 Main Street parcel, which will remain under the ownership of Franklin and Main LLC, from the rest of the project site, which will be acquired by RDI. The Greenfield Planning Board endorsed the ANR at a meeting on December 4, 2025. M.G.L. Ch.54A Process: The project abuts the CT River Main Line railroad tracks and contains land that formerly was owned by the railroad, so must go through a review with Mass DOT and railroad stakeholders prior to being issued a building permit. This is also a condition of the January 2, 2025, site plan approval. RDI met with Mass DOT in May 2026 for a preliminary review of the plans. On August 13, 2026, RDI and the project team met with the Greenfield Building Commissioner Mark Snow, and Greenfield Planning Director, Ella Wise, to provide updates on the project including the Mass DOT process. Commissioner Mark Snow subsequently issued a letter required as part of the application to Mass DOT. RDI’s team is currently working on updating the plans based on prior Mass DOT input and structural analysis of the site. We anticipate submitting our full application to Mass DOT by the end of October 2026 to initiate the review. NEPA Environmental Review: The project will need operating subsidy in the form of Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers, a federally funded program through HUD. An Environmental Review under the National Environmental Protection Act (NEPA) is required for projects using federal funds. The City of Greenfield, through its Community and Economic Development Department, is currently working with EOHLC to complete the Environmental Review. Community Outreach/ Public Meetings: We met with the following groups to gather input on the project: • • • • • • December 17, 2024: Greenfield Parking and Traffic Commission April 10, 2025: Greenfield Disability Access Commission May 19, 2025: Greenfield Business Association Downtown Property Owners Cohort June 2, 2025: Community Information Session at the John Zon Community Center June 17, 2025: LifePath Age and Dementia Friendly Task Force Housing Greenfield advocacy group – multiple meetings beginning in 2024 Anticipated Timeline: Currently the project is funded, and we are working towards acquiring the property, finalizing building plans, obtaining permits, and starting on site preparations for construction. Our anticipated timeframe moving forward is as follows: • • • • • February 2027: Acquisition of 176 Main Street, rear parking lot, and 188 Main Street parcels. This timeframe allows the current commercial tenants to remain through the holiday season. March 2027: Demolition of the existing building and soils assessment using the MassDevelopment Site Readiness funds and MassDevelopment Brownfields program. June 2027: Construction financing closing, start construction October 2028: Construction complete, begin lease up March 2029: 100% leased up We continue to diligently work towards bringing this investment of over $23M in public and private funds to Greenfield, helping to meet the urgent need for housing and building upon the work of the City and the community to revitalize the downtown. Based on the information provided, we respectfully request an extension to the site plan approval of January 2, 2025, for good cause. (9:15) Select Board Minutes Tuesday, September 29, 2026 7:00pm A regular meeting of the Select Board (the “Board”) of the Town of Harvard (the “Town”) was held virtually on Tuesday, September 29, 2026 in accordance with Chapter 2 of the Acts of 2025, An Act extending certain Covid-19 measures adopted during the state of emergency and signed into law on March 28, 2025. Select Board Participants: Ahmet Corapcioglu, Vice-Chair; Kara McGuire Minar; Eve Wittenberg; Eric Ward. Absent: SusanMary Redinger. Town Department Participants: Dawn Dunbar, Town Administrator; Julie Doucet, Assistant Town Administrator/Human Resources Director; Michelle Stockman, Executive Assistant to the Town Administrator. Additional Participants: Andres Correa, Energy Manager; Ellen Sachs Leicher, Harvard Climate Initiative Committee Chair and Harvard Energy Advisory Committee Member. A quorum was declared and the meeting was called to order by Vice-Chair Ahmet Corapcioglu at 7:00pm. Michelle Stockman kept the minutes of the meeting. The Vice-Chair opened the meeting to public communication, and there being no questions, comments, or concerns, proceeded to business matters. The upcoming Department of Public Works (“DPW”) information sessions, scheduled to be held on October 5 and October 8, were previewed. Prior Meeting Minutes Vice-Chair Corapcioglu asked whether the Board had any comments concerning the prior meeting minutes from September 1, 20261 and September 15, 20262 distributed and revised in advance of the meeting. There being no questions or concerns, Vice-Chair Corapcioglu declared them approved as revised. Appointments & Resignations In recognition of their service to the Agricultural Advisory Commission, the Board thanked Christiane Turnheim following their resignation on September 18, 2026.3 The Board also extended its gratitude to Rainer Park, who resigned from the Bare Hill Pond Watershed Management Committee on September 8, 2026.4 Next, a motion was made by Eve Wittenberg and seconded by Kara McGuire Minar to appoint Jo-Anne Crystoff, previously an alternate, as a regular member Select Board Meeting Minutes – September 29, 2026 1 of the Bare Hill Pond Watershed Management Committee.5 By a roll call vote, Wittenberg – aye, Minar – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was then made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to re-appoint Jim Lee as the Harvard Conservation Trust’s representative on the Open Space Committee.6 By a roll call vote, Ward – aye, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Following their resignation on September 19, 2026, the Board thanked Seth Trotz for their service to the Warner Free Lecture Trustees.7 It was noted that, although this was an elected position, the Board was able to appoint someone to fill the vacancy until the next election. The Chair of the Warner Free Lecture Trustees was working to identify such a candidate. For those interested in volunteering, Vice-Chair Corapcioglu highlighted the board and committee vacancies available, which could be viewed on the Town’s website. Amendment to One-Day License: Harvard Alpaca Ranch A motion was made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to amend the Harvard Alpaca Ranch’s one-day liquor license, changing the event date from September 26 to October 11, due to inclement weather.8 By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Energy Manager Report At the invitation of the Board, Energy Manager Andres Correa presented a year-one report on his work across four towns: Groton, Harvard, Ayer, and Shirley.9 The position was funded by a Mass Save Municipal Energy Management Grant, sponsored by National Grid, for which the four towns applied jointly with support from the school district, Groton Sustainability Commission, and Harvard Climate Initiative Committee. Mr. Correa highlighted grant awards totaling $734,851 in funding and an estimated annual savings of $60,286. Harvard, specifically, was awarded a $201,851 grant to fund the library’s heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (“HVAC”) system’s coil retrofit and replacement of equipment. The Board and Harvard Climate Initiative Committee Chair Ellen Sachs Leicher commended Mr. Correa on his strong contributions. They also expressed interest in continuing the position beyond the current three-year period. Local Action Unit Application for Emerson Green Project Speaking on behalf of the Municipal Affordable Housing Trust, Ms. Wittenberg provided an update on the Emerson Green affordable housing project, explaining that twelve units would be designated as local action units (each, an “LAU”) at 80% area median income, representing 25% of the total number of units in the development and helping the Town meet its affordable housing goals. Ms. Wittenberg summarized the Town’s application to the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (the “EOHLC”), which required the Board’s approval and signature.10 If the application was approved and the units deemed compliant, all 46 units would be included in the Town’s subsidized housing inventory and available to qualifying residents. A discussion ensued regarding the housing production timeline and plan. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Ms. Minar to approve the Town’s LAU application to the EOHLC, and that the Chair or Vice-Chair of the Board be authorized to sign it. By a roll call vote, Ward – aye, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Finalization of Special Town Meeting Warrant Vice-Chair Corapcioglu invited comments on the nine articles of the Special Town Meeting warrant (the “warrant”), distributed in advance of the meeting.11 There were no questions or concerns. It was noted that the Finance Committee would submit its recommendations separately. A motion was made by Ms. Minar Select Board Meeting Minutes – September 29, 2026 2 and seconded by Mr. Ward to close the warrant. By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Ward – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. The Board then proceeded to review and vote upon recommendations for each warrant article in turn. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Ms. Minar to recommend Article 1 to pay bills of prior fiscal years. By a roll call vote, Wittenberg – aye, Minar – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Mr. Ward to recommend Article 2 regarding the payment of $14,934 to cover the school ESSER grant deficit. By a roll call vote, Ward – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Minar – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Ms. Minar to recommend Article 3 to approve the Capital Planning and Investment Committee’s recommended expenditure for the acquisition of a police cruiser and water meters. It was clarified that the proposed police cruiser was a hybrid vehicle. By a roll call vote, Wittenberg – aye, Minar – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Ms. Minar to recommend Article 4 to amend Chapter 78 of the Town’s code, as proposed by the Personnel Board. By a roll call vote, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Minar – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to recommend Article 5 to replace Section 125-53 of the Town’s Bylaws with a new Clean Energy Facilities bylaw, as proposed by the Planning Board with consideration of resident feedback. It was clarified that this would align the Town’s solar bylaws with new State regulations. By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to recommend Article 6 to amend Chapter 125 of the Town’s Bylaws to conform with Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 40A as proposed by the Planning Board. Town Administrator Dawn Dunbar confirmed that the Planning Board had closed its hearing the previous night and that Town counsel had reviewed the final draft. By a roll call vote, Ward – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Minar – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to recommend Article 7 to reorganize Chapter 125 of the Town’s Bylaws pertaining to use regulations, as proposed by the Planning Board. By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 40. A motion was made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to recommend Article 8 to reorganize Chapter 125 of the Town’s Bylaws pertaining to dimensional regulations, as proposed by the Planning Board. By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Ms. Minar to recommend Article 9 to revise Section 125-60 of the Town’s Bylaws regarding the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority Communities Multi-Family Overlay District, as proposed by the Planning Board. By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Select Board Meeting Minutes – September 29, 2026 3 Before proceeding, the Board discussed next steps, which included preparing the motions and assigning responsibilities for the Special Town Meeting on October 20. Fiscal Year 2028 (“FY28”) Budget Guidance Eric Ward led the Board in a review of a draft memorandum (“memo”) outlining the FY28 budget guidance discussed at the September 22 meeting. The memo outlined the budget target and standards, submission guidelines, and revenue opportunities. Budget proposals would be due to the Board by November 30. A motion was made by Ms. Minar and seconded by Ms. Wittenberg to approve and distribute the FY28 budget guidance. By a roll call vote, Minar – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Ward – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. Position Letter re: H.5175/S.3166 Vice-Chair Corapcioglu presented a letter to Senator James Eldridge and Representative Danillo Sena concerning the Energy Affordability Conference Committee’s reconciliation of H.5175 and S.3166.12 The letter supported the Legislature’s goals of reducing energy costs and decarbonizing buildings, and asked that the final bill preserve municipal authority in implementing clean-energy policy, including protections for Mass Save funding and competitive energy supplier contracts. A motion was made by Ms. Wittenberg and seconded by Mr. Ward to approve the position letter as written and authorize either the Chair or Vice-Chair of the Board to sign it. By a roll call vote, Ward – aye, Wittenberg – aye, Minar – aye, Corapcioglu – aye, the motion carried unanimously, 4-0. All Boards Meeting Scheduling The Board addressed scheduling challenges and considered several dates for the upcoming Select Board and All Boards meetings due to conflicts with the Special Town Meeting, State election, and Veterans Day. The Board deferred the decision to its next meeting. Town Administrator Report (Attachment A) At the invitation of the Board, Ms. Dunbar delivered a Town Administrator Report. Project updates included: a pre-construction meeting on October 5 regarding the Ayer Road Transportation Improvement Program project; and the addition of a firebox to bring the Harvard/Devens Water System Interconnection Pump Station into compliance with safety requirements. With respect to personnel, Ms. Dunbar announced that Colin Hayes had been hired as an Equipment Operator/Mechanic for the DPW, effective September 29. Ms. Dunbar then reported on weekly meetings with NextGen, the Shirley Town Administrator, and the Ayer Town Manager, regarding the re-scoped budget for a $1M Municipal Vulnerability Preparedness Action Grant. Select Board Reports Mr. Ward noted upcoming Personnel Board meetings to discuss the annual cost-of-living adjustment. He reported that the School Committee was re-examining elements of the HVAC project while the Charter Review Committee continued its review work. Ms. Wittenberg reported on behalf of the Municipal Affordable Housing Trust, Conservation Commission, Open Space Committee, Tree Warden, and Agricultural Advisory Commission. The Affordable Housing Trust’s highlights included: a Habitat for Humanity Critical Repair Program information session to be held on October 13 in collaboration with the Council on Aging; and a housing development project awarded by MassDevelopment to Metro West Collaborative Developers for 65 affordable units at Adams Circle. The Conservation Commission planned to discuss the annual Bare Hill Pond drawdown further before making its Select Board Meeting Minutes – September 29, 2026 4 decision. The Tree Warden was developing a memorandum of understanding with the schools regarding responsibility for trees on school property. Ms. Wittenberg highlighted the Agricultural Advisory Commission’s need for new members. Ms. Minar reported that the Town Common flag, damaged in the recent storm, needed to be replaced. She also noted that funding for the Fivesparks grant through Senator Eldridge’s office remained pending due to unresolved budget matters. On behalf of the Park and Recreation Committee, Ms. Minar updated the Board on plans to reseed the field at Harvard Park. On behalf of the Community Media Access Committee, Vice-Chair Corapcioglu reported a successful open house following an expedited inspection of the new Harvard Media Cooperative production studio located at the school. Public Communication The meeting was opened to public communication. There being no questions, comments, or concerns, the Board briefly previewed the next meeting’s agenda. Not to reconvene in open session. Vil. ADJOURNMENT Rules of Procedure for Board Meetings of Lanesborough Select Board Meetings L IL. A. B. AGENDA The Town Administrative Assistant, in consultation with the Town Administrator and Chairman of the Select Board shall prepare an Agenda for the Select Board meetings. Any requests for matters to be placed on the agenda shall be submitted in writing to the Town Administrative Assistant by noon three business days prior to regularly scheduled meetings. Anyone requesting items be placed on the agenda shall provide the topic of the item and sufficient information and detail so as to provide a reasonable notice of the nature and purpose of the agenda item. Agendas will be posted a minimum of 48 hours in advance of any meeting on our Town website and Town bulletin board. Those wishing to speak in the public comment portion of the agenda shall provide their name and the topic of their comment. Topics shall be limited to matters of concem, official action or deliberation which are or may be before the Select Board. MEETINGS Public Notice of the meetings shall be advertised and posted by the Administrative Assistant as required by law. The Chairman of the Select Board shall direct the meeting. In the absence of the Chairman, the senior member of the Select Board shall direct the meeting and shall have all powers and duties of the Chairman. Ow > The Modern Rules of Order shall be used to conduct the meeting unless otherwise modified by these Rules or altered by the Select Board. The Lanesborough Select Board shall be addressed by their respective titles. Residents and/or taxpayers may use audio or stenographic recorders to record all or any portion of the meeting. Said recorders shall be operated froin the area set aside for the general public seating and may not be placed on the Select Board’s table without prior consent of the Chairman. © Video recorders may be used to record all or any portion of a public meeting. The operator of the recorder shall remain seated in the area set aside for the general public or stand in the rear or to the side of the general public seating area so as to not interfere in any way with the activities of the Select Board or the ability of the general public to observe the Board. PUBLIC COMMENT Residents and taxpayers of Lanesborough shall have the right to speak in the meetings during the Public Comment portion of the agenda. In order to conduct meetings in an orderly and productive manner the following rules and regulations shall govern such speakers: Comment from residents/taxpayers shall be received only after the speaker is recognized by the Chairman. The speaker shall announce his or her name and address prior to addressing the Select Board. The Chairman may rule out-of-order scandalous, impertinent, irrelevant, and redundant comments, or comments that attempt to disrupt or needlessly protract the proceedings of the meeting. The Chairman may request any individual to leave the meeting and may contact security to that end when that individual does not observe reasonable decorum. Further, the Chairman may request the assistance of law enforcement officers to remove a disorderly person when his/her conduct interferes with the orderly progress of the meeting. The Chairman may call a recess or adjournment to another time when the lack of public decorum interferes with the orderly conduct of the meeting. The Chairman may allocate available time among individuals wishing to comment. Time allocated for the public comment period at each meeting shall not exceed thirty (30) minutes and limited to citizens of Lanesborough unless prior approval is granted by the Lanesborough Select Board. Each speaker will be allotted three (3) minutes to present his or her topic. Said time limitations may be altered or waived at the Chairman’s direction. At the discretion of the Chairman conducting the meeting, a group of citizens registered to address the Select Board on the same issue may be required to designate a spokesperson.

text: RECEIVED AT CITY CLERK'S OFFICE By: X TML Date: November 05, 2026 MK Time: Novermber 10, 2026 CITY COUNCIL MEETING MATERIALS PS 2:30 PM RECEIVED AT CITY CLERK'S OFFICE Peter J. Oleskiewicz 69 Main Street #202 North Adams, MA 01247 By Tina Marie Leonesio Date:11/3/2026 EMAIL Time: 11:59 AM November 1, 2026 Dear Honorable Members of the City Council: I am writing to respectfully express my interest in being considered for appointment to the vacant seat on the North Adams City Council. As you know, I previously had the privilege of serving on the City Council for five years, having initially been appointed through the convention process. During my tenure, I served on several committees, including Public Services, Public Safety, and General Government. These experiences gave me valuable insight into our city's operations, the challenges we face, and the importance of thoughtful decision-making, collaboration, and responsible leadership. My commitment to public service has continued beyond my time on the Council. I currently serve on the Hoosac Water Quality District and the North Adams Planning Board, where I remain actively involved in matters that directly impact our community and its future. As a lifelong resident of North Adams, I care deeply about our city, its residents, and its continued success. North Adams is my home, and I take great pride in being part of this community. I have always believed that public service is about more than attending meetings and making decisions. It is about listening to people, understanding their concerns, working together to find solutions, and making a positive difference in the lives of those we represent. I truly miss being part of the City Council and having the opportunity to contribute directly to the progress of our city. Most importantly, I miss the opportunity to help people and be a voice for the residents of North Adams. I believe my previous Council experience, continued involvement in city government, and genuine dedication to our community would allow me to step into this role and make an immediate, meaningful contribution. I would be honored to serve the residents of North Adams once again and respectfully ask for your consideration and support in filling this vacancy. Thank you for your time, consideration, and continued service to our city. Respectfully submitted, Peter J. RECEIVED AT CITY CLERK'S OFFICE By Tina Marie Leonesio Date: Time: City of North Adams In City Council POSTED: November 4, 2026 Council Order Number: 12,572 X November 04, 2026 4:30 PM An Ordinance to Amend the Revised Ordinances of the City of North Adams, Chapter 21 Streets and Sidewalks, Sections 21-25, 21-25.1 and 21-25.2 for Wheeled Vehicle use on Public Ways. In City Council on October 27, 2026 A Motion by Councilor Lisa Blackmer, seconded by Councilor Bryan Sapienza, VOTED by Yea/Nay vote to Pass to a Second Reading and Publish as a Municipal Bulletin as required by Law. (9) Yea’s; Councilors Blackmer, Bona, Breen, Fitch, MacDonald, McCarron, Sapienza, Shade, and Zavatsky; (0) Nays; (0) Abstain. Attest, Ashley Shade, President City Council Tina Marie Leonesio, City Clerk PLEASE DO NOT REMOVE POSTING If you would like a copy, PLEASE SEE: Tina Marie Leonesio, City Clerk City of North Adams In City Council ___ ___ Ordained: Date: November 10, 2026 BE IT ORDAINED by the City Council of the City of North Adams as follows: An Ordinance to amend the Ordinance Chapter 21, Sections 21-25 entitled “Bicycle riding roller skating, in-line skating and skateboarding on sidewalks” Section 21-25.1 entitled “Roller skating, in-line skating and skateboarding in the Business District. Section 21-25.2 entitled “Shopping Carts” Delete Sections 21-25, 21-25.1, and 21.25.2 in their entirety and replace with the following: Sec. 21-25. Wheeled vehicle riding or use on sidewalks or public rights of way. 21-25.1.0. Definitions a.) Wheeled vehicle – A vehicle of pleasure, burden, or transportation, self powered or manually powered, equipped with wheels, not classified as motor vehicle in MGL. b.) Mobility Vehicle – A transportation device used by individuals with disabilities to gain or assist with mobility as defined by the Americans with Disabilities Act. c.) Electric bicycle, a bicycle or tricycle equipped with fully operable pedals and an electric motor, capable of speeds in excess of 20MPH. Specific classes of electric bicycles are described in Section 21-25.1.0.c.1 through 21-25.1.0.c.3. 1.) Class 1 Electric bicycle, an electric bicycle or tricycle equipped with a motor that provides assistance only when the rider is pedaling and that ceases to 1|Page City of North Adams In City Council provide assistance when the bicycle reaches the speed of 20 miles per hour. In accordance with MGL Chapter 90, Section 1 “Definitions” 2.) Class 2 electric bicycle, an electric bicycle or tricycle equipped with a motor that may be used exclusively to propel the bicycle and that is not capable of providing assistance when the bicycle reaches the speed of 20 miles per hour, in accordance with MGL Chapter 90, Section 1 “Definitions” 3.) Unclassified Electric Bicycle Exceeding Class 1 or Class 2 – any electric bicycle or tricycle equipped with a motor that is capable of speeds in excess of 28MPH. d.) Motorized scooter'', any 2 wheeled tandem or 3 wheeled device, that has handlebars, designed to be stood or sat upon by the operator, powered by an electric or gas powered motor that is capable of propelling the device with or without human propulsion. The definition of ''motorized scooter'' shall not include a motorcycle, electric bicycle or motorized bicycle or a 3 wheeled motorized wheelchair. e.) Public Thoroughfare – Any Publicly owned way or path that allows public passage. This includes streets and roads, walking paths, sidewalks, or other public right-of-ways. f.) Shared-Use Path or Trail – A public thoroughfare primarily designed for use by both pedestrians and bicycles. 21-25.1.1. Prohibition of vehicles on Sidewalks No person shall drive, wheel, or propel, any wheeled vehicle of pleasure upon or along any sidewalk or prohibited public right of way, except for the purpose of crossing such sidewalk or right of way to access property or buildings. If any such vehicle must be transported along a sidewalk to access the road or other area, it must be dismounted and pushed or carried by hand to such location as necessary and not ridden in any way. This prohibition does not apply to vehicles, exempted in Section 21-25.1.2. 2|Page City of North Adams In City Council 21-25.1.2 Exemptions to prohibition of vehicles on sidewalks The prohibitions of Section 21-25.1.1 do not apply to mobility vehicles, strollers and carriages, or hand powered vehicles of burden, such as wagons, personal shopping carts, or any other hand powered vehicle designed to carry goods or materials. Nor does this section apply to police officers or public safety officials on bicycles when engaged in the lawful performance of their duties. 21-25.1.3. Prohibition of wheeled vehicles on public thoroughfares during special events. No person shall drive, wheel, or propel any wheeled vehicle during designated special events, on public ways closed off to normal traffic or any other right of way when it is closed off to normal traffic for purposes of demonstrations or shows, unless such vehicle is part of the demonstration. If any vehicle that is not part of the event, must be transported through such a designated area, it must be dismounted, pushed, or carried through the area. This prohibition does not apply to exempted vehicles as described in Section 21-25.1.2. 21-25.1.4 Operation of wheeled vehicles on public roadways. Operation of wheeled vehicles on public road ways shall be in accordance with all state and local traffic ordinances. This includes the observance of traffic signs, signals, and pavement markings. 21-25.1.5 Operation of wheeled vehicles in crosswalks. No person shall ride any wheeled vehicle through a crosswalk. If it is necessary to use a crosswalk with such vehicles, the vehicle must be dis-mounted and pushed by hand through the 3|Page City of North Adams In City Council crosswalk. Wheeled vehicles as described in Section 21-25.1.2 are exempt from the prohibitions in this section and are considered the same as pedestrians. 21-25.1.6 Operation of wheeled vehicles on pedestrian bridges. No person shall ride any wheeled vehicle on any bridge for pedestrian use except wheeled vehicles exempted in Section 21-25.1.2. If a wheeled vehicle must use a pedestrian bridge, it must be dismounted and propelled by hand across the bridge. Pedestrians shall have the right of way, on any such bridge. 21-25.1.7 Use of Motorized vehicles on shared-use paths or trails. No motorized vehicles may be used on shared-use paths or trails, with the exception of Class 1 electric bicycles and motorized mobility vehicles as described in Section 21-25.1.2, unless otherwise posted. Speed of any vehicle on such trails or paths shall not exceed 15MPH. 21-25.1.8. Helmets, use of MGL Chapter 85, Section 11B1/2 Requires any person 16 years of age or younger operating in line skates, a skate board, a scooter or other manually-propelled wheeled vehicle or riding as a passenger on any such manually-propelled vehicle on a public way, bicycle path or on any other public right-of-way shall wear a helmet. Such helmet shall fit the person's head and be secured by straps at all times while operating in line skates, scooters, skate board or other manually-propelled wheeled vehicle and shall meet the standards for helmets established by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI Z 90.4) or subsequent standards or the Snell Memorial Foundation's 1984 standard for use in bicycling or subsequent standards. A violation of this section shall not be used as evidence of contributory negligence in a civil action. a). Helmets are required by persons of all ages while riding a vehicle described in 4|Page City of North Adams In City Council Section 21-25.1.0.a while riding on any public thoroughfare in the City of North Adams. This shall include passengers on any such vehicle designed to carry a passenger. 21-25.1.9. Prohibition of wheeled vehicles where posted. Operation of wheeled vehicles shall be prohibited, where posted by sign or ordinance. 21-25.1.10. Safe use of wheeled vehicles on public thoroughfares. Operation of all wheeled vehicles shall be in accordance with applicable MGL and local ordinances. This includes whether or not the vehicle is designed to carry a passenger. 21-25.1.11 Unsafe operation of wheeled vehicles. Persons observed to be operating any wheeled vehicle in an unsafe manner, or to be found in violation of this section, shall be issued a citation and may be subject to penalties as described in Section 21-25.1.11. MGL Chapter 85, Section 11e permits the citation to be issued to the parent or guardian of the operator, if the operator of such vehicle is under age 18. 21-25.1.12 Penalties Violators of this section shall be subject to one or more of the following penalties: a.) Fines in accordance with MGL Chapter 90, Section 1e as stated in Appendix D-8. b.) Confiscation of vehicle for a period of no less than 24 hours nor greater than 48 hours from the time of the infraction. 21-25.2. Shopping Carts 5|Page City of North Adams In City Council Store owned shopping carts are not permitted on any street, sidewalk, or public right of way and shall not be removed from the cart owner's property. This prohibition does not apply to personally owned shopping carts used to transport goods from store to home. This prohibition does not apply to personally owned baskets or carts attached to mobility vehicles. 21-25.2.1. Removal of shopping carts from sidewalks. Owners of commercial shopping carts must remove and retrieve shopping carts from public sidewalks or other public rights of way within 24 hours of a complaint by police or citizen reporting such abandoned carts. Carts not picked up by the owner shall be removed by the Public Works Department and disposed of accordingly. The Public Works Department shall not be responsible for returning said carts to store owners. 6|Page Date: ___October 27, 2026___ BE IT ORDAINED by the City Council of the City of North Adams as follows: Chapter 2.22 Remove “Reserved”. Insert Title as 2.22: North Adams Safeguards for Artificial Intelligence, Fairness & Equity (S.A.F.E. AI) Insert Sections in full as follows: SECTION 2.22.1. AUTHORITY AND SHORT TITLE This Ordinance shall be known and may be cited as the “NA S.A.F.E. AI Ordinance,” which stands for “North Adams Safeguards for Artificial Intelligence, Fairness & Equity Ordinance.” This Ordinance governs the municipal acquisition, deployment, and use of Artificial Intelligence systems by the City of North Adams and its departments. SECTION 2.22.2. PURPOSE, FINDINGS, AND CONSTITUTIONAL SAFEGUARDS The City Council finds that Artificial Intelligence technologies are rapidly transforming government operations, local economies, and civic life. Municipal adoption of AI must safeguard constitutional rights, civil liberties, and equal protection under the law. The purpose of this Ordinance is to establish safeguards governing municipal AI use; protect civil liberties, due process, privacy, and equal protection; prevent unlawful discrimination and automated harm; promote transparency and democratic accountability; ensure responsible innovation that strengthens the City of North Adams; and align municipal AI governance with constitutional principles and ethical public administration. The City affirms that technological efficiency shall not supersede individual dignity. SECTION 2.22.3. DEFINITIONS AI Audit: A documented review of a High-Risk AI System’s operation, accuracy, reliability, disparate impact, human overrides, data practices, security controls, compliance with this Ordinance, and material changes since the prior review. Algorithmic Impact Assessment: A documented evaluation of a proposed AI System that identifies its intended purpose, affected populations, data sources, decision-making role, foreseeable risks, accuracy and reliability concerns, potential discriminatory or disparate impacts, privacy and security risks, human oversight mechanisms, vendor obligations, and available mitigation measures. 1 | Page Anonymized Data: Data altered through removal or transformation of identifying information so that the data cannot reasonably be used, alone or in combination with other reasonably available information, to identify a specific individual. Articulable Suspicion: Specific and objective facts, together with reasonable inferences from those facts, that provide an individualized basis for investigative or enforcement attention. Artificial Intelligence System (AI System): A machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, processes data using machine learning, statistical modeling, generative techniques, or comparable computational methods to produce predictions, classifications, recommendations, content, or decisions that materially assist municipal operations or decision-making. Automated Decision System (ADS): An AI System used to materially assist or replace discretionary decision-making that affects legal rights, benefits, employment, public safety enforcement, housing, permitting, licensing, or access to City services. City Data: Information collected, created, received, maintained, purchased, licensed, or otherwise possessed by or on behalf of the City in connection with municipal operations, excluding information lawfully obtained by a Vendor independently of its work for the City. Civil Rights and Equity Impact Assessment: A documented evaluation conducted before deployment of a High-Risk AI System that examines whether the system may create or contribute to unlawful discrimination, disparate impact, unequal treatment, or impairment of civil rights or civil liberties, and identifies measures necessary to prevent, reduce, or remedy such risks. Continuous Indiscriminate Tracking: Ongoing or repeated monitoring of an individual’s location, movement, activities, or associations without an individualized investigative or other lawful basis. External Entity Access: The ability of any person, business, contractor, vendor, nonprofit organization, governmental entity, or other third party outside the government of the City of North Adams to view, search, retrieve, receive, obtain, or otherwise access City Data or data generated through a Cityoperated or City-contracted AI System. Generalized Behavioral Aggregation: The collection or combination of data concerning an individual’s activities, movements, associations, communications, or behavior for the purpose of creating a behavioral profile unrelated to a specific lawful investigation or municipal function. 2 | Page High-Risk AI System: An AI System used to Materially Influence decisions that: 1. Affect an individual’s legal rights, benefits, or access to public services; 2. Impact employment

Barrington, commented about DEi and comments from the last council meeting, stating DEi is a small economic portion of the city budget. Councilor Conant made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. COMMUNICATIONS FROM HIS HONOR THE MAYOR A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order to accept a grant funds in the amount of $10,500.00 from the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection. Councilor Conant made a motion to accept the grant carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order transferring and appropriating $67,504.00 from Public Works· Sewer Enterprise salary accounts to the Public Works Sewer Enterprise expense account. Councilor Conant made a motion to approve. Councilor Kavey asked Commissioner Morales to explain what happened with the two positions. The Commissioner stated these are multiple positions, the chief TPO is one position, and the head TPO has multiple staff. They had vacancies and transitions in leadership for two or three months and some have just been filled. Councilor Cunningham asked what the contractual services this will be used for. The Commissioner stated it is for service from a consultant and a series of related things to new management, safety, operational training, that they are outsourcing for training purposes. Councilor Cunningham asked if this has anything to do with the lab. The Commissioner said one of the services will look at the processes in the lab but not the space. Councilor Moody asked the Commissioner about open spots taken out of the budget during budget season in which the mayor said when negotiations are finished with the union he will return to ask for more money when positions are filled. She has concerns moving the funding from a salary account to an expense account. The Commissioner stated that the enterprise was not in that discussion, these employees are roped in to the compensation study, not part of the positions that were not funded. Councilor Moody asked about the $300,000.00 allocated towards consulting services. The Commissioner stated that we have ongoing services related to our permit. This is different than this. The motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order transferring and appropriating $200,000.00 from the Public Works Stabilization Fund for the purchase of equipment for the Department of Public Services. Councilor Conant made a motion to approve. Councilor Lampiasi asked the Commissioner about the timeline. Commissioner Morales stated that the equipment is necessary for a supervisor to go on the mains with a wing plow and to pick up that wing to go on a regular plow to go through the neighborhood streets. They have a vehicle that they have identified that can be expediated, so they do not have to wait the 10-12 months. Councilor Costa asked if this is going to increase our capacity to increase snow plowing. The Commissioner said it will. Councilor Cunningham asked if we have more plows than drivers. The Commissioner stated we have two plows like this currently that are spread out through the department. We have seven snow fighters, pickup trucks with plows, we do not have a plow truck with a wing and spreader capable of going on mains and neighborhoods. Councilor Warren suggested bringing things forward sooner and to inform the council when new equipment is necessary. The Commissioner stated he will communicate items like this in the future. Councilor White asked what type of truck will be purchased and can it be interchangeable. The Commissioner stated it is a one-ton pickup truck with attachments, plow, wing, and spreader. The motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. REPORTS FROM COMMITTEES Reports from the Public Health and Safety Committee A report from the Public Health and Safety Committee on a petition from Councilor White requesting an update from the EPA, DEP, and DPH concerning Building 71 and Hill 78, recommending to accept the report 4/0. Councilor Conant made a motion to accept the report and place on file. Councilor Warren asked Councilor Costa why the discussion did not touch on the public health component. Councilor Costa said this is an old petition. Councilor Costa stated that Richard Fisher from DPA gave an extensive presentation and answered many questions about the concerns for these areas. A follow-up question concerning storm water run off on Tyler Street Extension will be investigated. Councilor Moody is in communication with Mr. Fisher on this. Councilor Costa said there are plans to demolish the building 19 area and GE stated they have no plans to use the remaining buildings raised in that area for any purpose. They are considering a combination of fencing, plantings and grass with the final design not yet complete. The motion to accept and place on file carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. Councilor Amuso made a point of order, stating that item 13 will be viewer by the Ordinance and Rules Committee on November 23rd before it returns to the City Council. MATTERS TENTATIVELY REFERRED BY THE PRESIDENT UNDER RULE 27 These items do not require a vote for referral but may be raised for a vote by any Councilor. Referred to the Traffic Commission A petition from Councilor Cunningham requesting a "10 Minute Parking - Loading Zone" sign in front of That's a Wrap Cafe A communication from Mayor Marchetti on a Traffic Order amending parking regulations on Union Street Referred to the Director of the Berkshire Athenaeum A petition from Alex Blumin requesting a winter program presented each year by Law Library "Law movies" into wider education Referred to the Ordinances and Rules Committee A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Ordinance recommending that City Code, Chapter 16, Attachment 1 be amended At 6:32 p.m. Councilor Conant moved to adjourn, carried by a unanimous vote of the eleven members present. RILEY COUNCILLOR AT LARGE – ZIQIANG SUSAN YUAN CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-150 ORDERED: November 09, 2026 R ESOLUTION OPPOSING EFFORTS TO WAIVE STATE CONSUMERPROTECTION LAWS FOR A LONG-TERM LEASE OF QUINCY’S BIGGEST PARCEL OF PUBLICLY OWNED OPEN SPACE WHEREAS, Quarry Hills Associates (QHA) currently holds a long-term lease with the City of Quincy for approximately 240 acres of municipal property operating as the Granite Links Golf Club; and WHEREAS, the current lease agreement has 30 years remaining in its term; and WHEREAS, state law limits the lease of public land to 30 years (MGL Chapter 40 section 3) and requires leases of public land to be put out to bid (MGL Chapter 30B section 16); and WHEREAS, the mayor and previous council sent a home-rule petition to state legislators asking for these requirements to be waived so that Quarry Hills Associates could sign a new lease for an additional 50 years, ending in 2106; and WHEREAS, Quincy’s state senator paused action on the petition in the Senate over uncertainty about whether the deal was in the best interests of Quincy taxpayers, requesting a formal audit (as requested by the City Council) and analyses of the proposed lease’s cost and hospitality terms; and WHEREAS, the House then inserted the petition’s language in a package of budget amendments that it passed, circumventing the home-rule petition’s deliberative process; and WHEREAS, that leaves the long-term fate of Quincy’s largest single piece of publicly owned open space subject to a back-room process where budget amendments are traded like baseball cards; and WHEREAS, deep concerns have been raised by citizen advocates, fiscal watchdogs, and state legislators regarding the lack of research on the terms of the current and proposed leases and the implications of future construction at the site; and ORDER NO. 2026 – 150 Page 2 of 2 WHEREAS, residents have expressed ongoing concerns regarding public access to the land, promised trail connections to the Blue Hills Reservation, traffic, and maintenance of the site’s athletic fields; and WHEREAS, entering a commitment that binds the City of Quincy and its taxpayers through the next century requires the highest threshold of community engagement, independent financial auditing, and due diligence to ensure maximum public benefit; NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the Quincy City Council formally opposes any attempt to waive state laws that protect residents by limiting the lengths of leases of public land and by requiring open bids for leases of public land; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Quincy City Council urges the Massachusetts General Court to reject any consolidated budget amendments, home-rule petition, or other legislative maneuver that seeks to authorize this new lease without a comprehensive, independent fiscal analysis in the form of an audit and studies of cost and hospitality terms; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Quincy City Council requests that the Mayor’s administration halt lease negotiations and perform the requested financial accountability and due diligence to ensure that Quincy taxpayers get the most from any revenue-sharing formula; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that any proposed change to the current lease be returned to the Quincy City Council for discussion and oversight; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that a copy of this resolution be sent to Quincy’s state legislative delegation, the Senate president, the chairs of the House and Senate Ways and Means Committees, the Governor, and the Lieutenant Governor.
