title: Planning Board Agenda and Items
text: Page 1 of 4 Planning Board Minutes October 27, 2026 SEEKONK PLANNING BOARD Public Hearing, Regular Business, and Work Session Meeting Select Board Meeting Room October 27, 2026 Present: D. Sullivan, M. Bingham, P. Dunn, J. Perry, S. Smith, B. Hoch, and John Aubin (Town Planner) Absent with cause: S. Escaler Chair D. Sullivan opened the meeting at 7:02 PM Public Hearing: 1. Proposed amendments to the Zoning By-laws of the Town of Seekonk to Section 4.2.2 Institutional, Utility, and Recreational Uses. M. Bingham made a motion to open the public hearing. Seconded by B. Hoch. ROLL CALL: S. Smith: AYE, M. Bingham: AYE, P. Dunn: AYE, D. Sullivan: AYE, J. Perry: Recused herself from the public hearing, B. Hoch: AYE. P. Dunn made a motion to waive the reading of the public notice. Seconded by M. Bingham. ROLL CALL: S. Smith: AYE, M. Bingham: AYE, P. Dunn: AYE, D. Sullivan: AYE, B. Hoch: AYE. J. Aubin stated this is a petition received by the Town clerk that was then forwarded to the Select Board. This is the Planning Board’s public hearing on it and the Board will be making a report to Town Meeting. He was contacted by Christopher Rizzo to make a presentation. His understanding is that there will be a floor amendment proposed. This will be a question for the Town Moderator. The Planning Board is free to make a positive, negative, or no recommendation. Christopher Rizzo, of 305 Pleasant Street, made a presentation on the proposed amendments and gave a copy of that presentation to each Board member. Presentation entered into the record as attachment #1. C. Rizzo explained that due to deadlines for submittal, the original proposed language was overly complex. The language has since been simplified so that a floor amendment would be more easily digested. C. Rizzo further explained his research and reasoning for putting forth this amendment. D. Sullivan asked the Board if they had any questions for the applicant. D. Sullivan asked if there was anyone present to speak in favor the proposed amendments. John Alves, of 25 River Street, stated that he was on the Community Preservation Committee when the Medeiros Farm was purchased and passed at Town Meeting. He said that the purpose of the project was stated from the beginning. He stated that he hopes the Planning Board speaks in favor of this. Page 2 of 4 Planning Board Minutes October 27, 2026 Anne Miller, of 25 River Stret, wanted to make a comment on the presentation. There is a standard process for municipal projects and if there is going to be a Zoning Board review, the final design is brought forward so the Zoning board can make informed decisions. She is in favor of this amendment because she believes it eliminated any confusion about process and allows projects to move forward with less hoops while still providing adequate review. Jean Stocker, of 14 Washington Street, stated that she sees this proposed amendment as following what is already being done in the State. She believes that anything that can help make things less contentious is a good thing. She believes the process is very convoluted right now. C. Rizzo said he wanted to reenforce that this only talks about the principal use table. Anything else with zoning bylaws, still falls under the existing processes. D. Sullivan asked if there was anyone who wanted to speak in opposition of the proposed amendments. Ken Kazarian, of 12 Kenwood Court, wanted to speak. He asked the Chair if he knew how many municipalities are in Massachusetts. D. Sullivan answered 351. K. Kazarian made a point that C. Rizzo only mentioned 10 in his presentation. He then stated he felt this is a contentious discussion amongst residents because there are people who live 30 feet from the proposed active recreation field. K. Kazarian said he is concerned about the long-term maintenance plan to keep up with the fields and believes that the town will rent out the fields to help offset the cost. He stated that he is not against the project, but he would like there to be consideration or the neighbor who want to come home on the weekend and enjoy their own backyard. He believes this kind of project does not belong in the middle of a residential neighborhood but rather next to a school. D. Sullivan reminded everyone that the discussion tonight is strictly in regards to the proposed Zoning by-law language and not to details of the Mederios Farm project. Cynthia Ward, of 6 Kenwood Court, wanted to read a letter and submit it into the public record. This letter has been entered into the record as attachment #2. C. Ward said she is an abutter to the proposed project. She said she has greater concerns than just in relation to the Mederios Farm. She then read her letter to the Planning Board. Her letter ended with five requests. J. Aubin reminded the Board that they are here to make a recommendation to the Select Board on the proposed Zoning amendment that was submitted by petition. This is not something that the Planning Board came up with, but rather a petition submitted to the Town Clerk that the Planning Board is now reviewing. B. Hoch needed clarification on the proposal. The proposal would remove the 2/3 vote requirement and thus make municipal uses allowed by right. C. Ward had a question related to the process. She asked if the neighbors respond to the submitted proposal, how could a change be brought up after? J. Aubin said a change to the proposed language could only happen on the floor at Town Meeting and would ultimately be allowed by the Town Moderator. S. Smith made a motion to close the public hearing. Seconded by M. Bingham. ROLL CALL: S. Smith: AYE, M. Bingham: AYE, P. Dunn: AYE, D. Sullivan: AYE, B. Hoch: AYE. D. Sullivan said he believes the Board can only act on what was presented in the packet and certified by the Town Clerk. Page 3 of 4 Planning Board Minutes October 27, 2026 J. Aubin said the Planning Board can still take note of the testimony offered tonight and the statements made with regard to a floor amendment. Until the floor amendment is made, it is not being reviewed properly. D. Sullivan said he believes a positive recommendation would be inappropriate so it would come down to a neutral or negative recommendation. M. Bingham said the timing is not great. He also stated that he does not remember any municipal projects that got held up by Zoning in the past that would make this amendment a necessity. B. Hoch said he cannot support this amendment either as the Town Planner said the language was confusing. D. Sullivan agreed. M. Bingham made a motion to make a negative recommendation to the Select Board for the proposed amendment as submitted. Seconded by S. Smith. Vote: 4-0-1 (1 abstention by P. Dunn for feeling like she did not have enough information to make a recommendation. J. Perry was recused from this vote and discussion.) Regular Business: 2. Consider a recommendation to the Select Board on the laying out and acceptance of the roadway known as Matt’s Way, part of the Brigham Farm III 9-lot subdivision as a public way. Continued from October 13, 2026 J. Perry rejoined the Planning Board. J. Aubin stated this is a request for the acceptance of the roadway of Brigham Farm Phase III. The final paving has been completed and GPI completed an inspection with Mr. Sagar and M. Mariano today. A list of final outstanding items to be addressed was made and Mr. Sagar is aware of the list. M. Mariano, of Oakhill Engineering, was present to represent Sagar Services for Matt’s Way Road acceptance. He stated that the Board has the completed as-built of the road. The final paving happened last week. There have also been 2 notices of closeout performed. He also captured all the elevations and structures that have been reflected on the as-built. All the bounds had been installed two weeks ago. M. Mariano and G. Sagar went through the final list of items to be addressed from GPI for the Board. M. Bingham made a positive motion to the Select Board with the recommendations stated from GPI and the Town Planner in his report. Seconded by P. Dunn. Vote: 6-0-0 Work Session: 3. Discussion of SNEP Storm water utility technical assistance grant award J. Aubin stated that SNEP is an environmental collaborative of a number of nonprofit agencies and educational facilities that work on environmental technical assistance throughout Southeastern New England. J. Aubin said the Board has worked with them before on this project in 2024 to introduce the idea of a stormwater utility. Next stage includes looking at a feasibility study to assess what it would look like in Seekonk. J. Aubin clarified that this is not proposing anything to town meeting. This is really just an analysis to see what the stormwater costs are currently, what they are projected to be in the future, and how to deal with those costs and budgetary pressures associated. This is being driven by 21st century stormwater issues and storms with 19th century infrastructure. Also, Seekonk is subject to MS4 permitting through the State and the EPA. This was a subject that was discussed with the quad-board to develop a task force working group to work with SNEP to see what this would look like in Seekonk. It also brings into the conversation Home Owner Associations who are dealing with this right now. J. Aubin said the next steps are finalizing the scope of work with SNEP, present that to the Select Board, get their authorization into the agreement, and then start the process. 4. Correspondence Page 4 of 4 Planning Board Minutes October 27, 2026 None. 5. Approval of minutes from October 13, 2026 J. Perry made a motion to approve the minutes from October 13th as submitted. Seconded by S. Smith. VOTE: 5-0-1 (P. Dunn abstained for being absent) Adjournment 8:05 pm B. Hoch made a motion to adjourn. Seconded by J. Perry. VOTE: 6-0-0 Respectfully submitted by, Stephanie Iagatta, Secretary Planning Board Formally accepted on 11/00/2026 0 in favor, 0 against, 0 abstentions

title:
Notice of Public Hearing relative to determination of the percentages of the local tax levy to be
borne by each class of real and personal property for Fiscal Year 2027
text: RECEIVED By City Clerk at 5:54 pm, 11/5/26 CITY OF WESTFIELD NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING Notice is hereby given that Westfield City Council will hold a Public Hearing on Thursday, November 19, 2026 at 6:00 P.M. at the regular City Council meeting to be held at the Municipal Building, 59 Court Street, City Council Chamber. Public Hearing relative to determination of the percentages of the local tax levy to be borne by each class of real and personal property for Fiscal Year 2027, as required by Chapter 40, Section 56, as amended by Chapter 718, Section 2, Acts of 1989. At the hearing the Board of Assessors will provide all information and data relevant to the making of such determination and the fiscal effect of the available alternatives. All interested taxpayers are invited to attend and present oral or written information on their views. Written information may be emailed to k.bruce@cityofwestfield.org or be directed by mail to the City Clerk, 59 Court Street, Westfield MA 01085. If mailed, must reach the Clerk’s Office by 5:00 P.M. the day of the hearing in order to be available to the City Council prior to its determination. Kaitlyn Bruce City Clerk/Clerk of the Council

text: By City Clerk at 9:49 am, Nov 06, 2026 City of Amesbury Office of the City Clerk 1 Market Street Amesbury, MA 01913 MEETING NOTICE POSTED IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE PROVISIONS OF M.G.L. CHAPTER 30A §§18-25 Version 7.1.10 City Council Meeting Agenda Tuesday, November 10, 2026 City Hall Bartlett Community Room- 1 Market St. 7:00 PM The public can view this meeting: • In person • ACTV Channel 6 • the ACTV website: https://www.amesburyctv.org/public-government-access-television • or the ACTV Facebook Page: www.facebook.com/AmesburyCommunityTelevision 1. Call to Order 2. Pledge of Allegiance – Councilor Gilday 3. Roll Call 4. President and Vice President Announcements/Communications 6. Presentations from Mayor, City Staff, other Elected Officials, and Official Representatives of Boards and Commissions • City Clerk Jennifer Smith • Chief Bailey Presentation Police Budget/Operations Updates 7. Licenses and Permits- November 8. Public Comment - Public comment can be done in person during the meeting, or by emailing your comments to clerk@amesburyma.gov by 12:00 p.m. the Friday before the Council meeting, per City Council Rule 5G. Subject line PUBLIC COMMENT. Your comments will be read aloud at the appropriate time in the agenda and entered into the public record. 9. Council Response to Public Comment 10. Second Readings 2026-132 District 2 Vacancy- Councilor Claudel Frederique-Resignation a. Public Hearings: 2026-157 National Grid Chestnut St. Extension Pressure Relief Vault Petition Hearing WR #90000236921 (Continued from October 27, 2026, City Council Meeting) 2026-160 National Grid Pole Hearing Portsmouth Rd. WR #31227515 (Continued from October 27, 2026, City Council Meeting) 11. First Readings 2026-162 An Order to request the City Council to vote to declare as surplus various municipal vehicles and equipment. -Mayor Sponsor Summary: This order will authorize the surplus of the following vehicles and equipment belonging to the Fire Department 2026-163 An Order to request the City Council vote to hold the annual Classification Hearing to vote on four (4) separate items in order to establish the tax burdens for each class of property. -Mayor Sponsor Summary: Annually, the City Council must hold a Tax Classification Hearing to determine the distribution of the property tax burden among residential, commercial, industrial, and personal property classes. As part of this process, the City Council must vote on four separate items: the residential factor, open space discount, residential exemption, and small commercial exemption. The City Council is being asked to hold the required hearing and approve the recommended tax classification for Fiscal Year 2027. 2026-164 An Order to approve payment from the FY27 general fund operating budget for the below listed prior year invoices. -Mayor Sponsor Summary: The listed invoices below are for operating expenses related to supplies or services rendered in prior fiscal years but for which funds were not encumbered by the corresponding city department at fiscal year-end. This order requests payment be made to the listed vendors from the corresponding department’s current year (FY27) operating budget in accordance with M.G.L. c. 44 s. 64. This vote requires two thirds approval of the City Council. 2026-165 An Ordinance to amend the Amesbury Code of Ordinances by adding a new Chapter 446, entitled "Virtual currency automated teller machines,” to prohibit the installation and operation of virtual currency automated teller machines (ATM), commonly referred to as cryptocurrency ATMs, Bitcoin ATMs, or virtual currency kiosks. -Mayor and Councilor Stanganelli Sponsors Summary: This ordinance establishes a new Chapter 446 of the Amesbury City Code to prohibit the installation and operation of virtual currency ATMs, commonly referred to as cryptocurrency ATMs, within the City. Virtual currency ATMs have increasingly been used in financial scams and fraudulent activities, particularly targeting older adults and vulnerable residents. These machines allow individuals to convert cash into cryptocurrency, often through transactions that are difficult to trace and nearly impossible to reverse, making it challenging for victims to recover stolen funds. This ordinance is intended to protect residents from financial exploitation and prevent these machines from being used to facilitate fraud within our community. 2026-166 An Order to authorize the Mayor to accept and expend a MBTA Communities Catalyst Fund award in the amount of $500,000 to support the Route 110/150 Improvements project. -Mayor Sponsor Summary: This MBTA Communities Catalyst Fund award will support the planning and preliminary design of safety and traffic improvements at the intersection of Route 110 and Route 150. The project will include traffic studies, surveying, evaluation of intersection alternatives, and preliminary design to improve traffic flow, pedestrian safety, and connectivity. 2026-167 An Order to authorize the Mayor to accept and expend a HousingWorks Infrastructure Program grant in the amount of $5,000,000 to support the Clarks Road Reconstruction project. -Mayor Sponsor Summary: This HousingWorks Infrastructure Program grant will support infrastructure improvements along approximately 2,600 feet of Clarks Road, from Route 110 (Macy Street) to Main Street. The project includes roadway reconstruction, new sidewalks, traffic calming measures, pedestrian safety improvements, and upgrades to water and stormwater infrastructure. 12. Correspondence a. Communications from Mayor, City Staff, other Elected Officials, and Representatives of City Boards and Committees b. Council Communications c. Council Committee Reports 13. Act on Minutes – None at this time 14. Late Files 2026-169 An Order to accept the provisions of Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 40, Section 71, authorizing the use of school bus violation detection monitoring systems. -Mayor, Councilor Stanganelli, Councilor Welch, and Councilor Hogg Sponsors Summary: This order would authorize the City of Amesbury to establish a school bus stop-arm camera enforcement program pursuant to Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 40, Section 71, and Chapter 90, Sections 14C through 14E. 2026-170 An Order that $399,600 is appropriated from the Receipts Reserved for Real Estate Proceeds Fund (239 4193) and transferred to the Library Maintenance & Repairs capital fund (360 8039), with a portion transferring to the General Fund to offset legal fee costs of the purchase. -Mayor Sponsor Summary: This order will authorize the transfer from the Receipts Reserved for Real Estate Proceeds Fund (239 4193) to a capital account for library maintenance and repairs (less cost of related legal fees) with a focus on water infiltrations mitigation, including but not limited to roof, gutters, windows, masonry, exterior paint, soffits, eaves, and stairs. The $399,600 represents the proceeds from the sale of 5 and 9 School Street properties, authorized per Council Order #2024-133. Pursuant to G.L. c. 44, this order must be passed by at least a two-thirds vote of the entire membership of the City Council. 14. Adjournment

The virtual meeting will be live streamed on Andover46.com and broadcast on Comcast Channel 22, and Verizon Channel 45. Members of the public wishing to attend the public meeting may call or email the Conservation office at (978)623-8630 or CDPConservation@andoverma.us to obtain the link to access the meeting, in compliance with the Guidance on Holding Meeting Pursuant to the Act Extending Certain COVID-19 Measures. Members of the public who wish to communicate to the meeting can do so by emailing CDPCONSERVATION@ANDOVERMA.US. Residents are encouraged to email their questions or comments ahead of the meeting — however, staff will be available to present the Andover Conservation Commission with questions and comments received during the meeting. Please include your name and address with your question or comment. Every effort will be made to ensure that the public can adequately access the proceedings in real time via technological means. Section numbers correspond to agenda packets and are not an indication of the order of the agenda Page 1 of 1 Town of Erving Select Board Public Meeting Participation Guidance The Select Board welcomes residents to communicate questions, comments or concerns. Participants at Select Board meetings are notified that the meetings are both video and audio recorded, and comments provided will become part of the record. While offering public input, it is important that the Select Board is also allowed enough time to conduct their other business. The following guidelines have been established to make the best use of time at Select Board meetings. 1. To request time on the Select Board agenda, persons must contact the Town Administrator at (413) 422-2800, Ext.1102 or at SBRequests@erving-ma.gov by noon on the Tuesday before the meeting. a. Requests will be submitted to the Chairperson for consideration and scheduling. b. Supporting documentation related to the request must be provided to the Administrator’s office by noon on the Thursday prior to the meeting. The Chairperson may remove requested agenda topics that are made without supporting documentation. 2. The Select Board encourages public participation as follows: a. Town residents can bring comments before the Select Board that require discussion and are on the agenda, only after being recognized by the Chair. If your issue is not on the agenda, you may bring it up under “Future agenda items”. b. “Topics not anticipated” should be brought to the Chair for possible consideration prior to the meeting. c. Please try to keep your comments short and to the point. d. If it appears that the topic(s) being discussed will consume longer than the time allocated then, at the discretion of the Chair, the matter will be placed on an upcoming Select Board meeting agenda. e. If you believe that your topic will require more time or desire to make a more formal presentation than is allowed under these guidelines, please contact the Town Administrator to ask to be put on a future agenda so that we can properly allocate enough time. f. You are free to ask questions or to make your point for all to consider. However, engaging in active debate with Select Board or audience members will not be allowed. g. All comments and questions must be directed to the Chair of the Select Board per MGL Chapter 30A, Section 20(g). h. Participants are expected to speak from the presenter/guest table. 3. Employees and Board members who have business with the Select Board should be placed on the agenda beforehand (see Item # 1.). 4. Anyone wishing to contact the Select Board in writing may do so at: Town of Erving, Attn: Select Board, 12 East Main Street, Erving, Massachusetts 01344 Alternatively, members of the public can complete a Select Board submission form at the meeting sign in table and office staff member will follow up. The Select Board appreciates your cooperation in honoring these guidelines. From Massachusetts Attorney General Official Website What public participation in meetings must be allowed? Under the Open Meeting Law, the public is permitted to attend meetings of public bodies but is excluded from an executive session that is called for a valid purpose listed in the law. Any member of the public also has a right to make an audio or video recording of an open session of a public meeting. A member of the public who wishes to record a meeting must first notify the Chair and must comply with reasonable requirements regarding audio or video equipment established by the chair so as not to interfere with the meeting. The Chair is required to inform other attendees of such recording at the beginning of the meeting. While the public is permitted to attend an open meeting, an individual may not address the public body without permission of the Chair. An individual is not permitted to disrupt a meeting of a public body, and at the request of the Chair, all members of the public shall be silent. If after clear warning, a person continues to be disruptive, the Chair may order the person to leave the meeting, and if the person does not leave, the Chair may authorize a constable or other officer to remove the person. title: Board of Selectmen Agenda
text: Selectmen’s Meeting Teachers’ Lounge, Essex Elementary School, 12 Story Street November 16, 2026 This meeting will be conducted in-person, with the public welcome, but may also be made available to the public via remote participation to the greatest extent possible. See the final page of this agenda for remote connection details. AGENDA – OPEN SESSION 5:15 p.m. Call to Order. Reminder: This meeting is being broadcast and recorded. 6:00 p.m. Finance Committee to discuss final preparations for the Fall Town Meeting. 6:45 p.m. Adjourn to Fall Town Meeting Brendhan Zubricki: Presentation of his Town Administrator’s Report for the period October 31, 2026 through November 13, 2026, regarding the following:  Town Accountant Position Expected Vacancy Update  Essex Division Chamber of Commerce Leadership Group Meeting  Review of Final Fall Town Meeting Motions and Materials  Possible Advertising for Fundraising at the Field of Dreams  MPO Core Investment Highway Design Grant Application PUBLIC COMMENT. OTHER BUSINESS:  Approve the weekly warrant in the amount of $.  Approve the minutes for the Selectmen’s November 2, 2026, Open Meeting.  Consider a request from Douglas K. Woodman to close Woodman’s Restaurant at 119 Main Street for maintenance and repairs from Monday, January 4, 2027, until Monday, January 18, 2027.  Continue to consider whether the annual Festival held by the Essex River Cultural District can be considered a Town Event.  Review final version of proposed Town social media posting and management policy.  Ratify the Chairman’s signature of a contract for green crab harvesting from Essex coastal waters in the amount of $11,375.  Ratify the Chairman’s signature of a letter of support for technical assistance from the Metropolitan Area Planning Council with respect to the development of a regional Local Emergency Planning Committee Long Term Recovery Group, related to the Essex County Local Emergency Planning Committee that Essex is a part of. Selectmen’s Meeting Agenda Continued Page 2     November 16, 2026 Review and sign an Acknowledgement of Project Eligibility Notification form for a future possible project involving the improvement of the Castle Neck River crossing under Route 133 at the Essex/Ipswich line. Consider signature of a letter to oppose proposed funding cuts to the Mass Save Program. Ideas for agenda items for the next meeting. Items that could not be reasonably anticipated by the Open Meeting Law posting deadline. LICENSING: Antiques License Renewals (Calendar Year 2027):  Vincent W. Caravella, The Scrapbook, 34 Main Street  Tom Lang, Perim Lang Antiques, 18 Eastern Avenue  Michael March, Blackwood March Antiques, 3 Southern Avenue  Shelagh Schylling, Prezona Design, 72 Belcher Street  Salvatore Sorrenti, Ro-Dan Antiques, 69 Main Street Common Victualler License Renewals (Calendar Year 2027):  Paul Martini, ADP-ALB LLC, d/b/a Cape Ann Pizza and Subs, 65 Eastern Avenue  Adrian Wilkins, Essex Woods Meeting & Retreat Center, LLC, 1 Conomo Point Road  Kimberly St. Onge, Googan’s Galley, 1 Martin Street Annual Weekday Entertainment License Renewal (Calendar Year 2027):  Kimberly St. Onge, Googan’s Galley, 1 Martin Street Innholder’s License Renewal (Calendar Year 2027):  Adrian Wilkins, Essex Woods Meeting & Retreat Center, LLC, 1 Conomo Point Road REMINDERS:  The next regular Board of Selectmen’s meeting will take place on Monday, December 7, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. in the 3rd Floor Auditorium, Town Hall, 30 Martin Street. REMOTE CONNECTION DETAILS: Members of the public who wish to listen to and/or view the meeting may do so via two-way Video Call (with the option to show yourself on video or not and with the option to use a phone to call in, for two-way audio-only). Please note that while an option for remote attendance and/or participation is being provided as a courtesy to the public, the meeting/hearing will not be suspended or terminated if technological problems interrupt the virtual broadcast or its quality, unless otherwise required by law. Members of the public with particular interest in any specific item on this agenda should make plans for in-person versus virtual attendance accordingly. Selectmen’s Meeting Agenda Continued Page 3 November 16, 2026 Video On-line Link: https://join.freeconferencecall.com/bzubricki Meeting ID if prompted: bzubricki Please make sure you are joined in mute mode. Comments with only be taken from those that enter their name. The camera should be off, by default, when you join you may activate if you wish to do so. Dial-in Number: (425) 436-6352 and the access code is 1729820. Further, it is likely that this meeting will be broadcast by 1623 Studios over the local cable television network. Please check your cable listings for details if you are a Comcast cable television subscriber.

text: FITCHBURG CITY CLERK Nov 12 2026 11:38 am 11:52 am, Nov 12, 2026 WELCOME TO THE FITCHBURG CITY COUNCIL November 17, 2026 Fitchburg Legislative Building 700 Main Street Fitchburg MA 01420 7:00 PM This meeting can also be viewed live on FATV. Go to www.fatv.org/watch-fatv for more information on accessing this meeting. This is intended to help you understand the meeting format and assist you with the rules of the Council as they pertain to your participation. All meetings of the Fitchburg City council are open to the public. This does not mean that the public participates in all aspects of the meeting. It simply means that the meeting itself, including all discussions and votes, is open for public view. Executive Session The only time a Council meeting can be closed to the public is when the Council votes for Executive Session in order to discuss sensitive matters in private, such as pending litigation. Any votes taken however, must be taken in open session. OPPORTUNITIES FOR THE PUBLIC TO SPEAK DURING A COUNCIL MEETING: Public Forum The Public Forum occurs immediately following the Pledge of Allegiance. The President will ask if anyone in the audience wishes to speak on any matter appearing on the Agenda. If you wish to address the Council, you must stand and be recognized and follow these rules before speaking: 1. 2. 3. 4. State your name and city of residence. Approach the center table and either stand or sit. This allows you to be seen and heard clearly by everyone in attendance. You may speak only on items appearing on the agenda for no more than (2) minutes. Copies of the agenda are available on the center table prior to the meeting. Please state the petition, order, ordinance, or resolution number to which you refer. Public Hearings Public hearings are held on various issues such as Special Permits and Zoning changes. The same rules apply with the following exceptions: 1. You must stand and be recognized either “in favor” or “in opposition” when asked by the Council President. 2. You need not refer to the petition number. If you have any questions or comments either before or after the meeting, any Councilor would be happy to assist you. Thank you for your interest! I. PUBLIC FORUM This meeting will be open to the public. To participate in the meeting remotely citizens may join a Zoom using the information provided below. ZOOM DETAILS: Please click on the link: https://us02web.zoom.us/j/82648666603 or call 312-626-6799, meeting #8264866603. All participants will be automatically muted upon joining the meeting. In order to speak, participants will need to select the “Raise Hand” function to request to be unmuted. All speakers will be required to state their full name and street address before commenting. PUBLIC HEARINGS GENERAL BUSINESS: A. Limited Site Plan: 79 Grove St B. Extension: 164 Grove Street C. Final Form H: 240 East Central D. Final Form H: 15 Liberty Way E. Meeting Minutes: October 19 & November 2, 2026 This agenda is subject to change. The next meeting of the Planning Board is scheduled for December 14, 2026. Notice: The Franklin Planning Department has been made aware of fraudulent emails impersonating Town departments and requesting payment via wire transfer. The Planning Department will never request payment by wire transfer. All applicant fees must be paid by check and mailed or delivered to the Franklin Municipal Building. If you receive a suspicious email or are unsure if a request is legitimate, please contact the Department at 508-520-4907 to verify any outstanding fees related to your application.

Page 3 of 3 PAGE 3 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of November 2, 2026 Minutes of the Regular Meeting Monday, November 2, 2026 – 7:30 P.M City Council Chamber Roll Call Members Present: ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● President George C. Tyros Councillor Calvin D. Brooks Councillor Craig R. Cormier Councillor Aleksander H. Dernalowicz Councillor Dana M. Heath Councillor Brad E. Heglin Councillor Elizabeth J. Kazinskas Councillor Judy A. Mack Councillor Paul G. Tassone Councillor David R. Thibault-Muñoz Member Absent: ● Councillor Karen G. Hardern Open Meeting Law Announcement President Tyros announced that any person wishing to make an audio or video recording of the meeting, or transmit the meeting through any medium, was required to notify the Chair pursuant to Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 30A, §20. READING OF MINUTES OF PRIOR MEETINGS October 19, 2026 Regular Meeting Minutes Councillor Cormier moved to waive the reading of the minutes and accept them as presented. Councillor Tassone seconded the motion. Councillors Kazinskas, Dernalowicz, and Mack announced that they would abstain because they had not attended the October 19 meeting. The motion passed by voice vote, with the noted abstentions. Page 1 of 6 PAGE 4 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of November 2, 2026 Item 11968 – Public Hearing Pursuant to M.G.L. Chapter 40, Section 56, Regarding the Classification of Property for Taxation President Tyros opened the public hearing to determine the percentage of the local tax levy to be borne by each class of real property for Fiscal Year 2027. The hearing notice was read into the record. Mayor Michael Nicholson addressed the Council and recommended that the City continue to adopt a residential factor of 1.0, maintaining a single tax rate for all classes of property. Mayor Nicholson explained that Massachusetts General Laws permit municipalities to establish different tax rates for residential and commercial, industrial, and personal property. He stated that maintaining a single tax rate remained consistent with the City's economic development and housing development goals. The Mayor emphasized that the City's efforts to encourage both residential and commercial growth would be better supported by a uniform tax rate rather than shifting the tax burden between property classes. President Tyros called three times for anyone wishing to speak in favor of the proposed classification and three times for anyone wishing to speak in opposition. No members of the public came forward. There being no questions from Councillors, President Tyros declared the public hearing closed. Item 11966 – Appointment of Sean Kelley as Lieutenant to the Gardner Fire Department Councillor Heath thanked Mayor Nicholson and Fire Chief Loy for providing notification of the promotion of Sean Kelley to Lieutenant in the Gardner Fire Department. Councillor Heath recognized Lieutenant Kelley's service to the City since March 21, 2005, noting his more than 21 years of dedication to public safety. He specifically acknowledged Lieutenant Kelley's work coordinating the Student Awareness of Fire Education (SAFE) and Senior SAFE programs. Page 2 of 6 PAGE 5 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of November 2, 2026 Councillor Heath congratulated Lieutenant Kelley on his promotion and moved to place the communication on file. Councillor Heglin seconded the motion. Councillor Dernalowicz expressed support for the promotion, noting his longstanding friendship with Lieutenant Kelley and his family and recognizing their contributions to the Gardner community. Councillor Kazinskas also expressed support, recognizing Lieutenant Kelley's dedication, work ethic, and character. The motion to place the communication on file passed by voice vote. Following the vote, the Council briefly recessed while the City Clerk administered the oath of office to Lieutenant Kelley. Item 11967 – Finance Committee Update – Financial Outlook Reporting Councillor Dernalowicz provided an update regarding the Finance Committee's recent review of the City's financial condition. He reported that Mayor Nicholson and the City Auditor had presented a quarterly financial update to the Finance Committee covering revenues and expenditures for the first quarter of Fiscal Year 2027. Councillor Dernalowicz explained that the administration had compiled departmental revenue and expenditure information and was reviewing accounts that had expended more than 25 percent of their annual appropriations during the first quarter. He noted that certain accounts would have legitimate explanations for exceeding the 25 percent threshold, including annual or one-time expenditures, while others might require additional review and monitoring. Councillor Dernalowicz encouraged Councillors to review the Finance Committee's meeting and future financial updates. He stated that the spreadsheet containing the financial information would be distributed to Councillors and included with the Finance Committee's minutes for public review. He indicated that the Finance Committee would continue monitoring the City's financial condition and providing updates to the full Council. No formal action was taken. Page 3 of 6 PAGE 6 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of November 2, 2026 Item 11964 – A Measure Authorizing a Prior Fiscal Year Bill for the Veterans Services Department for W.B. Mason Councillor Dernalowicz explained that the measure concerned an unpaid Fiscal Year 2026 invoice from W.B. Mason for the Veterans Services Department that required authorization for payment using Fiscal Year 2027 funds. He stated that the item had been brought directly to the Council, rather than referred to the Finance Committee, to allow the prior-year obligation to be resolved and the accounting records closed. Councillor Dernalowicz moved to adopt the measure. Councillor Heglin seconded the motion. There being no discussion, a roll call vote was taken. The motion passed 10–0. Item 11965 – A Measure Authorizing the Payment of Prior Fiscal Year Bills Councillor Dernalowicz explained that the measure concerned unpaid Fiscal Year 2026 invoices for Konica Minolta copier services associated with three City departments. Councillor Dernalowicz moved to adopt the measure. Councillor Heglin seconded the motion. Councillor Heglin spoke regarding the circumstances that resulted in the invoices remaining unpaid and raised broader concerns about the City's accounts payable procedures. He explained that City Hall maintained three commercial copier contracts, with invoices initially directed to one department before being distributed to the other departments responsible for payment. Councillor Heglin reported that the invoices had continued to be directed to the former City Clerk after her departure, resulting in unpaid bills that were not identified until the vendor contacted the new City Clerk. Page 4 of 6 PAGE 7 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of November 2, 2026 He stated that the situation illustrated broader inefficiencies in the City's financial administration, including unnecessary duplication of work, excessive departmental involvement in processing routine invoices, and a lack of centralized oversight of recurring financial obligations. Councillor Heglin further noted that similar issues existed with recurring cellular telephone invoices, with more than a dozen separate bills being processed monthly for employees working within the same municipal building. He expressed concern that the City's current procedures were unnecessarily complicated, increased the likelihood of errors, and created vulnerabilities when employees left City service or were absent. Councillor Heglin recommended improvements to streamline the payment process, including greater centralization and the establishment of a comprehensive record of recurring municipal bills and the departments responsible for their payment. He emphasized that modernizing these procedures would improve efficiency, accountability, and the City's ability to manage its financial obligations. There being no further discussion, a roll call vote was taken. The motion passed 10–0. Item 11968 – A Measure to Determine the Residential Factor for Real Estate Taxation in the City of Gardner for the Fiscal Year Beginning July 1, 2026, and Ending June 30, 2027 Councillor Kazinskas moved that the residential factor for real estate taxation in the City of Gardner be established at 1.0 for Fiscal Year 2027, maintaining a single tax rate for all classes of property. Councillor Dernalowicz seconded the motion. There being no discussion, the motion passed by voice vote. Page 5 of 6 PAGE 8 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of November 2, 2026 COUNCIL COMMENTS AND REMARKS Councillor Brooks commented on the upcoming November 3, 2026 election. He expressed confidence in the integrity of the election process in Gardner and throughout Massachusetts, noting that existing safeguards, verification procedures, and audits were designed to ensure accurate election results and prevent interference. Councillor Brooks stated that the procedures in place provided substantial protection against attempts to manipulate election results and expressed hope that, following the election, officials and residents could return their attention to the work of governing. There being no further Council comments or remarks, the Council proceeded to adjournment. ADJOURNMENT Councillor Tassone moved to adjourn following the closing prayer. Councillor Kazinskas seconded the motion. The motion passed by voice vote. The closing prayer was offered, and the meeting was adjourned. Page 6 of 6 PAGE 9 Item 12012 City of Gardner – Mayor’s Office Mayor Michael J. Nicholson November 12, 2026 Hon. George C. Tyros, Council President And City Councilors Gardner City Hall, Rm 121 95 Pleasant Street Gardner, MA 01440 RE: A Communication from the Mayor Regarding Intent to Resign from the Office of Mayor and Mayoral Succession Dear Mr. President and Councilors, As you are aware, on November 3, 2026, I was elected to serve as State Representative for the Second Worcester District in the Massachusetts House of Representatives. I am deeply honored by the confidence the voters have placed in me and look forward to continuing my service to the residents of Gardner and the surrounding communities in this new capacity. In anticipation of assuming this new office, I am writing to formally notify the City Council of my intention to resign from the Office of Mayor of the City of Gardner, effective at 12:00 noon on Friday, January 8, 2027. This correspondence is intended to provide the City Council with advance notice of my planned departure so that it may begin preparing for the transition of municipal leadership and take any necessary steps consistent with the City Charter. My formal letter of resignation will be submitted separately at the appropriate time. Pursuant to Section 32 of the City Charter, when a vacancy occurs in the Office of Mayor during the final twelve months of the term, the President of the City Council shall succeed to the Office of Mayor for the remainder of the unexpired term. As my anticipated resignation will occur during the final twelve months of the current mayoral term, this provision will govern the succession. Accordingly, upon the effective date and time of my resignation, the President of the City Council will succeed to the Office of Mayor for the remainder of the term, which expires in January 2028. I am providing this advance notification to afford the City Council, City Clerk, and other appropriate municipal officials sufficient time to prepare for this transition and address any resulting organizational or administrative matters. Between now and January 8, I intend to continue fulfilling the responsibilities of Mayor and working closely with the City Council, department heads, and municipal employees to ensure an orderly and seamless transition. My administration will cooperate fully in providing any information or assistance necessary to facilitate that process. PAGE 10 Item 12012 Serving as Mayor of the City of Gardner has been one of the greatest honors of my life. I am grateful for the opportunity to have worked alongside the City Council in service to our community, and I look forward to continuing that relationship in my new role as State Representative. Thank you for your continued service to the City of Gardner. Sincerely, Michael J. Nicholson Mayor, City of Gardner PAGE 11 Item 11998 - 12006 City of Gardner – Mayor’s Office Mayor Michael J. Nicholson November 5, 2026 Hon. George C. Tyros, Council President And City Councilors Gardner City Hall, Rm 121 95 Pleasant Street Gardner, MA 01440 RE: A Communication from the Mayor Regarding the City’s FY2027 Financial Status Dear Mr. President and Councilors, I am writing to provide the City Council with an update on the financial challenges facing the City of Gardner and to submit a series of proposed budgetary adjustments intended to address the City's Fiscal Year 2027 financial obligations. Like many municipalities across the Commonwealth, Gardner continues to face significant financial pressures resulting from rising operating costs, increasing demands on municipal services, and revenues that have not kept pace with rising expenditures, particularly health insurance. These challenges require us to make difficult decisions while remaining mindful of our responsibility to taxpayers, municipal employees, and the residents who depend on essential City services. Following a review of the City's financial position, I have identified approximately $5.17 million in financial obligations and budgetary pressures that must be addressed. The identified financial obligations are as follows: Category Amount FY2026 Deficit $387,009.00 Anticipated Expenditure Shortfalls $3,920,067.00 Revenue Reductions $987,825.00 Term Leave Obligations $264,927.59 Total Financial Obligations $5,172,819.59 PAGE 12 Item 11998 - 12006 These figures demonstrate the extent of the financial pressures currently facing the City. The largest component involves expenditure shortfalls, reflecting the difference between available appropriations and anticipated financial obligations. At the same time, reductions in expected revenue estimates have further limited the City's ability to meet these expenses through existing resources. Proposed Financial Adjustments To address these obligations, my administration has developed a package of financial adjustments totaling approximately $4.59 million. Proposed Adjustment Amount Budget Reductions $542,553.93 Parking Meter Revenue $25,000.00 New Growth Revenue $266,895.00 Stabilization Fund $2,500,000.00 Corrected Indirect Costs $1,054,700.00 Enterprise Fund Reductions $200,000.00 Total Proposed Adjustments $4,589,148.93 This package reflects an effort to address the City's immediate financial obligations through several different approaches, rather than relying exclusively on reductions to municipal services. First, we have identified more than $542,000 in budget reductions, along with $200,000 in enterprise fund reductions. These adjustments represent an effort to reduce expenditures and limit the amount of additional financial resources required. Second, the package recognizes additional available revenues, including parking meter fees and new growth, as well as corrections to indirect cost allocations. These adjustments are intended to ensure that municipal expenses and available revenues are accurately reflected in the City's financial accounts. Finally, the proposal includes the use of $2.5 million from the City's Stabilization Fund. Such residents will be allowed as much time as the proponent of an item is permitted to have. GREAT BARRINGTON PLANNING BOARD DATE: October 22, 2026 TIME: 6:00 P.M. PLACE: Large Meeting Room FOR: Regular Meeting PRESENT: Brandee Nelson, Chair; Pedro Pachano; Jonathan Hankin; Jackie Kain Jeremy Higa Art Blumenthal, Associate Member Chris Rembold, Assistant Town Manager/Director of Planning & Development Ms. Nelson called the meeting to order at 6:00 PM. She said the meeting was being recorded. Roll call: Mr. Blumenthal;, present; Mr. Pachano, present; Ms. Kain, present; Mr. Hankin, present; Mr. Higaankin, present; Ms. Nelson present MINUTES: OCTOBER 8 & OCTOBER 15, 2026: Mr. Hankin made a motion to approve the minutes of October 8, 2026 as amended, Ms. Kain seconded, all in favor. Mr. Hankin made a motion to approve the minutes of October 15, 2026 as amended, Ms. Kain seconded, all in favor. SPECIAL PERMIT: 110 COTTAGE STREET: The Board had a ZBA special permit application to review and make a recommendation. The application was from James Toby Zucco to construct a larger garage on the same nonconforming footprint as the previous garage at 110 Cottage Street. Mr. Zucco was present to discuss the application. He said there in April there was a fire in the previous garage. He said he when he began the process to rebuild he was told he had to use the same footprint as the previous garage. He said he wanted to make the new garage higher than the previous garage. He said the previous garage had a second floor but there was only room to stand in the middle. He said he wanted to rebuild with a full second floor. He said the new garage is below the height limit in the zone. Ms. Kain said she drove by the property. She said she talked to the neighbor who was very happy with the new garage. Ms. Nelson said the code requires any lighting be downward facing. She said no flood lights. Mr. Hankin made a motion to send a favorable recommendation to the ZBA, Ms. Kain seconded, all in favor. 1 Mr. Higa arrived at 6:06 PM. ZONING AMENDMENTS: Sherdyl Fernandez from BRPC was present to discuss Cleanr Energy Siting. Mr. Rembold said he gave the Board a brief overview of the new law in May. Mr. Rembold said if an application for 25 megawatts is submitted there will be one permit issued for the project. The Planning Board would do site plan review or a special permit. If other permits are required the process would have to be completed in one year resulting in the issuance of one permit. Mr. Rembold said a denial of a permit will be reviewed at the State level. The current bylaw doesn’t address energy siting at all so the bylaw will need to be updated. Mr. Fernandez said he will be available to help with the creating a bylaw and the local permitting process. Ms. Kain said she waents a presentation. She asked what needs to be thought about for the processing an application. Mr. Fernandez said it is important to understand the permitting process as well as the portal in the website that will be used for the submission. Ms. Nelson asked about small commercial projects. Mr. Fernandez said a project under 25 megawatts will be processed by the Town. A project 25 megawatts and larger will be processed by the state. Mr. Pachano said a project that is 0-25 megawatts is under local control and over 25 megawatts goes through a State process. Mr. Fernandez said yes. There are different levels of review from the Town. A larger project goes through a more comprehensive process. Mr. Rembold said a roof top solar project is by right with SPR and a ground mounted solar project is by right with a special permit. Mr. Pachano said he understood. 2 There was additional discussion of the process. Mr. Rembold asked the Board to consider what they would like to have in a bylaw. He suggested the bylaw could include something like fire prevention. He said the Board should think about what could be included to strengthen the bylaw. Ms. Nelson said the next task is to look at what we have, what we need and what is missing. Mr. Fernandez said he will look at the sample bylaw to assist with what the Board wants to include. He said there are funds available for BRPC to assist with the getting a bylaw in put together. Ms. Nelson said currently there is nothing in the bylaws about battery storage so that use would not be allowed. Mr. Fernandez said there is nothing to call out that the use ais not allowed so, a consolidated permit could be applied for. Ms. Nelson said she wanted to know if there is a “back door” for what we currently don’t permit. Mr. Rembold suggested that the Board look at the model bylaw sent out in the meeting packet. He said the bylaw could be complicated. He said the State gives preference to solar. If battery storage is part of a solar project the battery storage would be allowed. Mr. Higa said he is concerned about fires and potential impact on abutting properties. He said he has questions about setbacks and if the Board can create a bylaw that would require maximum setbacks instead of minimum setbacks. He asked if we can limit the risk. Mr. Fernandez said the Town has control to require details, including emergency plans for day to day operations and impacts on abutters. Mr. Blumenthal asked if there would be noise. Mr. Fernandez said battery storage can generate noise. Mr. Rembold said it is the land court’s position that battery storage is a protected use, it can’t be prohibited. The bylaw needs rules to govern the use. Setbacks cwould be part of the rules but the rules have to be reasonable. Mr. Hankin asked if battery storage can be a freestanding use or does it have to be associated with solar. 3 Mr. Rembold said it can be a freestanding use. Ms. Nelson asked if clean energy applies to nuclear energy. She asked what other energy forms are considered clean energy. Mr. Fernandez said he would check out nuclear energy. He said wind is another form of clean energy. Mr. Higa asked if a project could exceed 25 megawatts. Mr. Rembold said yes. He said transmission, distribution and infrastructure could go through the Town for permitting of small projects. Large projects go through the State for permitting. There are different scales at what is controlled by the State. Mr. Higa said these projects could affect our livelihood including outdoor recreation. We need to control where they go. It is a great concern. Ms. Nelson said she looked up clean energy sources. She said nuclear is not considered a clean energy source. She said clean energy sources include anaerobic digestion, solar and wind. She said anaerobic digestion is not addressed in zoning. She asked if anaerobic digestion would be addressed through agriculture. Mr. Rembold said he wasn’t sure. Ms. Nelson asked how wind would factor in with the Scenic Mountains Act. Mr. Fernandez said the clean energy siting would supersede the Scenic Mountains Act. Mr. Rembold said East Mountain and Monument Mountain are protected. He said he looked into it years ago. Mr. Higa asked if there can be a residential use for wind. Mr. Rembold said yes. Ms. Nelson said the homework for the Board is to read the model bylaw. She asked Mr. Rembold and Mr. Fernandez to look at our bylaws and model bylaw to work out how to create a siting bylaw. 4 Mr. Higa suggested that the Fire Chief be part of a review process. Mr. Rembold said the Town would contact the Fire Chief. He said there was a proposal earlier this year that included battery storage. The application was withdrawn but staff was prepared to involve the fire department. Mr. Pachano said a project would be required to comply with electrical and fire codes. Mr. Rembold suggested there can be further discussion at the December 10 meeting. Vivian Orlowski said the Agricultural Commission was asked to meet with a local farmer about a solar project. The Commission made suggestions about how the land should be treated and what would go on the ground. The Commission encouraged pollination functions and other suggestions. She asked if that involvement would be allowed in the future. Ms. Nelson said our process already allows for involvement of other boards and committees. Mrs. Orlowski said she sent out information in September about data centers. She said there is a lot of negative impact associated with a datae center. She suggested the Board read the information she sent. Ms. Nelson said data centers are not currently on our agenda. Mr. Rembold said it can be kept on the agenda as a discussion point if needed but there isn’t time to consider. He said the Board could consider a moratorium. Mrs. Mooney said data centers and battery storage facilities are not the same thing. Ms. Nelson said correct. SEASONAL COMMUNITIES: Mr. Rembold said as part of the Seasonal Communities designation the Town will create attainable housing. There are several requirements that will need to be included in the bylaw including tiny houses as a primary year- round use and undersized lots to be developed for yearround residential housing. Mr. Rembold said tiny houses would be a principal use, not just an ADU. He said a new row would be added to the Table of Uses to allow. Mr. Hankin said movable tiny houses are currently defined as ADUs. 5 Mr. Rembold said there will be a new definition and possibly a new section under Section 8. He said this action will need to happen to comply with the Seasonal Communities designation. Ms. Nelson said a tiny house will be a dwelling under the definition. She said there could be multiple tiny houses on a lot. Mr. Rembold said they will need to be permitted, not necessarily allowed. The residential section will be amended. A tiny house will be considered a dwelling unit. Mr. Blumenthal asked what the square footage of a tiny house would be. Mr. Rembold said typically about 400 square feet. Mr. Blumenthal asked where manufactured housing fits in. Mr. Rembold said it is difficult. He said tiny houses are built according to the Building Code. Manufactured homes are built according to the HUD code. Mr. Hankin asked if the tiny houses are movable. Mr. Pachano said if the tiny house is movable it would be considered a trailer. He asked if the Seasonal Communities designation require a definition of tiny houses. He asked if we can just add the definition and say subject to residential zoning. Then we wouldn’t have to change the entire bylaw. Mr. Higa said Seasonal Communities would require a definition. Mr. Rembold said the model bylaw has useful definitions. Mr. Pachano said we need to decide if we are going to define movable as dwelling units or keep as is. Ms. Nelson said we may need to define movable differently. The model bylaw does not treat them the same. Mr. Pachano said we have to decide if we are going to regulate. He said he thinks they are two separate things. He said he will look at the Building Code. 6 Mr. Rembold said the Seasonal Communities require allowing undersized lots or small lots. He said the designation requires attainable housing meaning 250% AMI. He said there are income restrictions. Mr. Pachano said we can’t create a new law that doesn’t comply with zoning. Ms. Nelson said she is not clear about what action is needed because we already allow housing on a 5,000 square foot lot. Mr. Pachano said we could add a paragraph to the non-conforming section. Mr. Rembold suggested section 4 of the Table of Use that deals with minimums could be amended. Mr. Pachano said there could be a footnote in section 4 referring to #5. Ms. Nelson said Mr. Pachano can figure out a way to include. Mr. Pachano said we could provide some dimensional requirements. Ms. Nelson asked how AMI can be enforced from a practical stand point. Mr. Rembold said this can be further discussed at either the December or January meeting. He said enforcing tracking needs to be thought out. He suggested that the Board members send suggestions to him and he will try to put the information into a document for the December meeting. He asked that comments be sent to him no later than December 1. Mr. Blumenthal left the meeting at 7:37 PM. TOWN PLANNER REPORT: Mr. Rembold said the next meeting there will be a public hearing for 425 Park Street. The Board is the SPGA for this special permit. He suggested a site visit at 5:15 PM. He said Meat Processing will also be included for discussion. BOARD & SUB COMMITTEE ISSUES & CONCERNS: Mr. Higa said last week’s CPC meeting dealt with project updates. He said the Great Barrington Affordable Housing Trust gave a presentation regarding the housing project for the Rising ball field. He said the proposal isf for a 12 unit cluster development. There needs to be a RFP to go to be sent to the Selectboard. 7 Mr. Rembold said the draft is still being worked on. Mr. Higa said Step 1 submissions are due on November 6, 2026. The next meeting will be on November 10 at 5:15 PM. CITIZEN’S SPEAK TIME: Mrs. Orlowski said data centers are an issue. The State of New York has issued a 1 year moratorium. She said our Governor is leaving the responsibilities to local communities. She suggested Great Barrington put a moratorium in place and reach out to neighboring communities to suggest they do the same. Ms. Nelson said we are just looking into this. She said she will do some research. There were no other citizens who spoke. Having concluded its business, Ms. Nelson adjourned without objection at 7:44 PM. Respectfully submitted, Kimberly L. Planning Department’s Recommendations Recommendations If the Board is inclined to approve the application, then the Department of Planning and Development recommends the following conditions of approval for the Applicant: 1. The Applicant submit an application for an Approval Not Required (ANR) consistent with the Special Permit application materials within 6 months of Special Permit approval. 2. Summary of Special Permit Application The application is to reduce the dimensional requirements of the lot from the minimum of 200 feet of frontage to 180 feet of frontage. As explained by the applicant, the intent of the special permit application is to allow an Approval Not Required (ANR) division of land to create a new parcel for future residential use. The only requirement for an ANR is the minimum frontage. Section 200-5.3 Additional Dimensional Provisions of the Zoning Code allows for reduced lot dimensions. Section 200-5.3(E.2) reads: “The dimensional requirements for lots in any district may be reduced not more than twenty percent (20%) under a special permit from the Zoning Board of Appeals only if the Board finds that: (a) There is some difficulty in developing the lot which cannot be overcome without a reduction in the dimensional requirements or a site design is proposed which is more suitable for the lot than one which would be allowed under the permitted dimensional requirements; (b) Adjacent properties would not be adversely impacted; and 1 (c) The reduced dimensions would not be detrimental to the public good and would not substantially derogate from the intent or purpose of this ordinance.” 3. Planning Department’s Analysis The existing parcel has a frontage of approximately 430 feet. Therefore, the existing parcel has adequate frontage to be divided into two parcels. However, there is an existing building on the parcel near the center of the frontage that prevents the existing parcel from being split down the middle. The location of the existing building creates difficulty that requires a reduction of dimensional requirements. A potential alternative to the proposed reduction in frontage could be a reduction in the minimum side yard requirement of 20 feet. This could allow the proposed property line to be closer to the existing house. However, given that the ANR has not occurred, that reduction would apply to both the existing house and any new house on the newly created parcel. In that case, a new home could be built with a smaller side yard, and therefore built closer to the existing house than the 40-foot standard requirement. In contrast, the proposed reduction in frontage allows for all required yards to be met. Another potential consideration for the board is that Section 200-5.3(E.1) reads: “The Inspector of Buildings may issue a building permit for residential lots in the RA, SR, and H Districts with reduced lot area, frontage, and width requirements of not less than the average lot dimensions of residential lots within three hundred (300) feet on the same street.” This does not apply to the project under consideration, because it is in the RC district and there is no building permit application yet. However, consideration of the local neighborhood could inform the Board’s review. The table below shows the frontage of all lots within 300 feet of the site on the same street. text: City of GREENFIELD, MASSACHUSETTS ___ PLANNING AND DEVELOPMENT Virginia Desorgher Mayor PLANNING BOARD City Hall ● 14 Court Square ● Greenfield, MA 01301 Phone 413-772-1549 ● Ella.Wise@greenfield-ma.gov ● www.greenfield-ma.gov TO: Lora Wondolowski, City Council President Members of the Greenfield City Council FROM: Jeff Sauser, Chairperson, Planning Board DATE: September 3, 2026 RE: Planning Board initiation of proposed zoning amendments to Section 200-7.2 to allow multifamily buildings to consist of more than one building per lot. At its September 3, 2026 meeting, the Planning Board, after careful consideration and deliberation, took the following vote relative to the proposed zoning amendments to Section 2007.2 to allow multifamily buildings to consist of more than one building per lot. MOTION: Moved by Moschella, seconded by Brown-Anson, and voted 5:0:0 to initiate the proposed zoning amendment as further amended below to allow multifamily buildings to consist of more than one building per lot in the Central Commercial, General Commercial, Limited Commercial, and General Industrial zoning districts. --~ 200-7.2. Multifamily dwellings. A. Special permit required. The Zoning Board of Appeals may grant a special permit for multifamily dwellings under the following procedures and requirements. Multifamily dwellings in open space/cluster developments shall also comply with the requirements of ~ 200-7.1 of this ordinance. B. Procedure. (1) Applicants shall submit seven (7) copies of an application and the proposed site plan, prepared by a registered engineer, architect, or other qualified professional, showing proposed structures, parking, drives, landscaping, topography and drainage, plus architectural elevations of all proposed buildings and any other site plan submittal requirements specified in the Site Plan, ~ 200-8.4 of this ordinance. Where the development of a Priority Development Site (PDS) requires a special permit hereunder, the aforesaid application and site plan shall be submitted simultaneously The City of Greenfield is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity Employer, a designated Green Community and a recipient of the “Leading by Example” Award with any other permit application(s) required (a) by this Ordinance or (b) by the Code, generally, relating to the use or development of land, buildings or structures and not otherwise exempted by G.L. c. 43D. [Subsection 1 amended by Town Council on October 21, 2009] (2) Within ten (10) days of its receipt, one (1) copy of the application and site plan shall be forwarded by the Clerk of the Board of Appeals to the Planning Board, who shall submit a report of recommendations to the Board of Appeals within thirty (30) days. (3) The Board of Appeals shall not hold a public hearing on the application until receipt of the Planning Board report, or until forty-five (45) days has lapsed from the date of filing. Where the special permit sought hereunder is for the development of one (1) or more multifamily dwellings on a Priority Development Site (PDS), the Zoning Board of Appeals shall render a decision thereon no later than one hundred eighty (180) days from the date of submission of the application. [Subsection 3 amended by Town Council on October 21, 2009] (4) Multifamily dwellings may consist of one (1) or more buildings on one (1) lot in the Central Commercial (CC), General Commercial (GC), Limited Commercial (LC), and General Industry (GI) zoning districts. (45) Multifamily structures shall be served by a public way having sufficient width, suitable grades, and adequate construction to accommodate the increase in traffic generated by the site. (56) The site shall be designed so that access, grading, water and sewer systems, drainage, roads and sidewalks meet all applicable standards established in the Greenfield Planning Board Subdivision Regulations,1 and the specifications and standards of the Department of Public Works; no building shall be floodlit; driveways and parking areas shall be illuminated only by shielded lights not higher than fifteen (15) feet; no lighting shall cast observable shadows onto adjoining premises; major topographic changes or removal of existing trees shall be avoided and effective use shall be made of the topography, landscaping, and building placement to make maximum use of solar energy, protect the character of the environs, and protect scenic views seen from public ways. (67) Parking areas shall be screened from public ways and adjacent properties by building location, grading, fencing, or planting. Parking shall be off-street and shall provide for forward moving ingress and egress onto any traveled way. No parking area shall contain more than thirtysix (36) parking spaces. The City of Greenfield is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity Employer, a designated Green Community and a recipient of the “Leading by Example” Award (78) A development phasing schedule may be established by the Board of Appeals in accordance with ~ 200-8.3. (89) If the development will not be connected to a public water or sewer system, the applicant shall submit plans for an individual water supply system and a septic system designed by a registered sanitary engineer approved by the Greenfield Board of Health and if necessary, the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Quality Engineering. No septic system serving the development shall exceed two thousand (2,000) gallons per day sewage flow as determined under 310 CMR Section 15.02, Title 5 of the State Environmental Code. More than one (1) septic system may serve the site in order to meet this requirement. (910) A special permit for multifamily dwellings shall not be granted unless the Zoning Board of Appeals finds that the requirements of ~ 200-8.3 of this ordinance have been met. --Respectfully submitted, Jeff Sauser Chairperson, Planning Board The City of Greenfield is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity Employer, a designated Green Community and a recipient of the “Leading by Example” Award Official Zoning Map BERNARDSTON City of Greenfield, Massachusetts HA N HTS BARTO L MIL ! The Planning Board requests the initiation of the attached zoning amendments in order to allow residential adaptive reuse of accessory structures by Special Permit. The zoning amendment includes a new section in the “Special Regulations” article, as well as amendments to the “Use Regulations.” Recently, two local landowners have met with the Planning Director to inquire about converting existing accessory structures into residential units either for themselves or their family. The Planning Director proposed an amendment to the existing ADU ordinance to allow for ADUs larger than 900 square feet by Special Permit. However, the proposal to reconsider the ADU ordinance was met with pushback. Sincerely, Caroline Wiglesworth Account Manager, EPIC Entertainment and Sports CC: Andrew Ondrejack, Senior Account Executive TOWN OF HAMILTON TAX CLASSIFICATION FISCAL YEAR 2027 The purpose of the annual Public Hearing on Tax Classification is to record the Select board's vote on classification options of real property each having the potential to impact Hamilton’s FY2027 tax rate. The classification options are summarized as follows: Determination of a discount factor up to 25% for land classified as Open Space The Board of Assessors has determined that there exist no vacant land parcels in Hamilton that meet the statutory definition of open space (chapter land is specifically excluded from open space qualification). Consequently, the adoption of an open space discount by the Select board would fail to provide any taxpayer benefit. For this reason, the Board of Assessors recommends that the Selectboard vote no on the adoption of an Open Space Discount. Residential Exemption Determination of a Residential Exemption up to 35% of the mean residential valuation Adoption of this exemption is typically found in communities with a high percentage of second home properties (i.e., Nantucket) or communities with a high percentage of investor-owned residential properties (i.e., Cambridge). The exemption is designed to provide a measure of tax relief to owner occupants of residential property by shifting the tax burden to non-domiciled residential property owners. However, the overwhelming majority of Hamilton residential property owners consider their homes to be their principal residence. For this reason, the Board of Assessors recommends that the Select board vote no on the adoption of a Residential Exemption. Small Commercial Exemption Determination of Small Commercial Exemption up to 10% of valuation of eligible parcels This exemption is designed to provide a measure of property tax relief to owners of small business properties by shifting the tax burden to owners of larger commercial/industrial properties. The Town of Hamilton simply lacks the diversity of commercial/industrial properties necessary for the effective implementation of this exemption. Consequently, the Board of Assessors recommends the Select board vote no on the adoption of a Small Commercial Exemption. Residential Factor Adoption of Residential Factor to determine the percentage of tax burden to be borne by each class of property Adoption of a Residential Factor by the Select board is required for the purpose of determining the percentage of tax burden to be borne by each class of property. Adoption of a factor of “1.00” results in a single or uniform tax rate for all classes of property while adoption of any other factor will result in both a lower residential rate and higher commercial rate than would be realized under the uniform tax rate approach. Dual tax rate structures are typically found in municipalities with significant percentages of commercial, industrial, and personal property (CIP) valuation (i.e., Beverly). However, only 4% of the total taxable valuation of Hamilton is compromised of CIP valuation. For this reason, the Board of Assessors recommends that the Select board maintain a single tax rate by voting for a Residential Factor of 1.00.
