Markiewicz Assistant Town Manager/Finance Director Town of Hamilton P.O. Box 429 Hamilton, MA 01936 wmarkiewicz@hamiltonma.gov Office: 978-626-5215 Town of Hamilton Financial Policies FINANCIAL RESERVES PURPOSE To help the Town stabilize finances and maintain operations during difficult economic periods, this policy establishes prudent practices for appropriating to and expending reserve funds. With wellplanned sustainability, Hamilton can use its reserves to finance emergencies and other unforeseen needs, to hold money for specific future purposes, or in limited instances, to serve as revenue sources for the annual budget. Reserve balances and policies can also positively impact the Town’s credit rating and consequently its long-term cost to fund major projects. APPLICABILITY This policy pertains to short- and long-range budget decision making and applies to the Board of Selectmen, Town Manager, and Finance and Advisory Committee in those duties. It also applies to the related job duties of the Finance Director and Board of Assessors. POLICY The Town commits to building and maintaining its reserves so as to have budgetary flexibility for unexpected events and significant disruptions in revenue-expenditure patterns and to provide a source of available funds for future capital expenditures. The Town will strive to maintain overall general fund reserves in the level of eight to twelve percent of the annual operating budget. Adherence to this policy will help the Town withstand periods of decreased revenues and control spending during periods of increased revenues. There are multiple types of reserves, including free cash, stabilization funds, retained earnings, and overlay surplus. A. Free Cash The Division of Local Services (DLS) defines free cash as “the remaining, unrestricted funds from operations of the previous fiscal year, including unexpended free cash from the previous year.” DLS must certify free cash before the Town can appropriate it. The Town shall set a year-to-year goal of maintaining its free cash at five percent of the annual general fund budget. To achieve this, the Town Manager will propose budgets with conservative revenue projections, and department heads will carefully manage their appropriations to produce excess income and budget turn backs. Further, budget decision makers will avoid fully depleting the Town’s free cash in any year, so that the succeeding year’s calculation can begin with a positive balance. Moreover, as much as practicable, the Town will limit its use of free cash to funding onetime expenditures (such as capital projects, snow and ice deficits, or emergencies) and will appropriate any excess above five percent of the annual budget to build reserves or to offset unfunded liabilities. B. Stabilization Funds A stabilization fund is a reserve account allowed by state law to set aside monies to be available for future spending purposes, including emergencies or capital expenditures, although it may be appropriated for any lawful purpose. Prior to the adoption of this policy, Hamilton established a general stabilization fund and a recreation fields stabilization fund. Town of Hamilton Financial Policies General Stabilization: The Town will endeavor to maintain a minimum balance of five percent of the current general fund operating budget in its general stabilization fund. The Town will annually appropriate a minimum of half a percent of general fund operating revenues to the general stabilization fund until the target minimum balance is met. Withdrawals from general stabilization should only be used to mitigate emergencies or other unanticipated events that cannot be supported by current general fund appropriations. When possible, withdrawals of funds should be limited to the amount available above the five percent minimum reserve target level. If any necessary withdrawal drives the balance below the minimum level, the withdrawal should be limited to one-third of the general stabilization fund balance. Further, the Town Manager and Finance Director will develop a detailed plan to replenish the fund to the minimum level within the next two fiscal years. Special Purpose Stabilization Funds: Hamilton currently has a special purpose stabilization fund for recreation fields. The Town will annually review the need to appropriate to this fund, and any future special purpose stabilization funds, so that over time they achieve target balances sufficient to cover cash outlays for capital needs. The Town should consider establishing a capital stabilization fund and appropriate annually to this fund. The target for a town-wide capital stabilization fund should minimally equate to the total annual asset depreciation the Finance Director calculates under the requirements of the Government Accounting Standards Board’s Statement 34. Sustaining funding in these reserves enables the Town to pay outright for moderate-range capital expenditures and thereby preserve debt capacity for major, higher-dollar purchases or projects. This approach balances debt with pay-as-you-go practices and protects against unforeseen costs. C. Retained Earnings The Water Department’s finances are managed under an enterprise fund. By accounting for its revenues and expenditures in a fund separate from the general fund, the Town can effectively identify the utility’s true delivery costs—direct, indirect, and capital—and set user fees at a level sufficient to recover them. Under this accounting, the Town may reserve the water operation’s generated surplus For the water enterprise fund, the Town will maintain a minimum reserve amount of twenty percent of the operation’s total budget, but the reserve target may be significantly higher if major infrastructure improvements are necessary. The reserve will be used to provide rate stabilization and to fund major capital projects. To maintain the target reserve level for the enterprise fund requires the Board of Selectmen to annually review, and when necessary, adjust user rates. D. Overlay Surplus The overlay is a reserve the Town uses to offset uncollected property taxes and other unrealized revenue resulting from property tax abatements and exemptions. At the conclusion of each fiscal year, the Board of Assessors will submit to the Town Manager and the Finance Director an update of the overlay reserve with data that includes, but is not limited to, the gross balance, potential abatement liabilities, and any transfers to surplus. If the balance exceeds the amount of potential liabilities, the Board of Selectmen may request that the Board of Assessors vote to declare those balances surplus and available for use in the Town’s capital improvement plan or any other one-time expense. title: Select Board - Public Hearing
text: By Lisa M. Pedroli at 11:33 am, Nov 09, 2026 NOTICE OF CABLE TELEVISION PUBLIC HEARING Please take notice that the Board of Selectmen of the Town of Hopedale, Massachusetts, as Issuing Authority for a cable television license under M.G.L. c.166A, will hold a public hearing on November23,2026 at 7:00 p.m. The public hearing will be held in The Draper Room at 54 Hopedale Street. The purpose of the public hearing will be to determine whether to issue a cable television license to Verizon/Comcast. All applications, reports, statements and license drafts to be considered at the hearing that constitute public records under state law are available for public inspection during regular business hours and for reproduction at a reasonable fee. Members of the public are invited to attend and be heard on the topic: (a) whether the current cable operator is in full compliance with its currently existing cable license; and (b) what are the Town’s future community cable-related needs. NOTE: This notice, or one similar to it, must be published in a newspaper of local circulation, within the municipality, weekly for two successive weeks, the first publication date of which is at least two weeks (14 days) before the date of the hearing. (2) A copy of this notice should be sent, by registered mail, to the cable operator, as they are obligated to engage a reporter to record the proceedings. #396476

title: Tax Classification Hearing - Joint Hearing of the Board of Assessors and Select Board
text: Notice of Town of Hubbardston Board of Assessors Public Hearing 48 Gardner Rd, 1st Floor Meeting Room Hubbardston, MA Monday, November 16, 2026 6:30 PM In accordance with MGL Chapter 40, Section 56 as amended, the Hubbardston Select Board will hold a Public Hearing on Monday, November 16, at 6:30 p.m. at 48 Gardner Rd, Hubbardston, in the 1st Floor Meeting Room. The purpose of this meeting is to determine the percentage of the tax burden to be borne by each class of property for Fiscal 2027, known as the tax classification process. The public hearing is intended as a way for taxpayer to express their views and ask questions about whether the town should adopt different rates for the different classes of property. More information will be posted as we get closer to the hearing for public review. The hearing will include a presentation by the Board of Assessors outlining options available under Chapter 40, Section 56 of the Massachusetts General Laws. At the conclusion of the public hearing the Select Board shall determine whether or not tax classification shall be applied for the Fiscal Year 2027 tax rate. Currently the Town of Hubbardston taxes at a single tax rate for all property classes. All concerned taxpayers are encouraged to attend to present their views orally or submit them in writing to the office.

MASON, Town Administrator Chair to note: This meeting may be recorded and will be available on the town website. I. PUBLIC COMMENT Ill. OLD BUSINESS a. Update on mall property IV. ADJOURNMENT Rules of Procedure for Board Meetings of Lanesborough Select Board Meetings I. AGENDA A. The Town Administrative Assistant, in consultation with the Town Administrator and Chairman of the Select Board shall prepare an Agenda for the Select Board meetings. B. Any requests for matters to be placed on the agenda shall be submitted in writing to the Town Administrative Assistant by noon three business days prior to regularly scheduled meetings. Anyone requesting items be placed on the agenda shall provide the topic of the item and sufficient information and detail so as to provide a reasonable notice of the nature and purpose of the agenda item. C. Agendas will be posted a minimum of 48 hours in advance of any meeting on our Town website and Town bulletin board. TL Ow > Those wishing to speak in the public comment portion of the agenda shall provide their name and the topic of their comment. Topics shall be limited to matters of concern, official action or deliberation which are or may be before the Select Board. MEETINGS Public Notice of the meetings shall be advertised and posted by the Administrative Assistant as required by law. The Chairman of the Select Board shall direct the meeting. In the absence of the Chairman, the senior member of the Select Board shall direct the meeting and shall have all powers and duties of the Chairman. The Modern Rules of Order shall be used to conduct the meeting unless otherwise modified by these Rules or altered by the Select Board. The Lanesborough Select Board shall be addressed by their respective titles. Residents and/or taxpayers may use audio or stenographic recorders to record all or any portion of the meeting. Said recorders shall be operated from the area set aside for the general public seating and may not be placed on the Select Board’s table without prior consent of the Chairman. Video recorders may be used to record all or any portion of a public meeting. The operator of the recorder shall remain seated in the area set aside for the general public or stand in the rear or to the side of the general public seating area so as to not interfere in any way with the activities of the Select Board or the ability of the general public to observe the Board. PUBLIC COMMENT Residents and taxpayers of Lanesborough shall have the right to speak in the meetings during the Public Comment portion of the agenda. In order to conduct meetings in an orderly and productive manner the following rules and regulations shall govern such speakers: Comment from residents/taxpayers shall be received only after the speaker is recognized by the Chairman. The speaker shall announce his or her name and address prior to addressing the Select Board. The Chairman may rule out-of-order scandalous, impertinent, irrelevant, and redundant comments, or comments that attempt to disrupt or needlessly protract the proceedings of the meeting. The Chairman may request any individual to leave the meeting and may contact security to that end when that individual does not observe reasonable decorum. Further, the Chairman may request the assistance of law enforcement officers to remove a disorderly person when his/her conduct interferes with the orderly progress of the meeting. The Chairman may call a recess or adjournment to another time when the lack of public decorum interferes with the orderly conduct of the meeting. The Chairman may allocate available time among individuals wishing to comment. Time allocated for the public comment period at each meeting shall not exceed thirty (30) minutes and limited to citizens of Lanesborough unless prior approval is granted by the Lanesborough Select Board. Each speaker will be allotted three (3) minutes to present his or her topic. Said time limitations may be altered or waived at the Chairman’s direction. At the discretion of the Chairman conducting the meeting, a group of citizens registered to address the Select Board on the same issue may be required to designate a spokesperson.

text: 5/2/2026 Amended date: Town Meeting May 2, 2026 ZONING BY-LAWS TOWN OF LEVERETT, MASSACHUSETTS ARTICLE I. PURPOSE. These regulations are enacted to promote the general welfare of the Town of Leverett, to protect the health and safety of its inhabitants, to encourage the most appropriate use of land throughout the town, to increase the amenities of the town, and to reduce the hazard from fire by regulating the location and use of buildings and the area of open space around them, all as authorized by the provisions of the Zoning Act, M.G.L.A. ch. 40A, as amended, and by Article 89 of the Amendments to the Constitution. ARTICLE II. USE AND DIMENSIONAL REGULATIONS. 2100. Districts. 2110. Establishment. For the purposes of this By-Law, the Town of Leverett is hereby divided into the following districts: Residential/Village ... Residence/Rural ... Rural Outlying Residential …… General Business ... Commercial ...… RV RR RO GB COM Seven additional “overlay” districts are also hereby created: an Aquifer Protection District (pursuant to Section 4300), a Flood Hazard District (pursuant to Section 4400), a Stream and Lake Protection District (pursuant to Section 4500), a Scenic Road Protection District (pursuant to Section 4600), a Rattlesnake Gutter Overlay District (pursuant to Section 4700), an Upper Elevation Site Plan Review Overlay District (pursuant to Section 4960), and a Wireless Telecommunications Overlay District (pursuant to Section 4900). The boundaries of these districts are defined and set forth on the map entitled, “Zoning Map, Leverett, Mass.,” dated March 11, 2008, as may be subsequently amended by vote of Town Meeting. This map is on file with the Town Clerk. This map and all explanatory matter therein are hereby made a part of this Zoning By-Law. 2120. Boundary Definition. Except when labeled to the contrary, boundary or dimension lines shown approximately following or terminating at street, railroad, or utility easement center or layout lines, boundary or lot lines at water body shoreline or the channel of a stream, shall be construed to be actually at those lines; when shown approximately parallel, perpendicular, or at an angle to such lines shall be construed to be actually parallel, perpendicular, or at an angle thereto. When not located in any other way, boundaries shall be determined by scale from the map. The Rural Outlying (RO) Residential District shall commence 500 feet from the edge of the Right of Way of the road layout. 2130. Existing Lots. Where a district boundary line divides any lot existing at the time such line is adopted, the use regulations for any district in which the lot has frontage on a street may be extended not more than forty (40) feet into the other district. 2200. Use Regulations. 2210. General. No structure shall be erected or used or land used except as set forth in Section 2230, "Use Regulation Schedule", or in Section 2240, "Accessory Buildings and Uses", unless exempted by Section 2240, or by statute. Symbols employed below shall mean the following: Y - A permitted use. N - An excluded or prohibited use. SP - A use authorized under special permit as provided under Section 5300. SPR - Site Plan Review required as provided under Section 3900. 2220. Applicability. When an activity might be classified under more than one of the following uses, the more specific classification shall govern; if equally specific, the more restrictive shall govern, if equally specific, the more restrictive shall govern. 2230. Use Regulation Schedule. Districts 2231. Principal Uses. (For Accessory uses, see Section 2240.) RV RR RO GB CO Y Y Y Y Y Y N N Y N N Y N SPR Y N N Y N N SP SP Y SP SP Y SP SP Y SP SP Y SP SP Y Residential Uses (see Section 4880) Dwelling Single Family, shall include manufactured homes Two-family dwelling Multi-family dwelling (3 or more units) Flexible Development Non-family accommodations (boarding house, etc.) with 2 or 3 rooms for let Bed & Breakfast with 5 rooms or less to let Recreational occupancy of camping vehicle for not more than 14 consecutive days in any one month period 2 Districts RV RR RO GB CO Agriculture, silviculture, horticulture, Y floriculure or viticulture exempt from zoning regulations pursuant to G.L. c. 40A, s. 3 Other Agricultural Uses including Marijuana N Cultivation Private commercial campgrounds N Private commercial outdoor recreation area SP Commercial earth removal N Conservation area, public park Y Y Y Y Y SP SP SP SP SP SP N Y SP SP N Y N SP SP Y N SP SP Y SP SP Y SP SP Y SP SP Y SP SP Y SP SP Y SP Y SP SP Y SP SP Y SP SP Y SP SP Y SP S Y N SP SP N SP Y N SP SP N SP Y N SP SP N SP Y SP SP SP SP SP Y SP SP SP SP N N N N N N N N N N N N N N N N SP SP SP SP N SP SP SP SP 2232. Other Principal Uses. Having attributes similar to a use permitted (Y or SP) above Other principal uses ** = See Section 4970 for requirements and conditions, including requirement of SPR and SP ***= See Section 4900 for requirements and conditions 4 2240. Accessory Buildings and Uses. Any use permitted as a principal use is also allowed as an accessory use, as are others customarily accessory and incidental to permitted principal uses. 2241. Home Occupations. A business or profession may be engaged in as an accessory use of a dwelling by a resident of that dwelling, upon issuance of a special permit by the Board of Appeals, if conforming to the following conditions: a. The occupation or profession shall be carried on wholly within the principal building or within building or other structure accessory thereto. b. Not more than thirty (30) percent of the combined floor area of the residence and any accessory structures shall be used in the home occupation. c. The home occupation shall be accommodated within an existing structure without extension thereof. d. Not more than two persons not a member of the household shall be employed on the premises in the home occupation. e. Except for a permitted sign, there shall be not more than 300 square feet of exterior storage of materials, and no other exterior indication of the home occupation, or other variation from the residential character of the premises. f. No disturbance shall be caused as defined in Section 3420. g. Traffic generated shall not exceed volumes normally expected in a residential neighborhood. h. Parking generated shall be accommodated off-street, other than in a required front yard, and shall not occupy more than 10% of lot area. i. Home occupations in an Aquifer Protection District shall not use or store hazardous materials, as defined herein, in quantities greater than 5 gallons or 5 lbs. 2241.5 Small Home Occupations. If all of the conditions of Section 2241 are met and not more than one person not a member of the household shall be employed on the premises in the home occupation, and there shall be no exterior storage, then the business or profession may be engaged in as of right as an accessory use of a dwelling by a resident of the dwelling. 5 2242. Animals. Horses and other animals, including pigs, chickens, and other farm animals, used for non-commercial or non-agricultural purposes, may be stabled (as an accessory use) within the RR and RV districts. 2243. Accessory Scientific Uses. Uses, whether or not on the same parcel as activities permitted as a matter of right, which are necessary in connection with scientific research or scientific development or related production, may be permitted upon the issuance of a special permit by the Board of Appeals, provided that the Board finds that the proposed use does not substantially derogate from the public good. 2244. One house trailer, camping vehicle, or tent may be used as an accessory dwelling on a lot for not more than thirty (30) days in any twelve (12) month period. One mobile dwelling unit that does not qualify as an ADU or meet the conditions of Section 2400 may be used as an accessory dwelling on a lot for not more than thirty (30) days in any twelve (12) month period. One house trailer, mobile home, camping trailer, or similar vehicle, not used for dwelling purposes, may be stored out of doors on a lot. 2245. No building that does not qualify as an ADU or meet the conditions of Section 2400 shall be used as a dwelling unit if it is located on a lot with a principal structure serving as a residence. 2246. Rental of a single room in a principal residential structure is permitted as an accessory use. 2247. Dimensional Regulation: Accessory Uses. Accessory structures may not be placed within required yards, except that permitted signs may be located within a required front yard, and a permitted one-story accessory structure may be located within a required rear yard provided that it occupies not more than 25% of the required yard, and provided that it is not located within 10 feet of any property line , and a structure that qualifies as an ADU and meets the conditions of Section 2400 may be located within a required yard provided that it meets all dimensional requirements that apply to singlefamily dwelling units. 2248. Temporary Storage Units related to the construction of a home or business can be placed on a lot for 6 months or less provided that all setback requirements are met (see Section 2340. Dimensional Schedule). Extension of the time period to no more than 12 months may be granted by Special Permit from the Zoning Board of Appeals. 2250. Nonconforming Uses. Any use or structure not conforming with this By-Law may be continued if the use or structure was lawfully existing at the time it became nonconforming, subject to the following: 2251. Alteration, Extension, or Change. As provided in M.G.L.A. ch. 40A, s.6, a nonconforming single or two-family dwelling may be altered or extended provided that the Building Inspector determines that doing so does not increase 6 the nonconforming nature of said structure. Other pre-existing nonconforming 7 structures or uses may be extended, altered, or changed in use on special permit from the Board of Appeals, in accordance with Section 5300 herein, upon a finding by the Board that such alteration, extension, or change will not be substantially more detrimental to the neighborhood than the existing nonconforming use. Once changed to a conforming use, no structure or land shall be permitted to revert to a nonconforming use. 2252. Abandonment. A nonconforming use, which has been abandoned, discontinued for a period of two years (five years for agriculture, horticulture, floriculture, silviculture or viticulture), or changed to a conforming use, shall not be reestablished, and any future use of the premises shall conform to this Zoning By-Law. 2253. Restoration. Any legally existing nonconforming building or structure may be reconstructed if destroyed by fire or other accidental or natural cause if such reconstruction is commenced within twenty-four (24) months from the date of the catastrophe (unless a longer period is granted by special permit by the Board of Appeals). Notwithstanding the above, any structure so restored shall not exceed in volume or area the original non-conforming structure, except that where the original structure was non-conforming by virtue of its relation to the set-back, rear yard, or side yard requirements of this By-Law, any restoration may exceed in volume or area the original non-conforming structure as long as the foundation of the restored structure is not in greater noncompliance, as to set-back, rear yard, or side yard, than the original structure. 2254. Premises may be changed from one category of nonconforming use to another only on special permit from the Board of Appeals. Such special permit shall be granted only for uses no more damaging or inharmonious with the environs than the use being replaced. 2255. Additions and accessory buildings which are associated with existing residences that are non-conforming by reason of being closer to lot boundaries than is permitted by these by-laws may be built as close, but not closer, to the lot boundaries than the existing residence. 2300. Dimensional Requirements. 2310. General. No structure shall be erected or used, premises used, or lot changed in size or shape except in conformity with the requirements of this section, unless exempted by this By-Law or by statute (see especially M.G.L.A. ch. 40A, s.6). 8 2320. Multiple Principal Structures. Not more than one principal structure shall be erected on a lot, unless otherwise authorized in this By-Law, or unless pursuant to a special permit issued by the Zoning Board of Appeals in accordance with Section 5300 herein and the following conditions: 2321. No principal building shall be located in relation to another principal building on the same lot, or on an adjacent lot, so as to cause danger from fire. 2322. All principal buildings on the lot shall be served by access ways suitable for fire, police, and emergency vehicles; 2323. All of the multiple principal buildings on the same lot shall be accessible via pedestrian walkways connected to the required parking for the premises, and to each principal building. 2330. Rear Lots. Rear lots shall not be allowed in General Business or Commercial Districts. Individual lots in Residence Districts need not have the required amount of street frontage, provided that all of the following conditions can be met for each individual lot lacking such frontage: 2331. The area of said lot is at least double the minimum area normally required for the district. 2332. A building line is designated on the plan, and the width of the lot at that line equals or exceeds the number of feet normally required for street frontage in the district. For the purpose of this section 2332 only, the building line for a rear lot shall designate the line behind which the principal building on the lot shall be built. 2333. Lot width is at no point less than 30 feet, and lot frontage is not less than 30 feet. Frontage shall meet all of the requirements contained in the definition for "frontage" in Article VI, herein. 2334. Not more than one (1) rear lot shall be created from a property, or a set of contiguous properties held in common ownership as of April 30, 1988. Documentation to this effect shall be submitted to the Planning Board along with the application for Approval Not Required or Definitive Subdivision Plans under the Subdivision Control Law. The Building Inspector shall not issue a building permit for any rear lot without first establishing that compliance with this provision has been determined by the Planning Board. 2335. At the time of the creation of the rear lot, it shall be held in common and contiguous ownership with the front lot. 9 2336. The Planning Board shall not approve an application for creation of a rear lot unless the applicant submits a plan under the Subdivision Control Law depicting both the rear lot and the front lot from which the rear lot was created. 2337. Where a single-family structure is situated on a rear lot, the front, rear, and side yards shall equal or exceed those required in the district. text: TOWN OF MONSON) RECEIVED REGULAR MEETING AGENDA TOWN CLERK, MONSON, MA DATE: SPECIAL DATE - Monday, November 16, 2026 TIME: 7:00 PM LOCATION: 110 MAIN STREET ~ Public Meeting Room Call To Order We have assistive listening devices available for anyone who needs them. If you’d like to use one, please let a staff member know at any time during the meeting. M-PACT is recording this meeting. Any person may also record this meeting, after notice to the Select Board Chair. In order to run the meeting more efficiently, the Chair requests that persons who would like to speak on an agenda item, do so during public comment. No questions from the public will be taken during the business portion of the meeting. Public questions should be directed to the Executive Assistant at rmorse@monson-ma.gov and will be handled accordingly. Pledge of Allegiance Public Comment The Select Board shall provide a period not to exceed 15 minutes at the beginning of its semi-monthly meetings. Generally, there will be no discussion of topics raised. The following rules are intended to provide a structured format whereby constituents can provide information about, or comment on, items of select board business only. Only an individual recognized by the chair can speak. Audience members may not interrupt a recognized speaker nor the discussion of the body. The speaker is limited to two minutes for their comments. If they have additional remarks beyond this time limit, they may submit them in writing to the Select Board. Each speaker is allowed to speak only once during the public comment period and cannot yield their time to another speaker. The speaker must exercise conduct in an "orderly and peaceable manner". The Board encourages speakers to avoid repeating themselves, and if multiple speakers wish to talk on the same subject, they are encouraged to choose one spokesperson. The speaker may not approach the select board table, including to provide handouts or other materials. If a speaker or audience member violates any rule herein above, is disturbing or impeding the meeting, or threatens violence or incites imminent lawless conduct, the chair shall direct that such conduct shall immediately cease, and if it does not, the chair has the authority to stop the violator, take away any remaining time to speak, and/or in egregious cases, remove the violator from the meeting. Interim Contracts Check this option for an Interim Contract with a new Contractor whenever an existing Contract has been or will be terminated or suspended for any reason or whenever a current Contractor is unable to complete full performance under a Contract. An Interim Contract may be offered to the bidder that offered the next Best Value response under the original procurement and under the same terms and prices offered in that bidder’s original response. The duration of an Interim Contract shall be limited to the remaining time available under the duration stated in the original RFR, including any options to renew. If the Department is unable to negotiate a Contract with any of the original bidders who submitted responses, in their original rank order according to Best Value, and under the same terms as offered in their original response, the Department will be required to conduct a new competitive procurement. RILEY COUNCILLOR AT LARGE – ZIQIANG SUSAN YUAN CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-150 ORDERED: November 09, 2026 R ESOLUTION OPPOSING EFFORTS TO WAIVE STATE CONSUMERPROTECTION LAWS FOR A LONG-TERM LEASE OF QUINCY’S BIGGEST PARCEL OF PUBLICLY OWNED OPEN SPACE WHEREAS, Quarry Hills Associates (QHA) currently holds a long-term lease with the City of Quincy for approximately 240 acres of municipal property operating as the Granite Links Golf Club; and WHEREAS, the current lease agreement has 30 years remaining in its term; and WHEREAS, state law limits the lease of public land to 30 years (MGL Chapter 40 section 3) and requires leases of public land to be put out to bid (MGL Chapter 30B section 16); and WHEREAS, the mayor and previous council sent a home-rule petition to state legislators asking for these requirements to be waived so that Quarry Hills Associates could sign a new lease for an additional 50 years, ending in 2106; and WHEREAS, Quincy’s state senator paused action on the petition in the Senate over uncertainty about whether the deal was in the best interests of Quincy taxpayers, requesting a formal audit (as requested by the City Council) and analyses of the proposed lease’s cost and hospitality terms; and WHEREAS, the House then inserted the petition’s language in a package of budget amendments that it passed, circumventing the home-rule petition’s deliberative process; and WHEREAS, that leaves the long-term fate of Quincy’s largest single piece of publicly owned open space subject to a back-room process where budget amendments are traded like baseball cards; and WHEREAS, deep concerns have been raised by citizen advocates, fiscal watchdogs, and state legislators regarding the lack of research on the terms of the current and proposed leases and the implications of future construction at the site; and ORDER NO. 2026 – 150 Page 2 of 2 WHEREAS, residents have expressed ongoing concerns regarding public access to the land, promised trail connections to the Blue Hills Reservation, traffic, and maintenance of the site’s athletic fields; and WHEREAS, entering a commitment that binds the City of Quincy and its taxpayers through the next century requires the highest threshold of community engagement, independent financial auditing, and due diligence to ensure maximum public benefit; NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the Quincy City Council formally opposes any attempt to waive state laws that protect residents by limiting the lengths of leases of public land and by requiring open bids for leases of public land; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Quincy City Council urges the Massachusetts General Court to reject any consolidated budget amendments, home-rule petition, or other legislative maneuver that seeks to authorize this new lease without a comprehensive, independent fiscal analysis in the form of an audit and studies of cost and hospitality terms; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Quincy City Council requests that the Mayor’s administration halt lease negotiations and perform the requested financial accountability and due diligence to ensure that Quincy taxpayers get the most from any revenue-sharing formula; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that any proposed change to the current lease be returned to the Quincy City Council for discussion and oversight; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that a copy of this resolution be sent to Quincy’s state legislative delegation, the Senate president, the chairs of the House and Senate Ways and Means Committees, the Governor, and the Lieutenant Governor. Waiver applications should be made to the Licensing Department who shall review the request with relevant City departments and receive their approvals before forwarding the application with comment to the City Council for consideration. Any second and subsequent requests for waivers shall only be considered by the Licensing Department if the application is accompanied by documentation proving consistent sales and use of the outdoor dining area over the prior winter period when a waiver was granted. In the event of ice and/or snow, any sidewalk adjacent to the outdoor dining area must be kept free and clear of all snow and ice by the business. The City is not responsible for any damage to outdoor dining areas or associated furniture, furnishings, equipment, etc. due to City snow removal operations. Restaurants with approved winter waivers must keep outdoor seating areas and access to those areas, whether on the public way or private property, free and clear of snow and ice. A minimum clearance of 48” is required, while a clearance of at least 60” is preferred. The City reserves the right to reject future winter waiver applications from businesses that receive a winter waiver but do not utilize their outdoor dining area for consistent outdoor dining service over the winter season.” Action Contemplated Councillor Hapworth Moved Adopted or Refer to Comm. on Ord., Licenses and Legal Affairs Voted Ordered: Parking at all City owned lots, garages, and on-street spaces shall be free of charge on the following days: 1. Hoctor, P. Ellis, C. Holden, D. Sullivan G. Dunham, Town Manager Mr. Hoctor opened the meeting at 6:00 PM. PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE None. PUBLIC COMMENT REVIEW AND APPROVAL OF MINUTES Mr. Holden moved to approve the minutes of October 8, 2026. Seconded by Mr. Ellis. Approved unanimously (5-0) • • • • TOWN MANAGER REPORT The next Board meeting will be on November12, 2026 at 2:00 PM. There will be a Tri-Board meeting on December 3rd. The police did their annual review of liquor license inspections. Melissa will notify the license holders. The DOR will be trying to auction off the all-alcohol license from Carluccio’s on Tuesday, October 27th at noon at 100 Rte. 6A Wastewater update: the Oakridge and Forestdale Title 5 projects are complete. We are waiting for as built drawings to be submitted and reviewed and, once done, ﬁnal payment will be made to the contractor. Removal of unusable equipment will need a separate RFP. The middle/high school system is up and operational awaiting a ﬁnal check. Testing has been going on at Kiah’s Wood – monitoring wells with test holes onsite. There is a new state grant program for only Cape Cod; we will attempt to apply to continue efforts on three bays. The CWRMP update process is being ﬁne-tuned; we thank the water district for their help. Relative to the situation at JBCC, we have not received state feedback since a year ago; monthly meetings with the Base officials and Converge continue. Questions/Comments Mr. Hoctor asked about who would be overseeing the high school wastewater system. It needs oversight by a professional. We are asking for quotes for estimated monthly charges. Mr. Sullivan asked if there had been any word on the Verizon lease; not yet. CORRESPONDENCE/STATEMENTS/ANNOUNCEMENTS/FUTURE ITEMS/FOLLOW-UP Mr. Holden reported that lockdown drills at the schools went well. A new member of the Bikeway/Pedestrian Committee has been confirmed. There have been additional markings on the Service Rd. shared use trail at Quaker Meetinghouse and it is hoped that additional speed markings will be added at Round Hill Rd. Additional grant applications are expected to address crossings on Cotuit as well as Town Neck Rd.; the grant application is due October 31st. It is hoped that the Cape Cod Commission will accept the rack and equipment application. At the School Committee meeting the student representative submitted his initial report highlighting the bonfire event, which was well done. Congratulations to Grace Smith who won a race run out of 73 participants at the Cape Cod Fairgrounds. The Committee has requested commencement of negotiations from the Sandwich Education Association for successor collective bargaining agreements. The administration of a survey was undertaken to obtain student feedback in six areas: high expectations with rigorous learning, connection and community, whole child focus, customization, agency, and relevance. These cover grades three through twelve and results will be shared with the Committee. The Director of Student Services provided an update on the department including Department of Elementary and Secondary Education reviews, internal compliance improvements, professional development to include co-teaching and upgrades to the postgraduate program at Sandwich Middle/High school. Parents are invited to join the Sandwich Special Education Advisory Council (SEAPAC) by reaching out to seapacsandwich@gmail.com. On October 25th the Sandwich Police Department with support from the Sandwich Emergency Response team will be holding their Truck or Treat event at Heritage Gardens from 10 AM to noon. Enjoy a safe and happy Halloween. STAFF MEETING 6:05 PM Public Hearing New Private Livery License for ConJac Enterprises, LLC, 3 Little Acorn Lane Forestdale – Daniel J. Sherwood, Manager Mr. Hoctor read the public hearing notice. Mr. Holden moved to go into the public hearing. Seconded by Mr. Ellis. Approved unanimously. Mr. Sherwood said that this would be a sole operator business exclusively and with no advertising. He will provide airport and ferries transport and non-emergency medical appointment transport. He has one vehicle with livery plates and will submit his license paperwork next week and is awaiting his permission from MassPort. He has Progressive Insurance. All checks were fine. His office will be in his vehicle primarily. If he decides to expand, he will need to amend his license. Public input – an across the street neighbor saw this advertised and wanted to see what it was all about. He wondered if it would involve more vehicles in his driveway – no, only the one vehicle. Mr. Holden moved to close the public hearing. Seconded by Mr. Ellis. Approved unanimously. Mr. Holden moved to approve the New Private Livery License for ConJac Enterprises, LLC, 3 Little Acorn Lane Forestdale – Daniel J. Sherwood, Manager. Seconded by Mr. Ellis. Approved unanimously. OLD BUSINESS FY ’28 Budget Timeline & Process, Initial FY ’28 Thoughts The proposed timeline is in the agenda packet. Most of the milestones and time of month will stay the same. Mr. Dunham reported initial thoughts. This is a “vanilla” general government budget, primarily level services. We will not know about State aid for several months. Health insurance is increased again but we won’t hear about rates until mid-February. Free cash is not a problem; the capital budget will be slightly lower. There will be a draft operating budget, and he will be seeing department heads over the next two weeks. Relative to gas expenses at the DPW – so far, so good but the rate is currently locked in. We will be going out for a new bid soon. Mr. Hoctor asked about fuel expenses at the Marina. They are on them and focused on not exceeding their budget. Mr. Hoctor hopes they continue to manage what they have on hand and hope prices decrease. Mr. Dunham said that the Town will have a $300,000 to $350,000 match for the Marina Harbor Walk project. Planned DPW/Fire Substation Project Update – 11/12/26, 2:00 PM On November 12th, the team will be presenting to the Board; there will be ongoing public outreach. Other Matters Not Reasonably Anticipated for Old Business The Arts Alliance will be having two events at Town Hall this weekend. The floors are done, both main floor and stage. It should be fine to meet there on November 12th. There are 25 staff at the JBCC National Guard, and they are being outstanding at being conscious of the environment. Formal Colonel Matt Porter has been made a General. NEW BUSINESS Recommended Board & Committee Appointments Mr. Holden moved to appoint John Casey as a full member to the Recreation Committee. Seconded by Mr. Ellis. Approved unanimously. Mr. Holden moved to appoint Justin Jorgensen as an alternate member to the Zoning Board of Appeals. Seconded by Mr. Ellis. Approved unanimously. Mr. Holden moved to approve a change from alternate to full member of the Commission on Disability for Joann Lebherz. Seconded by Mr. Ellis. Approved unanimously. Other Matters Not Reasonably Anticipated for New Business None. None. PUBLIC COMMENT CLOSING REMARKS Mr. Holden says to continue to pray for peace, restraint among leaders, and protection of innocent life with justice guided by wisdom in our world. ADJOURNMENT Mr. Holden moved to adjourn the meeting. Seconded by Mr. Ellis. Approved unanimously. Public Hearing: The Warren Board of Selectmen will hold a public hearing on Monday, November 30, 2026, at 6:00pm at the Shepard Municipal Building, 48 High Street, Warren, MA, first floor Selectmen’s meeting room on the issue of tax classification. The Board of Assessors will present data relative to the setting of the FY 2027 tax rate and its effect on taxpayers for the different classification of properties in Warren. The Selectmen will vote whether a single tax rate will be maintained for residential, commercial, and industrial properties and whether an open space discount and/or residential and/or small commercial exemption will be approved for Fiscal Year 2027. The hearing will include a presentation by the Board of Assessors outlining the options available under Chapter 40, Section 56 of the Massachusetts General Laws. Currently the Town taxes at a single tax rate for all property classes. PROPOSED MOTION: SUMMARY: Project Seconded By: Moved By: Condition(s): VOTED: Yea Nay Abstain Wellfleet She11fish Department ~ •C.CCIIII 300 Main Street, Wellfleet, Massachusetts 02667 DATE: TO: FROM: RE: November 6, 2026 Selectboard Chair Yeston, Vice Chair Carboni, members Lyons, Wolf, Curley Shellfish Constable Nancy Civetta Proposed new CMRs outlining police powers under the Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission (POST), which would effectively strip Shellfish Constables of their authority Dear Selectboard members, Thank you for accommodating this time-sensitive issue on your Tuesday, Nov. 10, Selectboard agenda. Here is a time line of how this issue unfolded: • Friday, October 23: Johnny and I took a call from the Mass. Shellfish Officers Assn. (MSOA) Clerk Donovan McElligatt, who is Shellfish Constable for Oak Bluffs. He brought to our attention a new CMR the MSOA Board of Directors had just learned about, which if promulgated could strip Shellfish Constables of their authority. He reached out to us because we work for the Town with the largest aquaculture industry in the Commonwealth and are very involved with MSOA. He forwarded me his DRAFT public comment letter to help us understand the complicated issues and their impacts on how we currently work. • Wednesday, Oct. 28: Johnny and I attended the MSOA Fall Meeting, where a long discussion was held with attending shellfish constables and staff from the Mass. Division of Marine Fisheries about the impacts of these proposed CMRs. The membership agreed that we should request an extension to the public comment period (attached) and craft a letter that we could each use to bring this issue to the attention of our Town Administrations and Appointing Authorities. • Wednesday, November 4: Although I am not on the MSOA BOD, I was invited to join their call to approve the letter of request for the comment period extension and the DRAFT Notice to Municipalities. I received a copy of the DRAFT Notice to Municipalities. Next steps on outreach and actions were also laid out. I then requested a meeting with the Town Administrator. Chatham Shellfish Constable and MSOA President Renee Gagne had a meeting with Rep. Luddy and a legislative aide from Sen. Cyr's office briefing them on the issues. • Thursday, Nov. 5: I sent the TA copies of the DRAFT Notice to Municipalities and the DRAFT MSOA public comment letter from Oak Bluffs Shellfish Constable Donovan McElligatt for review before our meeting. (Both attached.) • Friday, Nov. 6: I met with the TA and the ATA and briefed them on the issue and next steps that MSOA members are taking and what we need from our regulatory authority, the Selectboard, which is also the Town's executive authority. I reached out to Shellfish Advisory Board Chair Chris Merl to discuss the issue. • The public comment oeriod opened on Oct. 23, the day we found out about this. It closes at 5 p.m. on November 17. There is a virtual public hearing on November 17, from 10 a.m. to 12 noon. wellfleet-ma. gov/shel lfish-deoartment Phone (508) 349-0325 nancy.civetta@wellfleet-ma.gov C[} Here is an update prepared by the President of the Mass. Shellfish Officers' Association (MSOA), Chatham Shellfish Constable Renee Gagne. I have edited it for third person, dates and to provide context. • • • • • • • • • The Mass. Division of Marine Fisheries (DMF) confirmed with their legal team that shellfish constables do fall under the purview of POST certification requirements. They also mentioned Harbormasters and cited their training did not provide all the necessary requirements. DMF also said they were limited in their ability to advocate for us. DMF suggested that this is a legislative issue and a "carve out" could constitute a legislative fix for shellfish constables and harbormasters. MSOA met on Wed., Nov. 4, to approve a letter to request a comment period extension, which was subsequently submitted to the POST Commission. MSOA drafted a Notice to Municipalities for their members to discuss with their appointing authorities. This was approved as a DRAFT for each town to tailor according to its Shellfish Constable responsibilities, duties and activities. Representative Hadley Luddy reached out to Renee and scheduled a Teams meeting with her team and an aide from Senator Cyr's office for Wed., Nov. 4. They were very supportive and will begin reaching out to the Coastal Caucus and Cape delegation to make them aware of the implications and work to discuss options. They discussed the extent of authorities required to conduct the enforcement duties shellfish constables currently provide to protect natural resources and public health, e.g. capability to search and seize catch. John Pappalardo from the Cape Cod Commercial Fishermen's Alliance also asked to meet with Renee on Wed., Nov. 4, and was made aware of the issue and will provide comment and reach out to their contacts. The Fishermen's Alliance also submitted a request to POST to extend the public comment period. MSOA is recommending to members that their appointing authority reach out to the Mass. Municipal Assn., their local representatives, and for Cape folks, the Cape and Island Municipal Association and Mark Forest (or local County rep). MSOA and DMF are still looking to find the proper venue to discuss our own certification course and incorporate training that would satisfy POST requirements. The Town Administrator and I are asking you to please authorize us to advocate for Shellfish Constables being "exempt from" or "carved out of' the requirements in the newly proposed 555 CMR 3.0 by the POST Commission at public hearings, with public comment, with municipal and state agencies, and our elected officials, etc. I will provide you with a public comment letter to sign. Thank you, ,. 1&-;;£,o Shellfish Constable Phone (508) 349-0325 Wellfleet Shellfish Department Fax (508) 349-0305 Massachusetts Shellfish Officers Association 261 George Ryder Road· Chatham, MA· 02633 November 4, 2026 To: Massachusetts Peace Officers Standards and Training Commission Re: Formal Request for Extension of Public Comment Period - Proposed 555 CMR 3.00: Regulated Agencies, Officers, and Conduct To Whom It May Concern: On behalf of the Massachusetts Shellfish Officers Association {MSOA), we respectfully submit this formal request for an extension of the public comment period for the proposed regulation, 555 CMR 3.00: Regulated Agencies, Officers, and Conduct. The proposed regulations were brought to the attention of much of our membership during the MSOA's annual Fall Meeting held on October 28, 2026. Upon reviewing the proposal, our members, who serve as appointed Shellfish Constables under the authority of Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 130, Section 98, expressed significant concern regarding the potential implications of these regulations. Specifically, the proposed regulations appear to have far-reaching implications for the historical statutory authority and responsibilities of Shellfish Constables, as well as for the autonomy and shellfish management practices of the local municipalities they serve. The potential scope of these changes warrants careful consideration and a meaningful opportunity for those directly affected to understand and respond to the proposal. Given the recent notification to much of our membership and the potential magnitude of the proposed regulatory changes, the current comment period does not provide sufficient time for our members to fully evaluate the proposal, communicate its potential impacts to their respective municipal officials and governing bodies, and facilitate informed input from local stakeholders. Shellfish management is inherently local, and these proposed changes could have significant consequences for the administration, oversight, and management of shellfish resources in coastal communities throughout the Commonwealth. It is therefore essential that affected municipalities have adequate notice and sufficient time to assess the proposal and provide thoughtful, informed, and substantive comments. Thank you for your consideration. Renee Gagne President, MSOA IMPORTANT MUNICIPAL NOTICE Potential Impact of Proposed Massachusetts POST Commission Regulations on Municipal Enforcement Personnel To: Massachusetts Town Managers and Town Administrators From: Subject: Proposed POST Commission Regulations- Potential Impact on Municipal Enforcement and Inspection Positions Date: Dear Town Manager: I am writing to bring an important regulatory matter to your attention that was discussed during the Massachusetts Shellfish Officers Association (MSOA) annual Fall meeting held on October 28, 2026. Although the discussion initially focused on the potential impact to municipal shellfish officers and harbormasters. the implications may extend considerably further, potentially affecting any municipal employee whose responsibilities include inspections, investigations, questioning. searches, seizures. or enforcement activities. The Massachusetts Peace Officer Standards and Training (POSTI Commission is a state agency responsible for establishing professional standards. training requirements. certification, and accountability for individuals serving in law enforcement positions throughout Massachusetts. The Commission has developed proposed regulations under 555 CMR 3.00- Regulated Agencies, Officers, and Conduct. These regulations raise important questions for municipalities regarding which employees qualify as peace officers under Massachusetts law. which positions may require POST certification, and how the proposed requirements could affect employees who perform specialized regulatory and enforcement duties but are not traditionally employed as police officers. For communities throughout Massachusetts, this is particularly important because many municipal departments rely on specialized personnel to administer and enforce state and local regulations. These positions include. but are not limited to, shellfish officers and constables, harbormasters, building inspectors, health inspectors, and herring wardens. 1. What the proposed regulations could change The proposed regulations seek to clarify which individuals and agencies fall within the Commission's regulatory authority. Of particular concern is the potential emphasis on an individual's actual responsibilities and enforcement activities rather than simply their municipal job title or department. ' Several provisions deserve particular attention: • Expanded definition of law enforcement personnel: An individual's authority, responsibilities, enforcement activities, and relationship to a law enforcement agency may determine whether they fall within POST jurisdiction. • Restrictions on police activities without certification: Individuals determined to be subject to POST requirements could face restrictions or sanctions for performing certain police functions without the appropriate certification. • Municipal accountability: Municipalities could face additional responsibility for knowingly permitting unauthorized police activities or failing to provide appropriate training and supervision. Activities that may raise concerns include arrests, detentions, searches, seizures of evidence or contraband, certain investigations, and other activities traditionally associated with law enforcement. Importantly, this does not necessarily mean that every municipal employee who conducts an inspection, issues a violation notice, or enforces a local regulation will be required to obtain POST certification. The distinction between regulatory enforcement and traditional police functions will be critical. 2. Municipal positions that could be affected The following municipal positions warrant review and clarification: Shellfish Officers and Shellfish Constables - Potentially Significant Impact Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 130, Section 98 specifically authorizes appointed shellfish constables and deputy shellfish constables to enforce shellfish laws and local regulations. The statute also provides limited warrantless arrest authority under specified circumstances involving the inspection of shellfish. This creates an important question: Can a municipal shellfish constable continue exercising the specific enforcement authority granted by state law without POST certification? Shellfish officers are specialized municipal employees responsible for protecting shellfish resources, inspecting commercial and recreational harvesting, enforcing licensing requirements, investigating illegal harvesting and possession, issuing warnings and citations, and responding to public health closures. The Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries has previously recognized that some municipal shellfish constables are not POST-certified and has advised municipalities to consult legal counsel regarding the extent of their enforcement authority. If the proposed regulations restrict certain enforcement activities by non-certified personnel, municipalities may be forced to reconsider how shellfish enforcement is conducted and rely more heavily on local police departments. Harbormasters - Potentially Significant Impact Harbormasters perform a combination of public safety, regulatory, and enforcement responsibilities, including enforcing boating and navigation regulations, investigating mooring and boating violations, managing vessel compliance, responding to marine safety incidents, and coordinating with police, fire, and other enforcement agencies. Certain activities, particularly detentions, investigations, searches, and enforcement actions, could raise questions about whether a harbormaster is performing functions subject to POST certification. Municipalities will need clarification distinguishing routine harbor management and regulatory enforcement from activities that constitute police functions. Building Inspectors - Potential Impact Building inspectors primarily perform regulatory and administrative functions, including construction inspections, building code enforcement, issuing violation notices, requiring corrective action, and referring unresolved matters for administrative or judicial proceedings. Routine inspection and administrative enforcement activities would generally be distinguishable from traditional police duties. However. activities involving detention, searches, or police-style investigations could create additional concerns. Health Inspectors - Potential Impact Health inspectors primarily enforce public health regulations and sanitary codes through food establishment inspections, public health investigations. permitting, violation notices, and corrective action requirements. Routine inspections and administrative enforcement should be distinguished from traditional police activities. Clarification will be important where investigations or other enforcement activities involve powers beyond ordinary regulatory inspection authority. Herring Wardens - Potentially Significant Impact 3 Herring wardens protect municipal herring runs and enforce applicable fishery regulations. Their duties may include monitoring harvesting activity, enforcing seasonal restrictions, investigating unlawful harvesting, and monitoring compliance with municipal and state regulations. Their exposure will depend on their specific statutory authority and whether their duties involve stopping individuals, conducting investigations, searches, or seizures. These positions illustrate why the proposed regulations deserve broader municipal consideration beyond traditional law enforcement departments. 3. Why this matters to municipal government The greatest concern is not necessarily that every affected employee will be required to attend a police academy. Rather, it is that municipalities could face uncertainty regarding which enforcement activities their employees are legally permitted to perform. Potential operational and financial consequences include: 1. Losa of enforcement capabilities: Employees may have to discontinue certain activities if they are classified as police duties requiring certification. 2. Increased reliance on police departments: Municipalities may need to redirect arrests, detentions, investigations, and other enforcement responsibilities to local police departments. 3. Increased municipal costs: Additional training, certification, staffing, overtime, and administrative expenses could create significant financial burdens. 4. Reduced enforcement coverage: Specialized municipal employees often provide enforcement coverage during early morning hours, weekends, seasonal activities, and other periods when traditional police coverage may be limited. 5. Potential municipal liability: Municipalities may face additional exposure if employees perform activities determined to be outside their authorized scope or if appropriate training and supervision are lacking. These concerns are particularly important for smaller communities that rely on specialized personnel to provide regulatory oversight and protect public resources without maintaining separate police enforcement divisions for every municipal function. 4. text: Select Board Hybrid Meeting Agenda Tuesday November 10, 2026, 6:00PM Lower Meeting Room, Town Hall Meeting link: Select Board Meeting Link Meeting ID: 822 8211 8413 Call-in number: 929-205-6099 Public Meeting Access Under state law, public bodies may continue holding hybrid and fully remote meetings without a quorum of the public body physically present, as long as adequate, alternative access is provided. Adequate, alternative access includes the opportunity to attend a hybrid or fully remote meeting, and a link to join the meeting is included in this Open Meeting Law posting. This meeting will be held over Zoom using the “meeting” setup. However, if there are interruptions, the meeting will be temporarily shut down and restarted as a “webinar”, which format Town Counsel has confirmed is compliant with law . Under those circumstances, the meeting ID will remain the same. If the webinar format is used, members of the public will only be able to see the Board members on the screen and will need to raise their virtual “hand” if they wish to be recognized to speak. If anyone is unable to rejoin, please contact the Town Manager at townmanager@westonma.gov. Be aware that members of the public will be placed in the “waiting room” during any portion of a meeting held in executive session, and, if the Board returns to open session after the conclusion of the executive session, allowed back into the meeting at that point. Agenda Time Agenda item 6:00 PM Call to Order 6:01 PM Resident Comments Historic Commission Appointment 6:11 PM • • • Alicia Primer John Thompson James Steadle 6:25 PM Review Articles and Vote Positions on the Articles and Set Members to Provide Motions 7:00 PM PUBLIC HEARING: Grant of Location, 34 Chiltern Road 7:20 PM Discussion on Used Car Licenses; Adopt Fee Structure & Develop Approval Process 7:55 PM Future Agenda Requests Time Agenda item Consent Agenda 8:05 PM o o o o o Approval of Minutes and Amendments Approve policy on Disposition of Public Property Approve MOA – Library Contract Accept gift in the amounts of $2500 from Sally Utiger of Weston and $100 from Lawrence Ardito of Andover to the Council on Aging Accept gift in the amount of $500 from the Edwin and Katherine Smith Fund to the Weston Public Library Notes Times stated above are approximate times for the discussion item unless the item is designated as a Public Hearing, which will start at the designated time but not before. Votes may be taken on any of the above agenda items, and the sequence and duration of agenda items may vary from what is indicated above, as the Board may deem necessary or otherwise appropriate. Items with a PP#xx notation indicate that item is supporting one of the Select Board’s Projects & Priorities list for the current year. Remote Attendance and Call-In Instructions • • • • • To use Zoom with video on a smartphone or tablet, download the Zoom app first. Then enter the Zoom Meeting ID. To use Zoom on a computer, download the installer the first time you join a meeting when prompted. After that, you can join meetings by selecting the meeting link. Use the call-in number to join in audio-only mode. This option is available if your computer does not have a microphone or speaker. You will enter a waiting room before joining the meeting. If you are calling in by phone, please remain muted. To unmute, press *6. Public Comment and Attendance Instructions • • • • • • • All participants will be muted when entering the meeting. Please remain muted until recognized. Please do not speak until the Chair asks for public questions or comments and recognizes the speaker. Persons who speak without being recognized may be muted, warned to cease speaking, and if not compliant, be placed in the waiting room for a period or removed from the meeting. To be recognized, select “Reactions” on the lower or upper toolbar, then select “Raise Hand”. If a request is made during a time when public participation is permitted, you will be placed in a queue and called upon in order. If you are calling in by phone, press *9 to raise your hand. The chat function is disabled. Participants cannot change their name during the meeting

E Nov. 11, 2026 Veterans Day Celebration 11 AM Nov. 27, 2026-Holiday Lights & Victorian Nights — French Sq. 3-6:30 PM ENT Page 2 TOWN OF WINTHROP OFFICE OF THE TOWN COUNCIL Town Hail, 1 Metcalf Square, Winthrop, MA 02152 Telephone: 617-846-1742 Fax: 617-846-5458 Motion by: Councilor Romano November 5, 2026 MOTION I move that the Winthrop Town Council to establish an amendment to Chapter 17.50 of the Winthrop Zoning Bylaw, Special Provisions Applicable to the Center Business District (CBD), for the purpose of designating the Town Council as the Special Permit Granting Authority (SPGA) for special permit applications within the Center Business District, in place of the Planning Board. I further move that: The proposed zoning amendment revise Sections 17.50.120 and 17.50.130, and any other applicable provisions of Chapter 17.50, to reflect the proposed designation of the Town Council as the Special Permit Granting Authority for the Center Business District. October 27, 2026 To: Winthrop Town Councit Ce: Senator Lydia Edwards; Winthrop Town Attorney Jim Cipoletta; Town Manager Anthony Marino Re: Formal Opposition to Proposed Transfer of Special Permit Granting Authority and Center Business District Zoning Amendments Dear Members of the Town Council, !am writing in my capacity as Chairman of the Winthrop Planning Board to formally express my opposition to the proposed transfer of Special Permit Granting Authority (SPGA) within the Center Business District (CBD) from the Planning Board to the Town Council, as presented in tonight's October 27, 2026, special meeting agenda. l respectfully but firmly believe that Special Permit Granting Authority should remain with the Planning Board, where professional expertise, technical review, and long- term planning considerations are central to the decision-making process. This proposal represents a significant change to Winthrop's land-use governance, removing permitting authority from a board specifically constituted to address planning and development matters and transferring it to a legislative body whose primary responsibilities serve a different purpose. Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 41, Sections 81A and 81D, establish the statutory framework for municipal Planning Boards and thelr role in guiding the long-term physical development of their communities, Section 81D specifically addresses comprehensive planning across land use, housing, transportation, infrastructure, and economic development. Chapter 40A, Section 9, further recognizes Planning Boards as eligible Special Permit Granting Authorities. These responsibilities are closely connected. A community's long-term planning objectives must ultimately be reflected in the individual development decisions that shape its physical environment. This is especially important within Winthrop's Center Business District, where individual projects collectively influence the character, economic vitality, and future of our downtown. Winthrop's Planning Board is composed of dedicated volunteers with professional experience in planning, architecture, design, development, and zoning. These individuals contribute substantial time and expertise to reviewing proposals involving site design, density, building massing, parking, circulation, infrastructure, and neighborhood compatibility. Their professional judgment provides a tevel of technical scrutiny, consistency, and institutional continuity that is particularly valuable in municipal development review. The Town Council serves an essential legislative role in establishing zoning policy and representing residents. The Planning Board serves a distinct and complementary function in applying those regulations through specialized, independent technical review. The authority to establish zoning policy and the responsibility to apply that policy to individual development applications are fundamentally different functions. Maintaining this distinction strengthens the integrity of the permitting process and helps ensure that individual decisions remain consistent with the Town's broader planning objectives. While Massachusetts law permits municipalities to designate different Special Permit Granting Authorities, no compelling justification or demonstrated public benefit has been presented for removing this responsibility from the Planning Board. Nor have deficiencies in the Board's administration of special permits been identified to justify such a substantial restructuring. A change of this magnitude should be supported by a clear demonstration that the existing process is inadequate and that the proposed alternative will better serve the community. Absent that justification, transferring this authority risks weakening the professional oversight and continuity that Winthrop's existing land-use review process provides. lam equally concerned that this proposal is being advanced alongside several other substantive amendments to the CBD zoning ordinance, including changes to parking requirements and associated mitigation fees, ground-floor residential restrictions, and building height limitations. Individually, these amendments warrant careful planning consideration. Collectively, they could materially alter the character, development standards, and future growth of Winthrop's downtown. The Council is effectively considering changes to both the rules governing development and the authority responsible for administering those rules. Such a consequential combination deserves comprehensive evaluation of its individual and cumulative impacts. Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 40A, Section 5, establishes specific procedures for zoning amendments, including Planning Board referral, public hearings, and an opportunity for formal recommendations before adoption. These requirements reflect the Legislature's recognition of the Planning Board's role in evaluating changes to municipal zoning. Given the significance of these proposed amendments, | respectfully request that the Town Attorney clarify whether tonight's motions initiate the zoning amendment process or seek final adoption and confirm that all applicable statutory requirements have been satisfied before any final legislative action is taken. | therefore respectfully request that the Town Council decline to support the proposed transfer of Special Permit Granting Authority and defer final action on the remaining CBD zoning amendments until the appropriate statutory review and planning evaluation have been completed. Winthrop is fortunate to have residents willing to volunteer their professional knowledge in service to the Town. That expertise should be meaningfully incorporated into decisions that shape our community, particularly when those decisions directly relate to the responsibilities and qualifications of the Planning Board. A Planning Board entrusted with guiding the future of its community yet removed from meaningful permitting decisions in its central business district, represents a troubling disconnect between long-term planning and the decisions that ultimately shape that future. This is a consequential decision with implications extending well beyond tonight's meeting. 1 ask the Council to preserve the Planning Board's established role, recognize the value of professional land-use oversight, and protect the integrity of Winthrop's development review process. Chairman, Wintlrop Planning Board Submitted in my capacity as Chairman. The views expressed are my own and do not represent a formal position of the Planning Board unless separately adopted by the Board. | respectfully request that this correspondence be distributed to all members of the Town Council and entered into the official meeting record.

AVAILABLE FUNDS Balances remaining in various funds that are available for expenditure. ENTERPRISE FUND A separate account for municipal services for which a fee is charged in exchange for goods or services. It allows a community to demonstrate the portion of total costs of a service that is recovered through user fees. This is a multi-year fund for which any end-of-year surplus is retained in the Enterprise Fund. OFFSET ACCOUNT An account set up to restrict fees collected by a particular department for expenditure by that department. Any surplus funds remaining at the end of the fiscal year are returned to the General Fund. FISCAL YEAR The Town’s fiscal year begins July 1st and ends on June 30th. FREE CASH Remaining, unrestricted funds from operations of the previous fiscal year including actual receipts in excess of estimates and unspent amounts in budget line-items. OVERLAY RESERVE An account set up to pay for real estate exemptions and abatements. RAISE & APPROPRIATE A phrase used to identify a funding source for an expenditure which refers to money generated by the tax levy or other anticipated local receipts. RESERVE FUND An account appropriated within the operating budget to provide for unforeseen expenditures during the fiscal year. Expenditures of funds deposited to this account require approval of the Finance Committee. Funds remaining at the end of the fiscal year are returned to the General Fund. STABILIZATION FUND A multi-year fund established as a “rainy day” account to address extraordinary or unforeseen future expenditures during the current or future fiscal years. This account can also be used to accumulate funds for capital expenditures in a future year.
