Select Board Recommends (5-0) Finance Committee Will Recommend from the Floor Capital Budget Committee Recommends (5-0) (Select Board) ARTICLE #3: Revolving Fund Bylaw: To see if the Town will vote to amend the General Bylaws of the Town of Yarmouth by adding a new section to establish and authorize revolving funds for use by Town departments, agencies or officers under Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 44, Section 53 E ½, or take any other action relative thereto. Departmental Revolving Funds 1. Purpose. This bylaw establishes and authorizes revolving funds for use by Town departments, boards, committees, agencies or officers in connection with the operation of programs or activities that general fees, charges or other receipts support all or some of the expenses of those programs or activities. These revolving funds are established under and governed by General Laws Chapter 44, Section 53E ½. 2. Expenditure Limitations. A department or agency head, board, committee or officer may incur liabilities against and spend monies from a revolving fund established and authorized by this bylaw without appropriation subject to the following limitations: a. Fringe Benefits of full-time employees whose salaries or wages are paid from the fund shall also be paid from the fund. b. No liability shall be incurred in excess of the available balance of the fund. c. The total amount spent during the fiscal year shall not exceed the amount authorized by Town Meeting on or before July 1st of that fiscal year, or any increased amount of that authorization that is later approved during that fiscal year by the Select Board and Finance Committee. 2 3. Interest. Interest earned on monies credited to a revolving fund established by this bylaw shall be credited to the general fund. 4. Procedures and Reports. Except as provided in General Laws Chapter 44, Section 53E ½ and this bylaw, the laws, charter provisions, bylaws, rules, regulations, polices or procedures that govern the receipt and custody of town monies and the expenditure and payment of the town funds shall apply to the use of a revolving fund established and authorized by this bylaw. The town accountant shall include a statement on the collections credited to each fund, the encumbrances and expenditures charged to the fund and the balance available for expenditure in the regular report of the town accountant provides the department, board, committee, agency or officer on appropriations made for its use. 5. Authorized Revolving Funds. The table establishes a. Each revolving fund authorized for use by a town department, board, committee, agency or officer. b. The department or agency head, board, committee, or officer authorized to spend from each fund. c. The fees, charges and other monies charged and received by the department, board, committee, agency or officer in connection with the program or activity for which the fund is established that shall be credited to each fund by the town accountant. d. The expenses of the program or activity for which each fund may be used. e. Any restrictions or conditions on expenditures from each fund. f. Any reporting or other requirements that apply to each fund, and g. The fiscal years each fund shall operate under this by-law. A Revolving Fund B Department, Board, Committee, Agency or Officer Authorized to Spend from Fund C Fees, Charges or Other Receipts Credited to Fund D Program or Activity Expenses Payable from Fund E F Expenditure Fiscal Years Limit Fire Training Facility Parkers River Landing Park Fire Department Facility Use Facility Maintenance $ 50,000 2027 and beyond Community Development, DPW Facility Use Facility Maintenance $100,000 2027 and beyond EXPLANATION: This article is required to create a bylaw enabling the Town to operate certain smaller and limited programs which bring in revenue that is required to operate the programs. This system of program delivery is termed a “revolving fund”, and it has the benefit of allowing much-needed services to be delivered that are financially self-sufficient while preventing them 3 from competing for limited revenues with services that do not generate their own revenues. The bylaw complies with the State requirements to provide structure and limitations to these programs, which are specifically laid out in the bylaw. This bylaw will cover the operation of the regional Fire Training Facility and the operation and maintenance of the Parkers River Landing Park. Purpose. To provide for the orderly operation of short-term rentals for residential properties that balance private, neighborhood and public interests, and will: 1. Protect and maintain the residential character of existing neighborhoods. 2. Protect public health and safety. 3. Protect and preserve year-round housing stock. 4. Inhibit the commercialization of housing for use as Short Term Rentals. 5. Enable residents to better afford to live in Yarmouth, maintain their properties and contribute to the community. 6. Ensure the continued revenues to the Town from the short-term rental excise tax. § 110-2. Definitions. OWNER – Any person, corporation, LLC, trust or other entity that, alone, or severally with others, directly or indirectly, has legal or equitable title or beneficial interest in any dwelling unit. 4 OPERATOR – A person or entity who is designated by an Owner to be responsible for the dayto-day operations of the Short-Term Rental and who serves as the local 24-hour emergency contact person with the Town of Yarmouth. An Owner may also be an Operator provided they are available 24 hours a day during the rental period to address operational issues at the Short-Term Rental. SHORT-TERM RENTALS (STR) - defined as owner-occupied, tenant-occupied or non-owner occupied residential property including, but not limited to, an apartment unit, house, cottage, condominium or a furnished accommodation that is not a hotel, motel, boarding or lodging house, or guesthouse, inn or bed and breakfast establishment, where at least one room or unit is rented to an occupant or occupants for 1-31 consecutive days at a time. STRs are characterized as transient in nature and not rented to the same occupant month to month. TIME SHARE, FRACTIONAL AND INTERVAL OWNERSHIP UNIT - Any Dwelling Unit which is owned by a limited liability company, corporation, partnership, or other joint ownership structure in which unrelated persons or entities own, sell, purchase or otherwise, for consideration, create or acquire any divided property interest including co-ownership or fractional or divided estates, shares, leaseholds, or memberships which are subject to, or subsequently bound by any agreement limiting the right or functional ability of interest holders or their designees to occupy or use the property to their respective interests or any other agreement which limits interest holders’ or their designees’ use of the property to fractional reservations through stay limitations of any duration. Such use is established by one or more of the following elements: 1) co-ownership or fractional or divided estates, shares, leaseholds, or memberships which are openly advertised, marketed, or offered for sale and sold individually at separate times; 2) centralized or professional management; 3) reservation systems; 4) maximum or minimum day limits on each interest holder’s occupancy or use of the property; or 5) management agreements or fees reflective of interval use or ownership, irrespective of whether the agreement may be cancelled individually or by any party. § 110-3. Ineligible Units. The following are not eligible to be rented as STRs. 1. Dwellings designated as income restricted or which are subject to affordability covenants or restrictions. 2. Approved Accessory Apartments, Accessory Dwelling Units, and Protected Use Accessory Dwelling Units, as defined in, and approved under, the Zoning Bylaw. 3. Dwelling units on a property containing an Accessory Apartment, Accessory Dwelling Unit or Protected Use Accessory Dwelling Unit. 4. Dwelling units with Time Share, Fractional and Interval Ownership. 5. Dwellings subject to any unresolved outstanding building, sanitary, zoning, conservation, or fire code violations. 5 § 110-4. Registration & Inspections. 1. All Short-Term Rentals shall be registered annually through the Yarmouth Health Department in accordance with General Bylaw Chapter 108 – Occupancy of Buildings; and shall be inspected annually by the Building Commissioner, or his/her designee, in accordance with 780 CMR – MA State Building Code; and shall adhere to all health and safety requirements. Overnight occupancy limitations shall be set by the Health Department based on inspections and septic capacity. 2. Rental Occupancy Certificate and Certificate of Inspection shall be displayed on the property in a prominent location and shall include 24-hour local contact information. All Certificates expire on December 31st of each year. 3. The Town reserves the right to post rental locations and contact information on the Town Website per MGL Ch. 64G, Section 14. § 110-5. General Provisions. 1. Trash Removal: All household trash shall be removed from the premises immediately after occupancy is concluded, and at a minimum once per week. 2. Parking: On-site parking area shall be provided and will be determined by the Health or Building Departments at time of inspection. There shall be no parking on lawns at any time and no expansion of parking into green space areas in front of the dwelling. No overnight street parking from 11:00PM to 7:00AM, and no street parking that impedes traffic or traffic safety at any time. 3. Duration: Renting for less than two (2) consecutive nights is prohibited. 4. Occupancy: Maximum overnight occupancy from 11:00PM to 7:00AM shall be the occupancy limit set by the Health Department in accordance with state and local bylaws and regulations, regardless of the number of bedrooms or places to sleep (i.e., beds, sofas, cots, bunk beds, etc.) provided in the STR. 5. Noise: All occupants of Short-Term Rentals shall adhere to General Bylaw Chapter 104 – Noise and shall respect quiet hours from 11:00PM to 7:00AM. 6. Type of Rentals: a. STRs are for Residential uses only. No large-scale events including, but not limited to, weddings; corporate events; graduation, fraternity/sorority, bridal or bachelor parties; and class/family reunions may take place in a STR or on a STR property. b. No events that include tents or amplified music may take place on a STR property. c. STRs shall not be used in a manner that adversely affects the residential character of the neighborhood or substantially and unreasonably interferes with a reasonable person’s use and enjoyment of their residence and property. An adverse effect may occur when, for example, a STR is used in a manner that results in the production of excessive noise, vibration, light, glare, trash, fumes, odors, traffic, parking congestion, or any other nuisance. 7. Pets: Adherence to any and all state and local regulations regarding pets. 8. Use of RVs, campers or sleeping tents as STRs or sleeping spaces is prohibited. 6 9. Short Term Rentals shall meet all local and state regulations, including but not limited to building and fire codes, health codes, water supply and wastewater disposal. § 110-6. Rental Listings, Advertisements and Booking Platforms. The following information shall be provided on all Rental Listings, Advertisements and Booking Platforms for STRs in the Town of Yarmouth: 1. Town Issued Rental Occupancy Certificate number. 2. MA Department of Revenue STR Certificate ID number. 3. Maximum number of cars a property can accommodate on-site as set by the Health or Building Departments. 4. No overnight street parking is allowed from 11:00PM to 7:00AM. 5. Maximum overnight occupancy from 11:00PM to 7:00AM as set by the Health Department. Number of sleeping spaces advertised shall not exceed this number. 6. Minimum booking of two (2) consecutive nights. 7. No large-scale events or parties. § 110-7. Penalties and Enforcement. text: Town of Yarmouth Per M.G.L.: All town and school boards, committees, commissions, and authorities shall post a notice of every meeting at least 48 hours prior to such meeting, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays. Notice shall contain a listing of topics/agenda that the chair reasonably anticipates will be discussed at the meeting. Notice of Meetings Name of committee, board, etc.: Planning Board Date of Meeting: November 16, 2026 Time: 6:00 PM Place: Dennis-Yarmouth Intermediate Middle School 286 Station Avenue, South Yarmouth Agenda (Topics to be discussed): 1. 2026 Special Town Meeting (STM): The Planning Board may meet in quorum at STM regarding Zoning Articles and General Bylaw related to Short-Term Rentals, and Zoning Article for Accessory Dwelling Units: a. Short Term Rental Articles: i) Article 5 - General Bylaw Chapter 110 – Short Term Rentals (1): New General Bylaw to regulate Short-Term Rentals, which would ultimately replace the regulatory provisions currently within Zoning Bylaw Section 418. ii) Article 6 - Short Term Rentals (2) – Zoning Amendment: Continue the STR Use in the Zoning Bylaw and extend the sunset clause to the effective date of the General Bylaw. This Article would be withdrawn if the General Bylaw does not pass. iii) Article 7 - Short Term Rentals (3) – Zoning Amendment: Extend Sunset Clause in Section 418 – Short-Term Rentals. This Article would be withdrawn if the other STR Articles pass. b. Article 8 - Accessory Dwelling Units: Amendments to the Accessory Apartment Zoning Bylaw to match the mandated changes from The Affordable Homes Act (Section 8 of Chapter 150 of the Acts of 2024) and regulations 760 CMR 71.00: Protected Use Accessory Dwelling Units, while maintaining as many existing provisions as allowed by the state regulations. c. Other Town Meeting Business 2. Adjournment Attachments: All exhibits are available for public review in the Planning Department, Yarmouth Town Offices, 1146 Route 28, South Yarmouth, MA, during normal business hours. Posted By (Name): Signature: Kathleen D. Williams Kathleen D. Williams Article 5: General Bylaw Chapter 110 – Short-Term Rentals (1) Motion by: Joanne Crowley, Planning Board/Dorcas McGurrin I move Article 5 as printed in the warrant. Select Board Recommends (4-0-1 abstention) Planning Board Recommends (6-0) Notes: (Planning Board) Page | 11 Article 5: Explanation This Article would modify and fine-tune current regulations related to Short-Term Rentals and convert regulatory provisions currently located within the Zoning Bylaw to a separate General Bylaw. At the 2022 Annual Town Meeting, Section 418 of the Zoning Bylaw was approved to allow for Short-Term Rentals while incorporating general provisions to regulate their use. This was done to codify the historic use of homes on Cape Cod as vacation rentals in response to 2021 case law that questioned this type of use unless expressly allowed in the Zoning Bylaw. The original STR bylaw was prepared expeditiously to ensure continued economic benefits and revenues to the Town from the short-term rental tax. STRs are a vital revenue stream for the Town, bringing in over $2.375 Million in Fiscal Year 26, with 75% going towards funding our wastewater program to improve our estuaries and water quality. As the bylaw was developed in an expedited manner, a sunset clause was included in the bylaw to allow time for further studies or analysis, with the STR provisions currently expiring on November 30, 2026, unless amended at Town Meeting. Subsequent studies conducted included a detailed Short-Term Rental Report by UMass Donahue Institute dated February 2026. This study analyzed demographics, the housing market, STRs in Yarmouth, impacts and benefits of STRs, reviewed existing regulations and identified potential new regulations. This study was presented to the Select Board at their March 3, 2026 meeting and recommended a multi-faceted strategy. In addition to looking at Page | 12 various ways to incentivize year-round housing, the study discussed tailoring regulations to inhibit future commercialization of STRs, strengthen compliance, and further address quality of life issues. The Planning Board used this study to start developing draft language and holding public meetings to garner community input. Some key provisions and modifications contained within the General Bylaw include: • further restrictions on types of dwellings that can be used as a STR • further clarifications on occupancy, parking, noise, and type of rentals • identification of specific information to be included within all STR listings, and • enhanced penalties and enforcement including the potential revocation of a Rental Occupancy Certificate related to verified violations. In addition to these bylaw enhancements, other administrative procedures will be enacted for the 2027 season, such as: • an on-line STR complaint form • improved education of the regulations to STR owners, and • collection of additional information in the application process including Department of Revenue Registration number. Town Planner Kathy Williams will give a brief presentation highlighting the main changes to the STR provisions included in this General Bylaw. Page | 13 Questions: Kathy Williams, Town Planner Joanne Crowley, Planning Board Page | 14 Article 6: Zoning Article – Short-Term Rentals (2) Motion by: Will Rubenstein, Planning Board/Dorcas McGurrin Motion if Article 5 – STR General Bylaw PASSES: I move Article 6 as printed in the warrant. Select Board Recommends (5-0) Planning Board Recommends (6-0) Motion if Article 5 – STR General Bylaw FAILS: I move to Withdraw Article 6. Notes: 2/3 Vote Required (Planning Board) Page | 15 Article 6: Explanation This Article would continue the use of Short-Term Rentals within the Zoning Bylaw in accordance with the provisions in the new General Bylaw Chapter 110 – Short-Term Rentals. The Sunset Clause in the existing Zoning Bylaw Section 418 has been extended until the new General Bylaw becomes effective on January 1, 2028 to avoid any gaps in regulations. Questions: Kathy Williams, Town Planner Will Rubenstein, Planning Board Page | 16 Article 7: Zoning Article – Short-Term Rentals (3) Motion by: Will Rubenstein, Planning Board/Joyce Flynn Motion if Article 5 – STR General Bylaw and Article 6 – STR Zoning Amendments BOTH PASS: I move to Withdraw Article 7. Motion if Article 5 – STR General Bylaw FAILS: I move Article 7 as printed in the warrant. Select Board Recommends (5-0) Planning Board Recommends (6-0) Motion if Article 5 – STR General Bylaw PASSES (majority vote) AND Article 6 – STR Zoning Amendments FAILS (2/3 vote): I move Article 7 as printed in the warrant. Select Board Recommends (5-0) Planning Board Recommends (6-0) Notes: 2/3 Vote Required (Planning Board) Page | 17 Article 7: Explanation Should other Articles related to Short-Term Rentals not pass, this Article would extend the sunset Clause contained in Section 418 to ensure the continuation of Short-Term Rentals in Yarmouth and the excise tax revenues they bring to the Town while further study and evaluation can be completed. This Article would be withdrawn if the other Short-Term Rental Articles pass. Questions: Kathy Williams, Town Planner Will Rubenstein, Planning Board Page | 18 Article 8: Zoning Article – Accessory Dwelling Units Motion by: Tom Pendleton, Planning Board/Joyce Flynn I move Article 8 as printed in the warrant. Select Board Recommends (5-0) Planning Board Recommends (6-0) Notes: (Planning Board) Page | 19 Article 8: Explanation This Article seeks to amend the current Accessory Apartments bylaw to comply with the requirements of the regulations issued by the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities (EOHLC) concerning Protected Use Accessory Dwelling Units (760 CMR 71.00) which arose from the 2024 Affordable Homes Act. The Affordable Homes Act requires all Towns in Massachusetts to allow accessory dwelling units as of right in all zoning districts that allow single family homes. In 2023, Yarmouth voters modified the Accessory Apartment zoning bylaw to promote the creation of year-round rental units by eliminating the Family Related and Affordability use restrictions while including provisions to protect the character of our residential neighborhoods. However, per 760 CMR 71.00, some provisions in our current zoning bylaw are no longer enforceable, such as the Special Permit requirement; minimum lot size; owner occupancy; certain parking requirements, and requirements beyond those required for a single-family home. The Planning Board worked with Town Counsel to retain as many of the current provisions as the state law allows such as meeting current setback requirements; not allowing ADUs to be Short-Term Rentals; not allowing separate ownership of the ADU; allowing only one ADU per lot; setting a minimum unit size of 350 sf; preventing parking in existing green space in front of the building; and no commercial uses other than limited Home Offices and Home Occupations. If passed, the Attorney General will review the Article for compliance with state Page | 20 regulations and will identify any provisions that violate state law which would need to be extracted from the Zoning amendment. Codifying these changes to the zoning bylaw to comply with 760 CMR 71.00 provides clarity for future applicants, makes it easier to enforce, and clearly outlines the provisions we want to retain within the constraints of the state law. City Council Action Requests: - Creation of an Easthampton Dog Park Donation Account - Creation of a Data Center Study Committee 3 Information         CITY COUNCIL MEETING – JUNE 17, 2026 Meeting held at 50 Payson Ave., 2nd floor meeting area and remotely by Google Meet 6:00 p.m. Members Present: President Koni Denham, Vice-President Felicia Jadczak, Councilors James “JP” Kwiecinski, Tom Peake, Tamara Smith, Jonathan Schmidt, Amanda Newton, Nathan Markee. Members Remote: Kiam Jamrog-McQuaid Pledge of Allegiance and Moment of Silence: Citizen Recognition: Fire Chief Christopher Norris and Chief Alexander recognized Nick Hebert and Stacy Elander for their actions during a motor vehicle fire on Strong Street on May 18, 2026 at approximately 7:20 a.m. Chief Norris stated that a vehicle left the roadway, struck a tree, and caught fire with an occupant trapped inside, and that Mr. Hebert and Ms. Elander, residents of Strong Street, broke the vehicle’s windows to gain access, used a garden hose to slow the fire, and removed the occupant to safety before police, fire, and EMS personnel arrived. On behalf of the City and the Police and Fire Departments, the Chiefs extended their gratitude and presented Mr. Hebert and Ms. Elander with life safety awards. Act on Minutes: None. Public Comment Summary: Cathy Wauczinski, Overlook Drive, read a petition submitted that day for a recount of the June 9 election, stating that the petitioners believe the records of votes cast are erroneous because, among other concerns, the vote count differs from totals recorded by the State, mail-in ballots arrived late or without a ballot in the envelope, some voters were denied the opportunity to vote in person, chain of custody for ballots may not have been maintained, and information about voting by mail and in person was unclear and inconsistent. She stated that many of these issues can be attributed to the election being rushed, that errors in the budget had not been corrected before the election, and that records requests had not been answered in a timely manner. She added that, according to the chief of elections, all concerns needed to be included on the petition to proceed beyond a simple recount. Jamie Paquette, 10 Meadowbrook Drive, Chair of the Easthampton Energy Advisory Committee and a member of the BEES Committee, reported that the Easthampton Community Electricity Aggregation Program, approved in 2024 and by the State DPU in 2025, was expected to hold a pre-bid meeting and bid day the following week through the City’s consultant, Good Energy, and that if favorable pricing is obtained the City would execute a contract beginning the following week, followed by a public outreach and education period. Chair Paquette reported that the Electrify Easthampton-Northampton program offers up to an additional $4,000 in rebates for upgrades such as heat pumps, on top of State incentives, and that committee members recently met with representatives of Senator Velis and Representative Gómez to encourage support for Mass Save, the Climate Bank, and simplified solar permitting. 1 Roger Anderson, Westview Terrace, stated that he was astounded by comments that residents were unaware of the election, noting the news coverage, social media, people holding Vote Yes and Vote No signs around the City for weeks, and an illuminated sign at the rotary. On motion made by Councilor Markee and seconded by Councilor Schmidt it was unanimously voted by roll call vote to open the Public Hearing. Public Hearings starting at 6:15 p.m. President Denham reminded councilors and the public to wait to be recognized by the President and asked residents to state all of their questions together so that they can be directed to the appropriate person. Fiscal Year 2027 City Budget Councilor Peake, Chair of the Finance Committee, stated that the budget would be continued because scheduled cuts, and additional cuts recommended by the Finance Committee, affected personnel and required impact bargaining, which Councilor Peake reported the Mayor had said had concluded, and that adjusted amounts were needed before final votes could be taken. He stated that the Finance Committee would meet on Tuesday, June 23 at 6:00 p.m. to take a final vote on the appropriation lines and that the City Council would meet the next day, June 24, to continue the item. Cathy Wauczinski, Overlook Drive, stated that the agenda had not been updated to show that the budget would not be taken up that evening, that many people were watching online or on the phone and had adjusted their schedules, and that discussion could have occurred on the parts of the budget that were not delayed. Councilor Peake stated that, because the Council would meet only to take up the budget and one item to be referred to the Property Committee, the hearing should be continued to 6:00 p.m. rather than 6:15 p.m. On motion by Councilor Peake, duly seconded by Councilor Schmidt, it was unanimously voted by roll call vote to continue the public hearing on the Fiscal Year 2027 City Budget to Wednesday, June 24, 2026 at 6:00 p.m. in these chambers. Supplemental Appropriations $20,000.00 for the remaining Fiscal Year required Medicare Tax (continued from June 3, 2026) Councilor Peake stated that the item had been continued because of questions about its effect on the next year’s budget. Councilor Kwiecinski restated the question, noting that the expense for the next year’s Medicare tax would be paid with this fiscal year’s dollars. City Treasurer Brooke Johnson stated that Medicare tax is paid 50 percent by employees and 50 percent by the City, that teachers may take a lump sum (“balloon”) payout before June 30, that the appropriation is made each year, that the Treasurer intends to reduce it each year, and that any amount not spent would close to free cash. It was clarified that the appropriation is $14,000.00 for school Medicare and $6,000.00 for the Medicare tax. Councilor Kwiecinski asked Treasurer 2 Johnson if this happens every year and why it was not anticipated as an expense. In response to Councilor Kwiecinski, Treasurer Johnson stated that the number of employees electing the lump sum is not known until late May or early June, that the FY 2027 budget is level-serviced at the same amount, and that part of the account is used for police outside details. Councilor Peake made the following supplemental appropriation as a motion: amount requested $20,000.00 to be transferred from free cash, $14,000.00 to School Medicare and $6,000.00 to Medicare Tax, to cover the remaining fiscal year required Medicare tax. On motion by Councilor Peake and seconded by Councilor Schmidt, it was unanimously voted by roll call vote to appropriate $20,000.00 for the remaining fiscal year required Medicare Tax. $10,000.00 for the remaining Fiscal Year legal expenses (continued from June 3, 2026) Mayor Derby stated that during last year’s budget the Council reduced the City Attorney fee line item, with the understanding that the Mayor would return for appropriations to cover legal fees. He said that this is the last request for the fiscal year and that the line item covers legal fees for all departments other than the Council, including impact bargaining, personnel issues, and public works projects. Mayor Derby stated that the City averaged $103,000 per year in legal fees over the last three years and, with this appropriation, would total about $42,000 this year; and that about $4,000 in fees were outstanding because the prior appropriation did not pass. Mayor Derby added that the request covers June expenses of the labor attorney and three months of the City Solicitor’s expenses. Councilor Newton asked if the full amount of the request for $10,000.00 would be spent. In response to Councilor Newton, Mayor Derby confirmed that any unspent amount would return to free cash. In response to Councilor Smith, Mayor Derby stated that $2,922.00 had been billed and that the remainder was forthcoming. Mike Carriveau, Line Street, stated that the Council should receive a detailed explanation of what legal fees are for before approving them. Councilor Peake stated that the concern was understood but that legal expenses may include matters, such as disciplinary situations, that should not be discussed at a public hearing, and that the City is obligated to pay bills it has incurred. Vice-President Jadczak stated that there is a difference between bills already incurred and anticipated expenses and asked that future requests include more detail on anticipated expenses. Councilor Kwiecinski stated that the Mayor should come to the Council in advance of expenditures and that the Council should consider the process for doing so. Mayor Derby stated that the Council’s questions risked legislative oversight of an executive function and that doing so would be inconsistent with the Charter, noting that the City keeps itemized bills available for review. President Denham and Councilor Kwiecinski stated that the Council did not intend to control the executive function but to respond to residents’ concerns and to know in advance what requests are coming. Councilor Newton stated that she preferred not to send unspent amounts to free cash. Councilor Peake stated that the Council’s decision to zero out the line was unusual, that the line has been restored at a lower level, and that the City 3 should discuss expenditures with the Council before funds are spent when they are not in the budget. Councilor Peake made the following supplemental appropriation as a motion: amount requested $10,000.00 to be transferred from free cash to City Attorney Professional Expenses, to cover the remaining fiscal year city legal expenses. On motion by Councilor Peake and seconded by Councilor Markee, it was unanimously voted by roll call vote to appropriate $10,000.00 for City Attorney Legal Fees. $135,000.00 for Easthampton Dog Park Construction (CPA) CPA Coordinator Eva Gerstle displayed the CPA available balance worksheet and stated that the figures are preliminary and unreconciled. She reported available balances before the pending FY 2026 appropriations of $39,769 in the open space and recreation set-aside, $27,751 in the historic preservation set-aside, $1 in the affordable housing set-aside, $618,052 in the undesignated account, and $30,877 in the reserve undesignated account, and balances of $1, $27,751, $1, $483,052, and $26,545, respectively, if both projects are fully funded. Joan Kurtz, 359 Main Street, President of Friends of Easthampton Dog Park, thanked the Council, the CPA Coordinator, and the Commission and asked for a positive vote. Julie Thomas, 6 Concord Drive, Precinct 1, thanked the CPA Coordinator for the balances and asked how residents can see what the CPA started with. President Denham and Ms. Gerstle stated that the CPA revenue history from 2002 to the present, the 2026 annual meeting presentation, and the preliminary end-of-FY26 available balance spreadsheet are posted under the Community Preservation Act Committee page on the City website. Councilor Peake made the following supplemental appropriation as a motion: amount requested $135,000.00 to be appropriated from the CPA undesignated fund to Dog Park Construction, to construct a dog park at Nonotuck Park. Councilor Kwiecinski stated that the CPA funds would leverage substantial additional funds. Ms. Gerstle stated that the Friends of the Dog Park received a $200,000 gift from a community member and that matching contributions total $205,000. On motion by Councilor Peake, duly seconded by Councilor Markee, it was unanimously voted by roll call vote to appropriate $135,000.00 for Easthampton Dog Park Construction (CPA). $44,100.00 for Mutters Field Renovation (CPA) Councilor Peake described Mutters Field as an accessible trail connecting East Green Street and East Street that has been affected by wear and by invasive plants. Ms. Gerstle stated that the project is a renovation of a conservation area acquired with CPA assistance in 2012, owned and maintained by the Pascommuck Conservation Trust, and includes replacing deteriorated wood edging along the accessible path with a more durable material, replacing a culvert stream crossing with a pedestrian bridge, renovating an access point, removing invasives, and adding native plantings, signage, and a bench. Marty Klein, 7 Stone Path Lane, a member of the board of the Pascommuck Conservation Trust, stated that the trail opened in 2016, that pressure- 4 treated edging lasts about 10 years in ground contact, that a 30-foot bridge will replace the culvert at the East Street end, and that the replacement edging is a composite material that is cut off-site, with the expected life of 30 or more years. Councilor Schmidt asked about the composite material and the risk of microplastics entering the adjacent stream; asked that any on-site cutting be done with vacuum collection and that capped ends be considered; and asked to be informed of the material selected. Mr. Klein stated that the Trust will make every effort to mitigate contamination. Councilor Smith spoke about the trail’s value as an accessible and intergenerational space. Councilor Markee, who lives near Mutters Field, stated an intention to vote yes. Mr. Klein stated that work on the trail could begin in August or early September and be completed in the fall. Councilor Peake made the following supplemental appropriation as a motion: amount requested $44,100.00 to be appropriated from CPA Reserve for Open Space ($39,768.00) and CPA Reserve Fund ($4,332.00) to Mutters Field Renovations, for renovation and improvements on the trails at Brickyard Brook Conservation Area between East Street and Mount Tom Avenue/East Green Street. Ms. Gerstle stated that the Pascommuck Conservation Trust has contributed $35,200 in matching funds. On motion by Councilor Peake and seconded by Councilor Markee, it was unanimously voted by roll call vote to appropriate $44,100.00 for Mutters Field Renovation (CPA). $50,000.00 for purchase of 10 fire hydrants Councilor Peake explained that Enterprise Retained Earnings is the Enterprise Fund’s equivalent of free cash. DPW Director Greg Nuttelman, (online), stated that a hydrant that cost about $1,800 earlier in the Director’s career now costs more than $4,000, that the hydrants are replacements for existing hydrants, with five to be installed immediately and five kept in stock, that the City has about 900 hydrants of which five are out of service. Communications from Elected Officials … will schedule a meeting, either the following week or the week after, to discuss the cell tower resolution and will coordinate with Councilor Smith, who represents the district involved. ADJOURN Note: Two-Thirds Vote: requires 6 votes Majority Vote: requires majority of members present and voting November 13, 2026 To: Town Council From: Jamie Hellen, Town Administrator Michelle Monsegur, Deputy Town Administrator RE: FY27 Budget Update and Reconciliation & FY26 Free Cash Update The Council will consider finalizing the FY27 budget reconciliation as required by statute prior to setting the tax rate on December 2, 2026. The following are the several recommended alterations to balance the FY27 budget: Revenue ● Final state aid was $170,615 less than assumed at the final June 10th Town Council vote. We have included the final cherry sheet. ● Estimated New Growth was $48,010 less than assumed at the final June 10th Town Council budget approval. The $218,768 in revenue loss represents .0014% of the town’s $152,134,537 town operating budget. It is worth reminding everyone the new growth trends continue to be a significant concern. Since peak new growth in 2020, the town has lost $1,047,418 in tax base. We would also remind the elected officials the state has officially named the members of the Foundation Budget Review Commission (with Legislative Commission website) and will begin Chapter 70 reform hearings in 2027 with a report due in 2028. “Hold Harmless” is a topic that elected and volunteer leaders should be discussing with members of the community to show how they can lend their voice to this process and/or why hold harmless chapter 70 aid is so critical to the school budget. How to make up the difference? To make up the difference for the revenue losses, we propose the following expenditure adjustments: ● Increase estimated local receipts to the maximum amount permitted under MGL c. 59, §23, Tax Rate Recap Page 3. As a general rule, the Department of Revenue (DOR), Bureau of Accounts, requires supporting documentation when estimated receipts for a revenue category vary from actual receipts by more than 5%. This figure is $143,642 added to the final FY27 budget reconciliation proposal. ● Cut the Health Insurance benefits budget by $75,126. So far we have implemented first year enrollment into the GIC within projections. The premium holiday commitment will be in January. Staff should have a mature Benefits budget update on costs come the first meeting in January, which will head right into the predictions for the FY28 budget filing. The Town has $304,345 remaining in the capital account for run out claims and health care consortium deficits. We have a goal of clearing our deficits within budget and to be in a position to not have to propose any additional resources on this problem. FY26 Free Cash Update certification We have attached the 2026 free cash and retained earnings certifications. The Town will have $3,943,191 in free cash for the FY28 operating budget and/or the upcoming FY27 capital plan. Staff have submitted capital plans for FY27 to the Deputy CFO/Budget Director. The deadline was last Friday. We anticipate a proposed FY27 capital plan along with the first FY28 budget model at the first Town Council meeting in February (which is right after the Governor files her budget). November 13, 2026 To: Town Council From: Jamie Hellen, Town Administrator Michelle Monsegur, Deputy Town Administrator Kerri Bertone, Chief Financial Officer RE: Tax Rate Workshop #3 The November 18th Town Council meeting will include the third and final tax rate workshop scheduled for this fall. The primary goal of this workshop is to continue to receive input from the community on maintaining a single tax rate versus adopting a split tax rate. Revaluation Update Under M.G.L. c. 40, § 56, Massachusetts cities and towns are required to complete a revaluation of all real and personal property every five years to ensure property is being assessed at full and fair cash valuation. FY27 is a revaluation (certification) year for Franklin. The Assessing Department has submitted Franklin’s FY27 property valuations to the MA Department of Revenue’s (DOR) Bureau of Local Assessment. FY27 values are the result of sales activity during calendar year 2025 and ownership as of January 1, 2026. DOR has completed its onsite and statistical reviews of Franklin’s preliminary FY27 valuations. These values have been posted on the Assessing Department’s website for public review as required by law pending preliminary certification. Following the end of the public disclosure period, November 12, 2026 through November 18, 2026, we expect to receive preliminary followed by final certification from DOR ahead of the December 2, 2026 tax classification hearing. Overall, FY27 preliminary values reflect the following trends: ● Class 101 (single-family homes) increased in value by 7.5% from FY26; ● Class 102 (condominiums) increased by approximately 5.5%; ● Classes 111-125 (apartments and other congregate housing) increased by 9%; ● The commercial class increased by 2.5%; ● The industrial class increased by 3%. Individual parcel valuations will vary from the overall class increase due to typical differences, data updates and corrections, new construction, and the effect of market trends for specific characteristics. Potential Tax Rate Scenarios The Assessing team has prepared the attached matrix to illustrate potential split tax rate scenarios. Because FY27 values have not been certified by the MA Department of Revenue, we are using preliminary FY27 property values and FY26 tax rates to estimate the impact of potential CIP shifts. The matrix shows the projected tax bill under these scenarios for the following properties: ● Median single family home ● Median condominium ● Median commercial property ● A few individual businesses as samples ● Median industrial property The Assessing team will provide updated potential split tax rate scenarios and estimates for the December 2, 2026 tax classification hearing. CIP Shift Research Our office spoke with Assessing staff in nine communities about their methodology for determining how much of the tax burden to shift from residential onto the commercial, industrial, personal property classes each year. The nine communities included: 1. Braintree 2. Easton 3. Milford 4. Needham 5. North Attleborough 6. Norton 7. Stoughton 8. Westwood 9. Wrentham 2 None of the nine communities cited a specific formula (percentage or dollar amount) that they follow to determine residential relief or the CIP shift each year. Most often, we heard that "it's a balancing act." A few communities aim to even out the increase across the residential and CIP classes. Needham and Westwood warned that going all the way to the maximum CIP shift leaves no room for residential relief in the future. The Assessing team notes that a rate shift will affect the valuations of those properties depending on the income approach to real estate value. Think of the real estate tax as an offset to the net operating income to the real estate. A tax increase for commercial and industrial properties will reduce the full and fair cash values in those classes. For apartment buildings (which are classified as residential per state law), a reduction in tax will increase the full and fair cash values in those classes. Additional Information We have included the following documents in the November 18th meeting packet to provide additional information on potential tax rate scenarios and exemption options: ● Matrix: Potential Tax Rate Scenarios ● Exemptions for Small Businesses (small commercial exemption and personal property exemption information) ● Senior Means-Tested Tax Exemption information ● FY26 Exemptions Granted and Dollars Abated (form MDM-1) ● Recent Years' Valid Arms-Length Commercial & Industrial Sales 3 November 13, 2026 To: Town Council From: Jamie Hellen, Town Administrator Michelle Monsegur, Deputy Town Administrator Kerri Bertone, Chief Financial Officer Kevin Doyle, Director of Assessing Renee Chen, Appraiser RE: Exemptions for Small Businesses Small Commercial Exemption Several Councilors asked about the small commercial exemption at the October 14th and 28th tax rate workshops. The Assessing team provided the following information in response: The small commercial exemption is offered under M.G.L. c. 59, § 5I. To qualify, the commercial property must have an assessed value of less than $1 million, and every business must have an average of no more than 10 employees across all locations during the previous calendar year. The maximum exemption is 10% of the value of the property. Fourteen of the 351 communities in Massachusetts have adopted a 10% small commercial exemption. The communities are: 1. Auburn 2. Avon 3. Bellingham 4. Berlin 5. Braintree 6. Chelmsford 7. Dartmouth 8. Erving 9. New Ashford 10. North Attleborough 11. Seekonk 12. Swampscott 13. Westford 14. Wrentham Looking at FY27 proposed commercial property data, 23 properties in Franklin would qualify for the small commercial exemption at this time (as shown in the following table). Address Composite Land Use FY26 Total Value FY26 Com. Value 105 BEAVER ST 013 - RES/COM $655,900 $63,730 76 CHESTNUT ST 340 - OFFICE $656,000 $656,000 33 COTTAGE ST 355 - FUNERAL $738,100 $738,100 41 DEAN AVE 340 - OFFICE $486,600 $486,600 43 EAST CENTRAL ST 333 - GAS STATION $989,900 $989,900 71 EAST CENTRAL ST 334 - SERVICE STA $876,000 $876,000 137 EAST CENTRAL ST 031 - COM/RES $465,700 $374,640 143 EAST CENTRAL ST 031 - COM/RES $416,700 $251,840 421 EAST CENTRAL ST 342 - MEDCL OFFICE $930,700 $930,700 5 EAST ST 340 - OFFICE $506,700 $506,700 11 EAST ST 031 - COM/RES $629,600 $536,175 76 EMMONS ST 342 - MEDCL OFFICE $494,600 $494,600 18 JAMES ST 013 - RES/COM $682,100 $32,235 5 JULIE DAWN DR 013 - RES/COM $775,500 $160,850 885 LINCOLN ST 031 - COM/RES $948,500 $480,900 68 MAIN ST 325 - SM RTL STORE $593,200 $593,200 49 MAIN ST 342 - MEDCL OFFICE $624,600 $624,600 804 POND ST 325 - SM RTL STORE $805,400 $805,400 1243 POND ST 031 - COM/RES $862,200 $435,850 264 UNION ST 031 - COM/RES $605,900 $305,150 338 UNION ST 326 - RESTAURT/BAR $637,500 $637,500 838 UPPER UNION ST 352 - COM DAY CARE $602,800 $602,800 4 WEST ST 340 - OFFICE $811,900 $811,900 2 Assuming the maximum 10% exemption, and using the FY26 single tax rate of $11.42, the total relief to the 23 property owners would be about $14,156. The benefit ranged from an estimated $37 (on a $368 tax bill) to $1,130 (on a $11,294 tax bill), with an average benefit of about $615. Under a split tax rate, the taxes and benefits would be higher. Please keep in mind that this exemption benefits the commercial property owner, who may not be the same as the business owner since many businesses rent their space. Please also note that the relief granted to those qualifying for the small commercial exemption will be borne by all the taxable properties in both the commercial and industrial classes, but not by those in the personal property class. For those applying after the tax and value files are finalized, the relief would be borne by all taxable property owners through the overlay account; this would be the case for FY27 if adopted. In our conversations with assessing staff in nine other communities, our office heard mixed results on the small commercial exemption. Braintree and Needham recommended offering it (both communities are at the maximum CIP shift). However, Easton, North Attleborough, and Westwood warned that it's too much work for too few eligible businesses, and that the tax break goes to the commercial property owner who may not be the business owner, as stated above. Personal Property Exemption The MA Department of Revenue explains that “Personal property generally includes tangible items that are not firmly attached to land or buildings and are not specially designed for or of such a size and bulk to be considered part of the real estate. This includes, for example, merchandise, furniture, machinery, tools, animals and equipment. Personal property is taxable unless a specific exemption provision applies.” Under M.G.L c. 59, § 5 (Clause 54), municipalities may exempt personal property from tax if the value of the personal property account does not exceed a minimum threshold established by the municipality. The established threshold cannot exceed $10,000 in value. According to the Town Code, Franklin accepted this statute in 2010 to allow a personal property exemption up to $1,000, which primarily benefits small, home-based businesses. Currently, 156 businesses in Franklin receive this exemption. This results in a total tax savings of $832 (under the current single rate of $11.42 per $1,000) for those 156 businesses. The cost of this exemption is borne by all taxpayers. The Assessing team points out that all personal property accounts, including those exempted, must be updated as to data and value annually even though they may be exempted. There continues to be ongoing consultant costs as well as assessing staff time. 3 Some of the nine towns we spoke with noted that a personal property exemption may help small businesses more than the small commercial exemption. Westwood offers a $2,500 personal property exemption, Needham $5,000, and Easton $6,000. The following table shows how many of Franklin’s 904 total FY26 personal property accounts would qualify for an exemption if the Town raised the amount above the current $1,000. Personal Property Exemption Number of Additional Qualifying Businesses Total FY27 Personal Property Value Total Personal Property Tax Break (at current rate) <$1,000 (current limit) 156 $72,880 $832 $1,000 to <$2,500 121 $211,710 $2,418 $1,000 to <$5,000 240 $655,790 $7,489 $1,000 to <$7,500 301 $1,030,690 $11,770 $1,000 to <$10,000 (max) 346 $1,419,780 $16,214 Should the Council decide to adopt a higher personal property exemption at this time, the change would go into effect for FY28. FY27 values for all property classes have already been submitted to the MA Department of Revenue and recommended for preliminary certification. The Personal Property exemption reduces the tax base and eliminates the opportunity for New Growth in the selected value range. 4 November 13, 2026 To: Town Council From: Jamie Hellen, Town Administrator Michelle Monsegur, Deputy Town Administrator RE: Senior Means-Tested Tax Exemption The Council asked for more information on establishing a senior means-tested tax exemption following the October 14th and 28th tax rate workshops. Current Tax Relief Options As background, the Town currently offers several exemptions under M.G.L. c. 59, § 5 for: ● Seniors under Clause 41C/41D (age 65+ with income and asset limits) and Clause 17D/17E (age 70+ or surviving spouses) ● Legally blind residents (Clause 37) ● Veterans and surviving spouses (Clauses 22 through 22F) ● Financial hardship (Clause 18) for taxpayers facing extreme personal or financial circumstances. The Town also offers a Senior Tax Workoff Program and a Veterans’ Tax Workoff Program through the Senior Center and Veterans’ Services Department, respectively. Participants in these programs can “work off” up to $1,500 of their property tax bills by completing up to 100 hours of work supporting Town departments. These programs are very popular and are beneficial to both the taxpayer and the Town. In addition, under Clause 41A, seniors may qualify for the tax deferral program. This program allows seniors to delay payment of property taxes until the property is sold or the individual passes away. As the State’s guide explains, deferring property taxes allows seniors to use resources that would go to pay taxes to defray living expenses instead. Members Present: John Ward, Jenn Waldron, Charles Garbiel Members Absent: None Others Present: Ray Purington, Town Administrator; Janet Masucci, Kate Savage. Review of Minutes: No minutes were available for review. RMB Roof Committee: Garbiel reported the Committee is getting quotes for asbestos testing of the roof shingles and other possible asbestos-containing materials that would be part of a roof replacement project. Once the asbestos samples are collected, the Committee has tarps it will install over the worst sections of the roof to help prevent leaks over the winter. The Committee has been discussing possible architects for the roof project. The Committee’s next meeting is November 4th at 5:30 PM at the Town Hall. RMB Use Committee: Waldron reported the Committee met last week and discussed various ideas for outside uses of the property, including a solar tracker system that might be available. Purington will attend the Committee’s next meeting on November 19th to answer various questions about the property, allowed uses, building, and contents. CDBG Housing Rehab Project: The Selectboard reviewed the 9/30/2026 quarterly report from the Franklin County Regional Housing & Redevelopment Authority outlining activities for the Gill-New Salem Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) for housing rehab projects. The goal of the grant is to complete 9 units of housing rehabilitation. Currently 7 applications have been reviewed and eligibility has been confirmed. One unit is under contract for rehab work, four are in the inspection and bidding phase, and two more are in process. Purington encouraged Gill residents who are interested in the program to contact the Housing Authority soon, before all the funds have been allocated. Gill Fix-It Day: Janet Masucci, who is a member of Gill’s Energy Commission, reported she will be meeting with Jan Ameen from the Franklin County Solid Waste District to discuss ways to hold a “fix-it” event for Gill’s residents. Gill Rec Soccer: Garbiel thanked the Gill Recreation Committee for the “phenomenal job” done for this year’s youth soccer program. There was heavy participation from all grades at Gill Elementary School, and the program fielded four teams this year, up from three last year. Warrants: The Selectboard reviewed and signed the FY 2027 warrant # 10 with totals of $93,151.10 for vendors and $36,213.54 for payroll. Waldron’s son Mitchell, a Gill firefighter and part-time police officer, appeared on this week’s payroll warrant. Due to the conflict of interest, Waldron abstained from signing the payroll warrant. The meeting adjourned at 6:05 PM. Minutes respectfully submitted by Ray Purington, Town Administrator Signed copy on file. Approved on 11/16/2026 ___ Jenn Waldron, Selectboard Clerk

Saltsman – Regional Assessor Carol Dearborn- Assistant Assessor Introduction Prior to the mailing of 3rd quarter tax billings, the Select Board holds a public hearing to determine the percentage of the Town’s property tax levy to be borne by each major property class. The responsibility and procedures are described in Chapter 40, Section 56 of the Massachusetts General Laws. The steps in completing the Classification Hearing are outlined below. Also provided is information about the levy, property assessments, and recommendations made by the Town Assessor. Steps in Setting Tax Rates Pre-classification Hearing Steps Step 1: Determination of the property tax levy (Budget Process) Step 2: Determine assessed valuations (Assessor) Step 3: Tabulate assessed valuations by class (Assessor) Classification Hearing Steps Step 4: Classification hearing presentation (Assessor & Select Board) Step 5: Determine tax shift options (Select Board) Step 6: Voting a tax shift factor (Select Board) Post Classification Hearing Steps Step 7: Sign the LA-5 Classification Form (Town Clerk, Assessor) Step 8: Send annual recap to DOR for tax rate approval (Assessor) Step 9: Obtain DOR approval of tax rates (DOR) Terminology The following are definitions of the terms frequently used in the discussion of tax rates. Levy: The Tax Levy (or Levy) is the amount of property taxes to be raised. The Levy amount is determined by the budget. The total amount of the approved budget less revenues from other sources like motor vehicle excise, municipal fees, and state aid is the amount to be raised from taxation. In Harvard, the Levy to be raised is estimated to be $31,265,650. This represents a 3.75% increase over last year's Levy of $30,136,861 Levy Ceiling: The Levy Ceiling is 2 ½ percent of the full value of the Town. Based on the Harvard aggregate valuation of $1,995,773,727, the town could not levy taxes in excess of $49,894,343 New Growth Revenue: Property taxes derived from newly taxable properties like new construction additions, renovations, subdivisions, and new personal property. The Assessors have tabulated new growth revenues of $170,546 Levy Limit: The Levy Limit is calculated by increasing the previous year’s Levy Limit by 2.5%, and adding the New Growth Revenue for the present fiscal year. Exceeding the levy limit requires an override of Proposition 2½. For Fiscal Year 2027, there was one new override voted, in the amount of $135,370 Maximum Allowable Levy: This is calculated by adding any excluded debt payments to the Levy Limit calculated above. The maximum allowable levy for Fiscal Year 2027 is $31,433,471 Excess Levy Capacity: Excess levy capacity is the difference between the actual Levy and the Maximum. Summary of Assessments (LA4) The interim year value adjustment requires the verification, analysis, and use of arms-length sales from calendar year 2025 for the single family and condominium classes. Sales from calendar years 2024 and 2025 were used to value all other property classes, including the apartment, vacant land, commercial, and industrial classes. Parties and Background This Agreement is between the Town of Harvard, a municipal corporation duly organized under the laws of Massachusetts, acting by and through its Select Board and having a usual place of business at 13 Ayer Road, Harvard, Massachusetts 01451 (the "Town"), and Advocates, Inc., a Massachusetts nonprofit corporation having its usual place of business at 251 Locke Drive, Marlborough, Massachusetts 01752 ("Advocates"). It is entered into as of [EFFECTIVE DATE] (the "Effective Date"). Whereas the Town of Stow has been awarded a contract from the Massachusetts Department of Mental Health ("DMH") for the Stow/Harvard Regional Jail Diversion Program ("JDP"), and Advocates provides the JDP co-response clinician under its agreement with the Town of Stow effective July 1, 2026 (the "Regional JDP Agreement"); Whereas a portion of the JDP clinician's hours under the Regional JDP Agreement is assigned to the Town of Harvard for co-response with the Harvard Police Department; Whereas the Town wishes to use part of those existing hours to support Harvard Fire-EMS through the Harvard Community EMS ("C-EMS") Program; Now, therefore, the parties agree as follows: 1. Work Statement and Description of Services The Town engages Advocates to extend JDP co-response services to Harvard Fire-EMS as part of the CEMS Program, using only clinician hours already assigned to the Town under the Regional JDP Agreement. The primary goal is to connect residents with behavioral health needs to appropriate community-based care and to reduce avoidable emergency responses. Under the direction of the Harvard Fire Chief or their designee for C-EMS scheduling, the Advocates CoResponse Clinician (the "Clinician") will serve as the behavioral health partner to Harvard Fire-EMS. Services may include: 1. Behavioral health, substance use, depression, and suicide or safety risk assessment, with safety planning when needed. 2. Brief clinical intervention, crisis intervention, and de-escalation. 3. Grief and bereavement support, including support following a sudden death when requested. 4. Support for older adults, caregivers, and residents facing isolation, illness, or major life changes. 5. Resource navigation, warm handoffs, and care coordination with providers and community agencies. 6. Focused behavioral health visits and follow-up after a C-EMS visit or emergency response. 7. Consultation with Harvard Fire-EMS personnel on behavioral health concerns and next steps. The Clinician remains an Advocates employee working under Advocates JDP policies and their own professional scope of practice. The Clinician does not act as EMS personnel. Medical assessment, treatment, and transport remain the responsibility of Harvard Fire-EMS. Each party keeps its own records, and the Clinician's clinical record is not part of the C-EMS patient care record. Information is shared only as permitted by law and Advocates policy. The Clinician will not use a personal vehicle for C-EMS activities. Harvard Fire-EMS will provide transportation in a department vehicle for scheduled visits. Any personnel or performance matters involving the Clinician will be brought to the attention of the JDP Program Supervisor or JDP Director immediately. 2. Clinician Hours and Priorities C-EMS services will be provided only within the Clinician hours already assigned to the Town under the Regional JDP Agreement. This Agreement does not add hours or change the Clinician's schedule. The Clinician is shared with the Town of Stow, and nothing in this Agreement reduces or changes services owed to Stow under the Regional JDP Agreement. C-EMS visits are scheduled, preventive work. Harvard Police co-response calls and mutual-aid requests from Stow take priority. When the Clinician must leave a C-EMS visit for one of these calls, Harvard FireEMS and the Harvard Police Department will coordinate the Clinician's transportation, and the visit may be finished by C-EMS staff or rescheduled. The Clinician will not be expected to leave a visit when doing so would create an immediate safety concern. 3. Term and Termination This Agreement begins on the Effective Date and continues through June 30, 2027, unless extended in writing by both parties. It may be renewed by written agreement of both parties. In no event will this Agreement extend past the term of the Regional JDP Agreement, and if the Regional JDP Agreement ends, this Agreement ends on the same date. Either party may end this Agreement for any reason by giving the other party thirty (30) days' written notice. Either party may end it sooner on written notice if continuing would create a safety risk or would violate law, licensing rules, or payer requirements. Either party may also end this Agreement immediately on written notice if the other party commits a material breach that remains uncured for fifteen (15) days after written notice of the breach. Ending this Agreement only ends C-EMS services to Harvard Fire-EMS. Police co-response services under the Regional JDP Agreement continue unless ended under that agreement's own terms. Upon termination, Advocates will make reasonable efforts to close out open cases and connect individuals being served with other providers. 4. Time and Place of Performance All services under this Agreement will be delivered within the Town of Harvard. 5. Compensation and Third-Party Billing Because services under this Agreement use existing Clinician hours funded under the Regional JDP Agreement, there is no cost to the Town under this Agreement, and the Town will not be invoiced for CEMS services. The Town agrees that Advocates may bill third-party insurers, including MassHealth, Medicare, and commercial plans, for billable services the Clinician provides under this Agreement, such as behavioral health assessments and crisis intervention, when clinically appropriate and allowed by the payer. Advocates will handle all billing in line with applicable law and payer rules. Advocates will not bill the Town or any individual served for any amount an insurer does not cover. Any insurance payments Advocates receives will not reduce or offset amounts owed under the Regional JDP Agreement. 6. Data and Written Reports The Clinician will use the JDP data collection tool to record C-EMS activity for operational analysis and outcome studies. Advocates agrees to all reporting conditions contained within the DMH grant award that funds the Regional JDP Agreement. 7. Confidentiality Client confidentiality shall be strictly maintained in compliance with applicable law, and client records will only be released when accompanied by a valid release form or as otherwise permitted by law. 8. HIPAA Compliance To the extent Advocates and the Town create, receive, maintain, or transmit Protected Health Information ("PHI"), as defined under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, as amended by the HITECH Act ("HIPAA"), in connection with the C-EMS Program, both the Town and Advocates shall use appropriate administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of such PHI, and shall limit any use or disclosure of PHI to the minimum necessary to carry out the C-EMS Program. 42 CFR Part 2: To the extent any records generated or accessed under this Agreement relate to the diagnosis, treatment, or referral for treatment of a substance use disorder, such records are subject to the federal confidentiality requirements of 42 CFR Part 2, and neither party shall disclose or permit disclosure of such records except as expressly permitted by 42 CFR Part 2 and applicable law. Any disclosure made pursuant to a client's written consent shall be accompanied by the notice prohibiting further redisclosure required by 42 CFR Part 2. 9. Breach Notification The Town shall notify Advocates promptly upon discovery of any improper or unauthorized use, disclosure, or access of PHI or client records relating to the C-EMS Program. 10. ADJOURNMENT *Public Comment: please see attached Public Comment Policy which can also be found at https://www.nantucket-ma.gov/DocumentCenter/View/51055/Public-Comment-Policy---Adopted-bythe-Select-Board-on-February-12-2025-PDF. **New Business: Topics not reasonably anticipated by the Chair 48 hours in advance of the meeting may be brought up for discussion in accordance with the Open Meeting Law. 3 Town of Nantucket Public Comment Policy Adopted by Select Board February 12, 2025 A. Purpose: This Policy is adopted to facilitate orderly and efficient public comment periods at meetings of Town public bodies. It will protect the ability of the residents of Nantucket, and other persons, to provide feedback or information to pertinent public bodies regarding matters of public interest, Town initiatives, operations, services, and programs. To allow speakers a fair opportunity to address a public body, and to ensure the public body may accomplish its stated business in an efficient manner, these guidelines seek to ensure compliance with the Open Meeting Law and meet other legal and constitutional obligations. Meetings of public bodies in the Town of Nantucket should be places to engage in orderly and peaceable discourse. B. Authority: Principles of free speech and freedom to petition the government, fundamental rights protected by the United States and Massachusetts Constitutions, prohibit public bodies from preventing all speech that may be upsetting or offensive. As such, this Policy establishes reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions sufficient to facilitate orderly and peaceable public comment periods at meetings of elected and appointed public bodies of the Town. C. Legal Standards: Meetings of public bodies are subject to the requirements of the Open Meeting Law, G.L. c. 30A, §§ 18-25. The Open Meeting Law empowers the chair of a public body to preside at and regulate the proceedings of meetings. Pursuant to G.L c. 30A, § 20(g), no person shall address a meeting of a public body without permission of the chair, and all persons shall, at the request of the chair, be silent. Any person wishing to speak at an open meeting must first be recognized by the chair. All questions raised and all comments made by a duly-recognized speaker must be directed to the chair of the public body alone, not to individual members of the public body, staff, or the public. The chair is authorized to maintain order, and, although a rare occurrence, has authority, after appropriate warnings are ignored, to take action up to and including removal of a person who is disrupting a meeting. D. Application: To secure the rights of the public to participate in public comment periods in the Town of Nantucket in a manner consistent with law, and, to thereby protect the Town and members of elected and appointed bodies from civil rights claims, this policy shall apply to all public bodies in the Town of Nantucket. E. Procedures: 1. All agendas of multiple-member bodies in the Town of Nantucket shall include a period for Public Comment, subject to the limitations set forth in paragraph 3. Where to place Public Comment on the agenda is at the discretion of the chair. If public comment is invited during a separate agenda item, this Policy shall govern. 2. While statements made during a Public Comment period are not required to address an agenda item for that particular meeting, such comments must relate to a matter within the public body’s jurisdiction. Public comments on matters outside the public body’s jurisdiction may be ruled out of order by the chair. To avoid due process issues, a person seeking to provide comments on a matter appearing on the same agenda will be asked to defer until the specific agenda item is reached. 3. Each speaker will be allowed to speak once for up to 3 minutes. The chair will curtail verbal comments exceeding the allotted time. 4. A recognized speaker may not cede or assign their time to another unless such an assignment is required as reasonable accommodation for such person because of a disability. All speakers who may need an accommodation are strongly encouraged to contact Town staff or the chair of the public body at least 48 hours prior to the meeting. That said, to facilitate an efficient public comment period, groups that have multiple speakers with the same viewpoint may consider consolidating their comments or designating one person to speak on their individual behalf’s. F. Disruptive Conduct/Unprotected Speech: Disruptive conduct and engaging in other unprotected speech, including but not limited to the following, may be grounds for the chair of a public body to curtail speech and take other action as appropriate: 1. Speaking without being recognized; 2. Continuing to speak after the chair has curtailed additional verbal comment; 3. Interrupting a recognized speaker; 4. Speaking about matters not within the jurisdiction of the public body; 5. Engaging in conversations while another person is speaking; 6. Making true threats of violence directed toward a particular individual; and 7. Making comments inciting imminent lawlessness. G. Public Body Response: 1. A public comment period is a listening session, and the public body is there to listen. The public body, in fact, should not respond to matters raised at the meeting unless they are on the agenda for the same meeting. 2. Matters raised during public comment periods are not required to, and are unlikely to, be addressed or resolved by the public body at the same meeting. Such matters may be appropriately deferred to a noticed-agenda item at a future meeting due to Open Meeting Law considerations. 3. At the sole discretion of the chair of the public body, matters raised during public comment may or may not appear on a future agenda or be referred to the Town Administrator for appropriate action, if any. 4. A public body cannot demand that persons attending meetings or participating in public comment be civil to one another. Nevertheless, the Town, or the members of the public, and those that appear before them are encouraged to make any/or all residents of the Town feel welcome, including listening to them speak, and acknowledging that speakers may have a different viewpoints. Disclaimer: A Public Comment period is not a time for debate or response to comments by the public body. Comments made during the Public Comment period do not reflect the views or the positions of the public body. Because of constitutional free speech principles, the public body does not have the authority to prevent all speech that may be upsetting and/or offensive during the public portion of the meeting. H. Enforcement: Concerns about Public Comment Periods may be brought to the attention of the Town Manager, who will discuss the concerns with the chair of the public body, and take appropriate action. Failure to comply with this Policy may be deemed a violation of the Town’s Code of Conduct, and grounds for the removal of an appointed official. text: AGENDA November 19, 2026 Pursuant to Chapter 131, Section 40 MGL, The Tolland Conservation Commission will hold public hearings November 19, 2026 at 5:00 PM. Via Zoom. Zoom link available by emailing – conservation@tolland-ma.gov– before November 19. For the following purposes: Open Hearings 1. NOI 306-0103 submitted by Frederick Stone, 263 Lakeside Drive to build an accessory shed near Cranberry Pond. Continued from October 29, 2026. 2. RDA submitted by Olivia Lawry, 211 Moreau Road to remove dead trees. 3. NOI 306-0104 submitted by Vicki Bartels, 443 North Trail to replace an existing dock on Noyes Pond. 4. NOI 306-0105 submitted by Joshua Freedmann to replace an existing dock on Cranberry Pond. Close Hearings: New Business:  Approve minutes of October 29, 2026.  Set next meeting date – December 17, 2026 at 5:00 PM via Zoom Old Business: Any other business not reasonably anticipated 48 hours prior to meeting. Adjourn Comments are limited to Tolland residents and property owners only. Please note the Conservation Commission is here to listen. The public comment period is not designed to be a discussion. Accordingly, please do not expect the Commission to respond to your concerns or questions tonight. Your voice is important and we strive to address your concerns appropriately. We may respond at a future meeting or have someone reach out to you. Speakers are to conduct themselves in a civil manner. Inflammatory statements will not be tolerated. Each speaker will be limited to 2 minutes and you will be informed when your time is up so that everyone who wants to speak has the same opportunity to do so. Les Cohn- Chair

text: WINTER PARKING BAN Parking Permits Now Available DECEMBER 1, 2026 TO MARCH 31, 2027 (Applies to All Town Streets) The following rules and regulations apply from December 1st through March 31st and for all plowable snowstorms. On-street parking is not permitted during this time period between the hours of 12:00midnight and 7:00am. Vehicles may instead purchase a pass at Town Hall to park in municipal lots located on Parker Street and Pleasant Street. 1. Residents wishing to park overnight during the winter months in either municipal lot shall register their vehicle at the Parking Clerk’s Office (located in Town Manager Suite, Monday-Friday, 8am-4pm). Each vehicle will receive a municipal parking sticker, valid 12/01/26-11/30/27. This must be displayed on the rear window, driver’s side, lower corner. 2. Vehicles parked overnight in Municipal Lots without a sticker will be ticketed and may be towed. 3. Vehicles must be moved out of Municipal Lots during snow events from 7:00am AND 10:00am. Vehicles in the lots during those hours will be towed. 4. The Town reserves the right to modify these rules due to public safety needs. After conversing with the DPW Director, Building Commissioner, and Planning Board, not much has changed in terms of current conditions for these private roads from the 2025-2026 schedule. The Planning Board wishes to provide the following recommendations: BELAIR DRIVE (Belair Estates): • It appears that no repairs have been made to this road for some time. • We recommend that Belair Drive continue to NOT be plowed or sanded COLDBROOK DRIVE (Pennybrook Estates): • The road is in good condition. • We recommend that Coldbrook Drive be plowed and sanded by the Town this winter. Photo 1 LEE ROAD • The DPW has plowed this private road in the past. • There are two easements placed on Lee Road for the purposes of plowing, drainage and general road maintenance. • We recommend that Lee Road be plowed and sanded this winter. WILDFLOWER DRIVE & BRIAR CIRCLE (Isabella Ridge): • Roads are showing early signs of deteriorating. • We recommend that Wildflower Drive & Briar Circle be plowed and sanded by the Town this winter. 1|Page WILLISTON DRIVE • Only the eastern section of Williston Drive has been accepted by the Town (see photo) • The DPW has historically plowed and sanded the entire length of this road so that the trucks could turn around easily • Roads are showing early signs of deterioration. A couple patches will be made prior to the winter season. • We recommend that the entirety of Williston Drive be plowed and sanded this winter. SUMMARY The Planning Board recommends directing the DPW to manage sanding and snow and ice removal on the private section of Williston Drive and on the private roads, Coldbrook Drive, Lee Road, Wildflower Drive, Briar Circle, Williston Drive, during the winter of 2026/2027. 2|Page Town of Ware Rural Community Priorities Survey Dear Residents of Ware, The Town of Ware stands as a proud symbol of resilience, hard work, and community spirit. For generations, families, farmers, workers, small business owners, and neighbors have built this town with determination, integrity, and an unwavering commitment to one another. Ware’s strength has always come from its people. As we look ahead, we face both challenges and opportunities shared by many rural Massachusetts communities: maintaining roads and infrastructure, supporting public safety and emergency services, expanding economic opportunity, improving communication and transparency, addressing housing needs, and ensuring that young families, seniors, veterans, and longtime residents can continue to thrive here in Ware. But Ware has never backed down from challenge. Our history proves that when this community comes together, we move forward stronger than before — “The Town That Can’t Be Licked.” To help guide the future of our town, the Selectboard is asking every resident to participate in this Community Priorities Survey. Your voice will help shape: ● the town’s highest priorities, ● areas where services can improve, ● infrastructure and economic development needs, ● and opportunities to strengthen our community while preserving the character, values, and identity that make Ware unique. Whether you were born and raised here, recently made Ware your home, own a local business, are raising a family, or have spent a lifetime serving this community — your perspective matters, and your voice deserves to be heard. The survey will take approximately 5–10 minutes to complete. Every response will be reviewed carefully, and the results will be shared publicly to help guide future planning, budgeting, and decision-making for the Town of Ware. This is our town. This is our future. Together, we can continue building a Ware that remains strong, proud, welcoming, and prepared for generations to come. We encourage every household to participate. TOWN OF WELLFLEET DATE _ _ _ __ IN TOWN COUNCIL A RESOLUTION SUPPORTING THE CREATION AND SUSTAINING OF THE WELLFLEET CULTURAL DISTRICT WHEREAS, the Town Selectboard and the Town of Wellfleet wish to pursue the establishment of a state-designated Cultural District through the enabling legislation MGL Chapter 10, Section 58A, and; WHEREAS, Wellfleet has a geographical area of a city or town with a concentration of cultural facilities located within it defined through formal mapping exercise, and; WHEREAS, Wellfleet recognizes the value a Cultural District designation brings to its local economy, provides contributions, financial or otherwise, for project and program delivery and sustained staff leadership to support its efforts, and considers the District in policy, zoning and municipal planning strategies, and; WHEREAS, Wellfleet has created a diverse partnership of stakeholders, formalized through a Cultural District Partnership Agreement, to provide leadership and oversight of the Cultural District in order to maintain its good standing annually to retain state designation and to align the work of community stakeholders in support of state and local District goals, and; WHEREAS, Wellfleet commits to measuring state-wide program goal metrics as well as locally relevant measures for success and report these yearly to the Massachusetts Cultural Council, and; WHEREAS, Wellfleet has engaged the larger cultural and creative communities during the planning processes, through at least one publicly accessible community input meeting, collectively contributing to a plan demonstrating how the community at-large will benefit from, and be included in, the work of the Cultural District. WHEREAS, Wellfleet ensures its Cultural District will strive to be accessible to and by all, committing to actionable items that will increase the inclusive design of its cultural and creative spaces to ensure equitable access to all who choose to participate, and; WHEREAS, the Massachusetts Cultural Council will be petitioned in accordance with its guidelines and criteria to designate said Cultural District; NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, by the Selectboard and the town of Wellfleet that the application to create a state-designated Cultural District be submitted designating the WELLFLEET CULTURAL DISTRICT, and in doing so, the town agrees to: attract artists and cultural enterprises to a community, encourage business and job development, establish tourist \ destinations, preserve and reuse historic buildings, enhance property values and foster local cultural development; further, the city/town will appoint a municipal official to represent the city/town within the District partnership of said Cultural District, will encourage all who own businesses and properties within the Cultural District to involve themselves in the development and success of the District, and will direct city/town agencies to identify programs and services that could enhance or support the development of the District and ensure that those programs and services are accessible to the Cultural District.
